RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. NOBRY CON DO'T LIKE A WIFE. Sum chaps think ther sharp un discernin', Un wee! up P knowledge—tip-top; They'll deny womankind's onny larnin',— That's wheer they ged in a hot shop. Forrud foes, heaw they booast, crow, un swagger, O'er th"' lord o' creation "—proud anon! Yet, for o thad, ther's nod an odd bragger, As cute as a woman, nod one! Iv they will, they con keep freawns th' distance, Iv they choose, they con kindle up strife; To bring sualeet or cleawd to existence Ther's nobry con do't like a wife. Iv yo've bod perseverance, wi' study An inseet to mooast things yo'll ged, Bud ther's one subject far woss un muddy, Than owt else beside as yo've bed. Thad is to find th' depth ov o th' skeeomins Unfawseness P sum wimmin's brains; It's a subject for gret thowts un dreomin's, Bud yo'll ne'er ged reward for ye'r pains. Thad notion's a quare mess to handle, For id changes like th' 'mates ov a fife ; Ut thad job a mon kornd howd a candle,— Ther's tufty con do't like a wife. Wod blessin's a woman con carry When hoo's gradely, to every place; Wod a terribul look o' "Owd Harry," 800 beg, when Hate glows on her face. Wod soft gentle speech hoo con utter When boo's wheedlin' for summat ut's new. • Wod whirlwinds o' gab hoo con splutter, When her tongue's driven hard wi' a foo. / Her Voice seswnds like music's sweet measure, I' peace, bud it's discord P strife: Hey! to fill Life's cup full o' rare pleasure, Ther's nobry con dot like a wife. I' distant climes dornd seech for comfort, For bliss, o'er the wide ocean ne'er steer; Bud look bi yor fireside ut hooam fort, Iv yo' her a reight partner it's theer ! Tiler's nowt liks a lass, cleyn un gradely, As looks after hooam un id cares; One as anus is modest un staidly, Un neex polies naybur's affairs. Sitch like cherish husbands on childer; Un 'do ther' nook" oth' way thro' life: To Cum smilin' fro' cares as bewilder Ther's nobry con do't like a wife. Woman's th' soother o' mon in his sorrotv, No trubble her heart grip con stur; Ut a pinch, to scrape up, skeeom or borrow, Ther's nooan as con do id like her. Hao'l remind yo' o'er gam done afooartime, 0' th' pay-day, on meet ye' ut th' door, Hoo'l smile, then hey th' cheek to want mooar ! After o, wi' hur fawts un her failin's, Tho' higs hur words cut like a knife. Mon's best mate, thro' his toils, hooapes, un ailing, Is tared deawn good, true, honest wife. JACK o' Arm's.

A Scotch minister began an extempore marri r age service in these words: "My friends, marriage is a blessing to a few, a curse to many, and a great uncer- tainty to all. Do ye venture?" After a pause he re- peated, with great emphasis, "Do ye venture?" No objection being made to the venture, he then said, "Let's proceed." THE Docron AMONG THF! ESIETMOB.—Once a baby was brought to . him, evidently reduced to a very low state from the want of sufficient nourishment; immediately realising the nature of the ailment, a large syringe was procured from the medicine-chest, and "warm tea and milk was." I was informed, "squirted down the baby's throat until it fairy ran over !" The remedy, although an apparently severe one, was, I believe, efficacious, for under this treatment the baby thrived wonderfully, but we will hope that the poor little thing was not filled up to overflowing each time the prescription was adminis- tered. On another occasion; an old woman, who had been long ailing., was brought to the station-house for treatment. The case was a difficult one, for the illness was, to all appearance, old age and exhausted nature. In this dilemma Pain Killer" was prescribed, doses of which were administered both externally and internally. This cam terminated less successfully than that of the baby, for after a course of three weeks of the Above- mentioned treatment the old lady died, Let. us hopta the "Pain Killer" did not Accelerate her end !—Commo. dare A. n atnitirftt, Oft6o ...irrs TO radfilttler.—Not wholly witimut grudging does a worker in the fields of literature see the manner in which labour is lightened for his suc- cessors. Where, a score years ago, a writer had boy pain- -Tul NlsearWh tC:. verify every allusion and test every re- ference, his successor, by tha aid of a not very extensive' library, may find in a few minutes the facts of which he is in search, and perhaps even sume others, no less use- ful, of which previously he was ignorant. Absolutely detestable are in my estimation some of the books for the supply of sham erudition—books wherein, for in- stance, a man may find, under the head of any great man, all that has been said concerning him by those of his contemporaries or successors with whose works the compiler is acquainted. By the aid of such books a man, knowing neither writer, may begin his sentence with "As Coleridge brilliantly remarks of Swift," Sm. It is, however, in the nature of compilers of second-class books to give second-hand information; and one who trusts td works of this kind will sooner or later, in the choice lan- guage we have borrowed from sport, "come a cropper." The quotations are scarcely ever taken from original works, and are not seldom garbled or wrongly given. In scarcely any instance is the source advanced so that a man can refer to it; and not seldom, on mere hearsay report, a phrase to which he has no right is assigned to a celebrity. No man with any self-respect or claim to scholarship will trust to these ready-reckoners of liter- ature.—Gentle»ian's Magazine. STUCK Ix THE NEEDLE'S Ere.—There is a pleasant tale of some worthless, phrasing Frenchman, who was taxed -with ingratitude: "Ii ,faut saroir gamier l'indipendance du ctsur," cried he. I own I feel with him. Gratitude without familiarity, gratitude otherwise than as a name- less element in a friendship, is a thing so near to hatred that Ido not care to split the difference. Until I find a man who is pleased to receive obligations, I shall con- tinue to question the tact of those who are eager to confer them. What an art it is, to gi+e, even to our nearest friends; and what a test of manners, to receive! How, upon either side, we smuggle away the obligation, blush- ing for each other ; how bluff and dull we make the giver; how hasty, how falsely cheerful, the receiver! And yet an act of such difficUlty and distress between near friends, it is supposed we can perform to a total stranger and leave the man transfixed with grateful emotions. The last thing you can do to a man is to burthen him with an obligation, and it is what we propose to begin with! But let us not be de- ceived: unless he is totally- degraded to his trade, anger jars in his inside, and he grates his teeth at our gratuity. We should wipe two words from our vocabu- lary: gratitude and charity. In real life, help is given out of friendship, or it is not valued ; it is received from the hand of friendship, or it is resented. We are all too proud to take a naked gift: we must seem to pay it, if in nothing else, then with the delights of our society. Here, then, is the pitiful fix of the rich man; here is that needle's eye in which he stuck already in the days of Christ, and still sticks to-day, firmer, if possible, than ever: that he has the money and lacks.the love which should make his money acceptable. Here and now, just as of old in Palestine, he has the rich to dinner, it is with the rich that he takes his pleasure: and when his turn comes to be charitable, he looks in vain for a recipient. His friends are not poor, they do not want; the poor are not his friends, they will not take.—Begyars, by Robert Louis Stevenson, in Scribner's Mayadne. THE GLACIAL Onion; OF Laxks.—Some years have elapsed since Ramsay boldly stood forth as champion of the theory which ascribed the formation of lakes to the action of glaciers, an action of twofold nature: first, the erosion of lake basins by direct grinding of the rocks over which the glacier had advanced; and second, the piling up moraine barriers across river valleys, and thus damming up the stream to form the lake. This explan- ation was received with considerable Scepticism, and I plead guilty of being among the unbelieavnersuentinla, t whatthe I have seen in Scandin in avia, Scotland, a Ireland, latter more especially, convinced me that Ramsay is right in general. Roughly speakinp, I estimate that at least 95 per cent, of the lakes of the world are due to such glacial agency. A mere glance at a map of Europe is very suggestive. The most remarkable group of lakes in Europe is that on the east•side of the great Scandin- avian range, all of them at the foot of great glaciated valleys, just where the erosive action of the ancient glaciers.was most effective and also where the valleys were most readily dammed by terminal moraines. The north-west of Ireland, especially Connemara, where lakes are dotted like plums in a pudding (see the ordnance map of the district between Galway Bay, Lough Corrib, and the Killeries) is the most instructive region I have directly examined, and one to which I commend the attention of all mho would study the subject. Ins re- cent publication by the Geographical Society of Vienna, a broad and important generalisation by Dr. Bohm is , discussed. He shows that the elevation it which groups of lakes occur varies inversely with the latitude. The higher the latitude the lower the lakes. With certain modifications due to aspect, Scc., these modifications cor- respond to those which modify the variation of the snow line; or, otherwise stated, the general or average eleva- tion of lakes varies with the general or average elevation of the limits of perpetual snow, the lake level being con- siderably lower than the snow line, corresponding to what we see in the Alps, Sze., where the glaciers descend far below the snow lire. Ile divides the lakes into two classes, those of the valleys and those of the mountains. The first are much larger than the second class, and form a horizontal zone corresponding to lakes limits of an earlier glacial period. The Mountain or rtis, much smaller, are due to more recent glacial extension gt o the ..„detritusthis During us and are of ephemeral character,, owing uri - they receive and their varying drainage. century about a hundred lakes have disappeared in the Tyrol—Gentleman's Mayarine. PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY HUGH BETTE. VIII.—L'ENFA NT TERRIBLE. - Although a son is expected to speak respectfully of his father, it seems to be the privilege of a father to please himself whether he speaks well of his son or not. This is no doubt as it should be; for while a boy never has been a man, a man has been a boy, and. therefore knind all about it. "The child is father to the man." Granted; but he isn't thereby privileged to play drum solos on tte most tender part of the man's anatomy; nor does the aforesaid man pay him that deep respect due to a fathef; he only pays damages for what the child does. Hor ever, we will not go further into the relations between porent and child for fear of getting mixed. t The son I wish to speak about is the sturdy youtig chap of from four to five years of age. A son of thetas tender years, to those who haven't dealt with him, may seem entirely unworthy of notice; but I can assure you upon oath, that in every family where he exists, he counts at least one, and don't you forget it. At sea, when the thermometer falls, and there is every prospect of a storm, all loose articles on the upper decks are securely lashed ready for its arrival. When the average boy has passed his third year, batten down the hatches, close the port holes, lash every loose article, and, to drop metaphor, insure the house. This four-year-old is a nice little chap to talk to and play with when you have a few minutes' leisure, but if you take your eyes off him for one short minute, you spoil his character. His maiden aunt says he is " a dear little fellow,' and "the best child that ever born." Well! he may be. I don't profess to have the sole judgment in such matters, but when I find five pairs of boots set down to him in one quarter's bill, I shall not argue that he isn't dear. So far we agree; but when she buys him a little hammer, and after she has gone away he hunts up an old nail and drives it firmly into one of the piano legs, we agree to differ. She says I make him out to be worse than he really is, but it isn't likely I should blacken his character, when he grows up he might come to be a lawyer, or even an insurance agent. You select clothing for yourself with a view to elegance or warmth, or both. Not so for the four-year-old. The whole of the designer's ingenuity, the manufacturer's skill, and the parent's scrupulosity is put on the opposite scale against the wear of this little tyrant, dnd Weighs Thf,T9 is a fortune ready for the man who invents a ^itith that eAno9t be cut with a stray orying-tfe, Or that won't fray with pollthiilga treken bottle On it. Por what purpose do you supply the four-year-old with clothing? Simply to keep him from flaying himself alive. You never heard of a four-year-old's clothes getting too little for him; such a thing is virtually impossible, only in the sense that a pair of trousers with one leg torn off are too little for two legs. Knowing this four-year-old tolerably well, you select only the strongest-made toys for him; but that doesn't make any difference—he isi// see how they are con- structed. The 'way he detaches the members from a strong wooden doll is to find a hole in the yard wall, in- sert one of the doll's legs, and then swing on the dolL Ditto with the remaining lea and arms. The body he saves until he can borrow the cleaver. I once supplied h four-year-old with a wheel-barrow made, expressly for him, of oak an inch thick. I smiled as I thought it would come in for his children or even grandchildren. It "came in" the same afternoon with the bottom board split in two, and no report could be got out of the four-year-old as to how it had been done. I don't thing he knew the way to any of our large iron foundries, and if he did I shouldn't have thought they Would let him use the steam-hammer. Anyway, if I have to deal with another four-year-old, before buying him any more toys, I shall wait till some enterprising firm turns them out in wrought Steel. A woman decks up her baby in all the finery at her command, and struts off in great pride to show it to Mrs. Blank; but she doesn't do this with her foss-year-old boy. It is a most solemn duty taking him to a friend's house. She certainly dresses him plainly but neatly, be- cause people would "talk if she didn't, but she is all the time aware that it isn't much use. Before starting, she promises him all the horrors of war if he is a bad boy, and all the plenty of peace if he is a good boy in the presence of Mrs. Blank. As it isn't any use trying to read his intentions from his face, and as they wouldn't be worth anything as a guide if she could, she takes fast hold of one of his hands to keep him from trying to get down some grate, and sallies forth. Arrived at Mrs. Blank's his fascinating inquisitiveness comes into full play, and he hasn't been in the house long before he has everything off the hooks that he can reach, and his questions of "What's dis ?" "What is dese for?" "Where did you get 'em ?" &e., are not stopped by his mother telling him that she'll never bring him out again. She knows very well that she daren't leave him out of her sight, and so does he. Mrs. Blank says, "Oh ! never mind him, he's doing nothing wrong." When Mr. Blank comes home, however, she seems to alter her mind, for she describes her youthful visitor as a "little wretch," and wonders why parents don't teach their children manners, &c. While I feel it my duty to inform you that it is very wrong to call a four-year-old a little wretch, I wont swear that I haven't done it myself. It is all nonsense talking about teaching him manners; you might as well try to teach a mule to sin, alto. When you have yelled at him till you feel ashamed to own him, and boxed his ears (a very injurious practice, thoughyou don't 'remem- ber it in time) till his mother calls you a brute, you would think that your humiliation was complete; but it isn't always. This four-year-old seems to be absorbed in drawing liquid kangaroos on his slate while you are talking eves family matters, and doesn't seem to notice anything yost say; but I warn those who are about to have the un- qualified pleasure of training a four-year-old, that thij drawing business is the sheerest hypocrisy. When Uncle James drops in, and takes this innocent child on his kneta, -the four-year-old says, " Unco James, have you some pennies?' "Yes!" says Uncle James, looking somewhat surprised. "Have you a good rot ?" "Yes 1 a few," answers Uncle James. "Are dey all yours?" is the next question, and although you begin to sweat in anticipation of what is coming, you dare not interrupt. "All raine? Yes, of course," answers Uncle James. "What makes you ask that ?" And, while you are holding your breath the enfant terrible replies, 'Mine papa said you hadn't a penny to call your own." If this is the result of a quiet chat with your wife re Uncle James' affairs, it will be well if you stifle any murderous feelings that may he en- gendered, for all your capabilities will be required to explain the joke to Uncle James. The theological questions of the four-year-old are barrowing. He says "Papa,was Noah a butcher?" This reaches your ear perhaps, when you are right in the middle of the news of last night's House of C,ommons, and it takes about thirty seconds for the meaning of the question to dawn upon you. Then you say, "A butcher, child, no !" He then ages, "Well, what did he want all dem elephants, and eowses, and sheepses for?' Then syts sanguinary rui pg.piuruei nrssay," eae present tozoology." n HI Lookaotoguuyhrs. , natural e, wife, just give this boy a lesson in ic hoTfislti cooeryminarogfuments of a statesman e nof oNnonaha. If renNontastoi soluble lein any of his he el animals in the manner that this boy treats all the t TiTeodfousrl-Tzfoal.dbigchuseful in running errands—for himself. He can fetch a pound of sugar from the grocer's across the way, in less than an hour, provided always i n thestrheeatw;evoarrr thoagrt that an- grinderthe inisn'tanothere then ext y .Imustbo confess, was anneunitntonrrtfailure. said, of ,Thoimin, jasustanrunerarann y and fetch fbeotch me a oil." •I gave him a penny, and winked at my wife a very meaning wink. I repeated, "Now you understand' strap oil?" Oh! Yes! he understood. He hadn't been absent more than five minutes when he returned. , I opened the paper he brought, and it contained—the salve for all his wounds, a sweet sell for me—sugar toffy. I passed it finally over to him, feeling very much brdwned. Another case of virtue rewarded. With the fact staring me in the face that I was once four years old myself, I cannot say that there'is no hope for other four-year-olds, when one has developed into a man who pays twenty shillings in the,pound-, i.e. when •he pays anything at all.

PRESENTATION TO MR. AND , MRS. F. MONKS. On Saturday evening Mr. F. Monks, J.P. wee, presented on behalf of the workpeople of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., with an illuminated address, and Mrs Monks was presented with'a fine full- length oil-painting of her husband. The presenta- tion took place at the Drill Hall, Warrington, in the presence ot over 550 of the workmen employed by the firm at their Warrington and Wigan works, and their wives and families. Those from Wigan. numbering about 250, were brought to the town in a special train which left Wigan about four o'clock. Prior. to . the presentation, the workmen and those who accompanied them partook of an ex- cellent knife and fork tea, catered for by Mr. Mas- sey. of the Roebuck Inn, Bridge-street. Amongst the invited friends, present in addition to Mr. and Mrs Monks. were Miss Monks. Mr. and , Mrs F. W. Monks, Mr. and Mrs Thomas Hall, Miss Hall, the Rev. Priestley Prime, Mr. Prime (of Birmingham), Alderman Joseph Davies, J.P:, Mr. William Owen, Mr. and Mrs T. Birchall, Mr. and Mrs W. Pletcher, Mr. and Mrs A. H. Eathbone, Mr. C. Twiss, Miss Twiss, Mr. and Mrs 14 (keening, Mr., and Mrs John Henry Knowles, Mr. and Mrs Joseph Monks, Mr. William Longshaw, Mr and Mrs W. J. Forshaw, Mr. G. Riley, Miss Riley, Mr. E. Walker (Walker Bros., Wigan), Mr. Robert Mawson (Wigan Coal and Iron Company), Mr. John Eatock (Douglas Forge Com- pany), Mr. F. Dobson, Mr. and Mrs.. Hudson, Mr. and Mrs. James Gandy, and Mr. Criteh- ley. The oil-painting is the work of Mr. Jas. Charles, formerly of Warrington, and has the merit of being an unmistakeable-likeness of the original. The address is contained in an album of beautiful design and is a very fine example of the art of illuminating. The artist in this case was Mr. 'James Orr Marples, of Liverpool and London. The following are the words of the address:—" Frederick Monks, Esquire, „LP. Sir,— We, the managers and workmen employed at the War- rington and Wigan works of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., welcome the opportunity of presenting this address to you, and the accompanying portrait of yourself to Mrs Menks. We desire to 'express our respect, high esteem, and thorough appreciation of your uniform kindness, affability, and earnestness, and the business capabilities which have erialAed you to tarry ou,tbe works tliiongh.the Past thirteen years of 'great deprei- sion=years which might be designated as the most dg- estrous and the darkest that have veiled the iron trade of this district—during which you have, nevertheless, developed the works to their presen,t important dimen- sions, and ensured to your employes the regular worE which is so necessary for the comfort and happiness of their homes and families. It IS our earnest hope that you may long be spared to direct the interest of the firm, which, under yeur able and judicious Management,' has been so successful in the past." Then follow the follow- ing signatures of the Presentation Cammittee of the War- rington and Wigan Works :—Warrington : T, Burton, J. Woolley, J. Plant, 11. Ikin; J.Burthem, A. Riddlesworth, T. McCue, T. Birch, S. Dunn, T. Woolley, R. Jones, S. Jones' J. Timminkof. Conroy, T. Penti, W. Miles, T. Worra.ll, W. Pemberton, H. Tranter, W. Gleave, .7. Bed- dard, M. Wilkes, J. Corradine, E. Brown, J. Egerton, W.. Moody,. R. Schofield, T. Davies, . Elwell, M. Waterhouse. Wigan: F. M. Dobson, W. Burton, D. Davies, J.. Jackson, P. Caswell, E. Pincher, J. Radford, F. Taylor, D. Ross, R. Ainscough, J. Smith, H. Billing. ham, W. Thomas, E. Thomas, R. Gwinett," B. Hickson, J Griffiths, F. Crane, R. Hill, W. Hotchkiss. After tea the chair was taken by Mr. T. Hall. The programme besides addresses, included glees by a glee party, a pianoforte solo by Miss Hall, and songs by Mr. Ikin, Mr. j'avlor, and Mr. Radford.' The Crteramax, in his introductory address; mentioned that it walk/ very soon be fourteen years since the cere- mony of cutting the first sod of the Warrin,gton works took place. It was cut with: a determination to make the works a success, though if the struggle for exist- ence they had experienced for about'seven years could have been foreseen, he feared they should have hesi- tated, since it was admitted that trade had passed through such a crisis as no man remembered before for severity and endurance. (Hear, hear.) They had also had ground cut from under their feet from time to time owing to the various Changes which had'taken place in the iron trade within the past few years, and they had been' compelled almost for sheer existence to change and develope their works, and therefore all the more honour was due to the man at the helm. (Applause.) Their effort had always been to run their works regularly week by week, and so find constant employment, and it was no boast for him to say that, in spite of depression in trade, they had fairly succeeded in their efforts. (Ap- plause.) Short addresses were next given by Mr. S. Dun and Mr. P. Caswarx, the fOriner as the representative of the Warrington, and the latter, of the Wigan workmen. . Mr. T. Bunrcm next presented the illuminatedaddress to Mr. Monks. He said he felt it a pleasure to take part in the movement which had brought them together that knight, a movement which they all had at heart, and if he might 'be allowed the expression, thousands of people outside. (Hear, hear.) There were one or two words set forth in the address which he *felt constrained to make a few remarks upon. With regard to the words " kindness " and "affability," he might say that he had been in the employ of Mr. Monks for more than 18 years, and it was a pleasure to look back over those years, in- asmuch as he had always received the greatest consider- ation and much kindness at the hands of Mr. Monks. He had noticed also during those years that a spirit of leniency, of kindness, and affability had always been demonstrated on the part of Mr. Monks towards the people employed under him, an affability which had rendered it easy at all times, whenever, any grievance had cropped up between employers and employed, to settle those grievances in a pleasant and amicable way, andin a way which had been satisfactory to both the parties interested. And he hoped and trusted that as the works had been carried on during the past 13 years, they would be carried on in the future, without having re- course to those foolish strikes and lock-outs which had proved so disastrous to the people concerned. (Hear, hear.) The address also reminded them of the earnest- ness and business capabilities which had enabled Mr. Monks to carry on the works during the past years of revolution in the iron trade. It was long since they had observed those qualities exemplified in Mr. Monks, and it was to them that they largely attributed the success of the company, and as employes they wished to recog- nise Mr. Monks' best efforts, whichhad been so beneficial ' both to the company and its employes. (Applause.) The address was then presented to Mr. Monks. Mr. W. BuirroN, in presenting the painting to Mrs. Monks, remarked that while Mr. Monks's life had been a successful one, it had also been successful as far as the employes were concerned—both at the Warrington and Wigan works—inasmuch as Mr. Monks had succeeded in gaining the high esteem which they met there that night to manifest,. (Applause.) The painting was next formally presented by Mr. Burton. On the lower part of the frame the following words were inscribed :—" Presented, to Mrs. M. Monks by the managers and workmen of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Company, Limited, Warrington and Wigan works. March 3rd, 1888." It was explained that the date "March 3rd" was due to the fact that it had been intended to present it a week earlier, but this intention was frustrated by the illness of the artist. Mr. F. MONKS, on rising to acknowledge the gift, was received with applause. He said that first of all he would answer for his wife, at her request, and say how' much she appreciated the gift, and particularly the spirit which had prompted it. He would not venture to refer to domestic matters further than to say he believed the workmen owed a great deal to her, and those who had good wives would know the fulness and the meaning of the words when he said that he had one of the best wives a man could have. (Applause.) He would accept the address which they had been good enough to present in the same cordial, kindly, generous feeling 'which had prorhpted the gift of the portrait to his wife and family. There were times in a man's life, when, if he lived long enough, he'could look back, and he was reminded that it was about 25 years since he was planning how he was to realize the ideal of his life. He simply referred to the matter then because there were men in that room who knew the truth of what he was saying. 11113 had an ideal which he tried to realize, but which jealousy-, he would not say ignorance, of the workmen with whom he was connected prevented the realization of. He was thank- ful that he had sufficient tact to see that there was no use wasting time, and he and a friend of his who was in that room struck out in a direction which they hoped wou.ld ultimately lead to what they considered the regeneration of the people—namely, the establishment of the Warring- ton Co-operative Society. (Hear, hear.) He was as firm a believer in the vkine of co-operation that day as he was 25 or 27 years ago. Perhaps the time had not come for its full realization, but he was hopeful it would come, though he could not say that he was so hopeful as to bo- i lieve that he should live to see it, but he hoped his son and grandson would live to see the time when the work-. ing people of this country would become their own capitalists and their own employers. (Applause.) Thete was nothing which he had been able to do fur the con- cern with which he was connected before be eitablished the present works, but what the working people of this country could do for themselves if only they had the thrift, prudence and wisdom which was so necessary for the conduct of all btisiness. There were certain condi- tions which were as necessary for the success of business as bread was necessary for the sustenance of life. Alt employment must be remunerative. It must be re- rinmerative to the capitalist and also to workmen, and when these conditions were present to both they had a successful concern. (Applause,) Another essential was this: In a small business, were a man could look after it himself, he might, to a large extent, make it dependent upob, him- self, but in a large business those who had the conduit of departments were just as essential as the head of the concern. (Applause.) In accepting the address that night, and the portrait which they had been pleased to give to his wife, he did so in the spirit in which he sup- posed a general would accept the honours paid him, remembering that those who had servedunderhim, even down to the private soldier, had all contributed to the victory and to the success achieved. And so that night ~he accepted the address in that spirit, not taking the , • ,

He was not fool big enough to believe that every workman was of the right stamp. but he would say that from the firet day almost that he engaged a man they had been, he thought, re- markably well served. Perhaps they would excuse,him if he referred to an old man now dead and gone, but whose memory wasTespected. He was the first man he thought he ever employed, and it was no discredit to say that, although he was only what they would call an Irish day labourer, there existed up to the time of his death 'a mutual. respect and affection, which he should be glad to see more universal than it was. Ha was in his way as devoted, as loyal, and as kind- hearted a man as they would wish to meet, and they had ' had had many a kfit of fun and chat together. He dare say many of them would know to whom he referred— old Patrick Rohan. (Applause.) He was only a type of many men they had_had, and he could narrate many in- stances of men they had had in their employ in their own works, and when he was at Whitecross, who had more frequently than he would like' to say expressed their gratitude for services which they felt had been given them.. He mentioned these matters in the hope that if there were any young men in the assembly who aspire as he hoped there were, to become managers, and ultimately employers, that they would never, lose cour- age, and that they, would never become faint-hearted. (Hear, hear, and applause.) If a man would do his duty to those who were about him, and treat them cour- teously—treat the Irish day labourev,with as much cour. tesy and gentlemanly feeling as he Svould ids banker-7 he would succeed. He might netstieceedinaccumulating as large a fortune as Many, but he would succeed in that higher spirit of management which all were anxious to attain to. (Applause.) The occasion which had brought about that presentation was really; he thought, the removal of himself and family from Lovely-Jane to Walton—not very far away, and. In itself . they might say a very trivial thing. 'But it had givenTise to a de- monstration like that which helped one, mid he hoped that their removal to Walton • would not in any way lessen their interest in those about them.' (Applause). :In conclusion he said that those who had to do with t the management of large businessesknew the strain that cAme upon those who had the charge of them; and he begged of them, on behalf of the managers who were more directly over them', to show their consideration to ' them, and as far as they were able to second t ie efforts in the interests not only pf themielVes bit Of llibelong- inkte thenrand dbolt them. (Applause.) , 'long as lc that-,spirit yppit maintained hi the *Oki; he VentufM tb i say that it woUld-require a very-I:Teat deal of competi- tion tp knock them completely out of time. (Loud AP- plause.) Alderman DAVIES was the next sneaker, an conclu- eluded by prtosing. ,‘ Success .t 6 Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Corimany, a proposal which' was honoured with -hearty cheering. .. div.head: OUR LONDON LEITER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LEITER.

LONDON. - THURSDAY NIGHT. There is something ever marvellous in the ease and rapidity with which tremendous personal changes are accomplished. This time last week the Emperor William was stiil alive, and though his condition was known to be dangerous, there were doubts whether he ;night not survive the Crown Prince. To-day the old Emperor is no more, and all Germany is vibrating with the shout of "Long live ;the Emperor!" There has been something very 'touching in the unfeigned sorrow of the German people at the death of then-old Sovereign. He bad had time to outlive the memories of his earlierpub- lie acts, when, armed to the teeth and followed by his grenadiers, he rode over and through the people when they made any effort to resist the personal ,tyranny of the sovereign. Ido not suppose anyone would contend that the Emperor William was a great max. An infinitely greater is the soldier- statesman to whom, years ago. he committed the welfate of Germany and' his own personal fortunes. But for Bismarck there would never have been a German Empirp, and it is even doubtful whether King William would have been able to keep the iron crown of Prussia, which in imperious, net to say insolent contempt of popular rights, he put on his own head. _ _

The Emperor's position in the early days of his reign in Prussia is graphically illuktrated by an in- cident described by Mr. Forbes in his biography, just hastily published, of the Emperor. When he was setting out to take part in the Seven Weeks' War, he spent his last night in Berlin in selecting and packing up his private papers. As Mr. Forbes says, he hoped to March on Vienna: But in the meantime it was wise to secure a safe re- treat from Berlin. Had he been beaten then, he would no more have ventured back to his capital than Napoleon 111. dared return to Paris after Sedan. But when Bismarck had founded an empire for him, and his great captains and gallant soldiers had won the day against France, the Emperor might. do as he pleased. What he pleased to do in his mel- lower old age was much kinder and wiser than his earlier riding, booted and spurred, through the popular ranks. The people grew fond of the old man, saluting them from his window in the palace Tinter den Linden, and he always add/timed them and came to look upon them as his "Kinder." The people of the present generation really liked him, but still having Bismarck they get along very well without him, and have transferred theiraffection to the much finer individuality ef his son. The House of Commons is plodding along an ex- cellent fashion under the new rules. It meets at half-past three, breaks up at midnight, and, what is more, does something in the interval. The great salvation of the dignity of the House, and thepros- perity of public business is the closure—that ex- I pedient against which, less than six years ago, all the 'Conservative forces were desperately arrayed. and which within the past month they have urged a not unwilling Opposition to adopt. It has of late been discovered that Mr. Smith has no monopoly of "the pounce." Twice this week the privilege has been exercised by private members with excellent effect. On Tuesday night, when a division on Mr. Slagg's motion, touching the frontier policy, in India, was imperilled, Mr. Caine moved t closure, and a divi- sion was taken. On Wednesday the angry and baf- fled residuum of Tories in the House of CommonS tried as a last resort to defeat Mr. Bradlaugh by talking out his Oaths Bill. The member for Northampton, in humble imitation of the illustrious example of the leader of the House, moved the Clo- sure, and the House had an opportunity of declaring its opinion upon the issue. It b:comes daily more and more clear that the closure is an indispensable agent in Parliamentary Procedure. Its effects are much wider than is apparent from the line in the Parliamentary Reports, which states that the clo- sure has been moved. The knowledge that this rod is in pickle deters obstruction, for obstructionists know thatthey are ineffectively wasting their own time by prolonging debate., At the proper, moment the closure will be moved, and the division will be taken. It might, therefore, as well be taken early in the evening as late. Mr. Bradlaugh hal a great triumph on Wednes- day when he carried his Oaths Bill by a majority of 100. That would be a great feat in whatever cir- cumstances it was accomplished. But in the pre- sent condition of parties in the House of Commons the mere statement of the arithmetical fact implies the wholesale conversion of the Conservative party. When, five years ago, Mr. Gladstone, then at the head of an overwhelming majority available for general purposes, attempted to pass a bill having the same object, he was defeated by a small major- ity, What Mr. Gladstone. Prime Minister and Ileader of a great party, could not do in 1883, Mr. Bradlaugh did on Wednesday with a majority of 'lOO. Mr. Bradlaugh, indeed, accomplished more than Mr: Gladstone vainly essayed. The Affirmation Bill of 1883 merely proposed that members returned to the House of Commons might, if they ,pleased,inake

, affirmation insteadtofitaking :the `oathATheAbill passed by the. Hbuse of Commons on Wednesday extends the deliverance ifrom the oath to all the. ordinary relations of puhlic life. It provides that any person on objecting to being sworn shall be permitted to make affirmation in all places, and for , all purposes, where and when an oath is at present I required by the law. It will be strange newS for Sir Henry Wolff, on his way to Teheran, to hear how matters fared in the House of Commons on Wednesday. It was this question of Mr. Bradiaugh being permitfed to take the oath that directly led to the creation of the fohrth party. Now, whilst the Mr. Gorst of those days is Sir john, whilst 3mr. Arthur Balfour is Chief Secretary for Ireland. Lord Randolph Churchill votes with Mr. Bradlaugh prac- tically to abolish the oath, and the bill is carried under a Conservative Government by a majority of 100!

Cemplaint is made among the large body of doc- tors in average practice in London that the leaders of the profession do not charge for ordinary con- sultation more than the regulation fee. If a sick man has plenty of time he may go to the, rooms of Morel! Mackenzie. Robson Roose, or Doctors Gull and Jenner, pay his guinea and have their advice upen his case. It is true that most of these prac- titioners charge two guineas for the first interview, and a guinea for each succe.e_ding visit. But that does not remove the cost far beypnd what is paid,to, an ordinary &moulting doctor whose' 'name is less familiar on the public tongue. The difficulty is that to the ordinary patient a visit to a fashionable doc- tor means the expenditure of a whole morning, and even then it may happen that at half-past one, when the great Than is called away to his luncheon, the turn of the weary patient may not have collie. and he may have to begin again on the next day. But even this infliction, in some cases more costly than the fee itself, does not deter the crowds from assembling at the shrine of. a fashionable doctor. What the rank and file of the profession say,is that these great men should charge a minimum fee of two guineas for au interview,-thus leaving some chance for others to pick up The odd guineas. But if the lights of the professiou consent to shine in their own rooms at the regulation fee of guinea,- they, make it . up pretty well in Kpecill 'cases. Sir Morell,Mackenzie haa received as a pre- liminary fee from the Crown Prince 'a cheque for .E 3,000. Now that he has brought his patient round to be mperorit is pretty certain that the scale of remuneration will be increased. A doctor whose name was not known hi London three years ago, told me at dinner the other night that he had just returned from a visit into one of the home counties at the peremptory call of alentlenian once well known in the House of Commons, but •whose iden- tity is pow disguised in theyeerage. His house was sithitted just ninety miles from London and the doctor's fee for attendance was 60 guineas. The regulation fee for a leading consulting physician it', London, called into the country, is fourteen,' shit- • lingo a mile, and it is the custorn to late thelee at two-thirds of the mileage in guineas. Thus a ninety mile journey_ makes , up. a little doc- tor's bill of 60 guineas. It is just poesible that the interposition of the local doctor would have been equally efficacious, for my lord was not really very ill. Rut it did-him good to post-off his servant in the dead of the night to call up v., ,faShionable Lon- don doctor at five o'clock in the bacrrning and to in- cur a little bill of 60 guineas. , . But for occasional references. in the newspapers, the Silver Wedding might hate passed over without one,in a hundred thousand people knowing that so interesting an event had occurred. I remember when Lord Mayor de Keyser. was 'stepping into office hearing him speak with enthusiasm of what he was going to do in the Silver Wedding year. It Seemed a certain baronetcy. and he was prepared to purchase it at a' lavish price. I suppose he got a hint that such a demonstration was not desired in high quarters. At any rate the proposed civic cele- bration Was eondentied into the presentation of an address. The conduct of the affair is highly credit- able to the good sense and good taste of the Prince of Wales. Even if there was nothing against the Jubilee levy, it 'would have been obviously hard upon the public to have had something similar hi the the following year. There were a considerable num- ber of valuable presents made, but 'happily the Silver Wedding on Saturday passed off without any of that uubluehing systematic banding round of the hat which marred the spontaniety of the Jubilee t ejoicings,

"BRITANNIA RULES THE WAVES ."—Frorn The Ports- mouth Times and Naval Gazette.—When one has visited the Royal Dockyards at Woolwich and Chatham, and in- spected the great ships of war with their powerful artna- ment which the Admiralty are providing for the protee- .___. . . . .

, . tion of Her Majesty's extensive coast lines, he is at once satisfied that ," Britannia still rules the waves." While there are obvious differences of opinion between experts relative to the value of large and small war-ships in action, one has only to come to Portsmouth Harbour and see such formidable ships as the Inflexible, the Iron Duke, the Devastation and others of equal armament, costing upwards of a:million sterling to produce, with myriads of small torpedo craft, to become convinced that in the matter of naval construction, England is not only keepirig abreast with other countries but isexcelling them. Portsmouth Dockyard and Portsmouth Harbour are names familiar throughout the civilised world. It is here that that all the war vessels and magnificent troopships of Her Majesty's service are fitted out, for foreign stations. It is said that these ships are supplied with every conceivable necessity for the comfort of the officers and men; every precaution is taken to provide against sickness and disease caused by the sudden change of climate to which the troops are subjected. It is said that every vessel belonging to Her Majesty) ser- vice leaving Portsmouth is not considered ready or sea without a liberal supply of St. Jacobs Oil. This marvel- lous remedy is not only used extensively on shipboard, but also in the several dockyards above mentioned. Mr. Frederick Payne, who lives at 82, Gladstone Street, .Landport, Portsmouth, and who has been connected with the Portsmouth Dockyard for upwards of fourteen years, hands us the particulars of the most miraculous cure effected by the use of St. Jacobs Oil in the case of his wife, who tor eight years had been a fearful sufferer from rheumatism. Her limbs and shoulders were swollen to three times their natural size; he arms and hands were shapeless; much of the time her right shoulder was swollen to that extent that the top of the shoulder and the side of the face came together, and she suffered the most intense pain. Four years ago the disease settled in her back, making her completely help- less, the heart became so much involved that she Was unable to make the slightest exertion without experienc- ing great difficulty in breathing. The only way she could lie in bed was by having the back of a chair set up behind her, and padded with pillows. Her husband , was obliged to carry her up and downstairs, night and morning, and she suffered Such excruciating agony that she repeatedly fainted away. She became so much re- duced inlesh that Mr. Payne says she was little more than a skelton. She was treated by the best medical skill in Portsmouth and vicinity, employing four • medical gentlemen in all, each of whom told her and her ; husband that they could do nothinr, whatever for her— that her case was chronic and pos.s'lll hope of .recovery.

Her ease was considered by her neighboui's and members Of the church to which she belongs as past help. Last summer the medical man then in attendance upon Mrs. Payne said, that she might possibly be made more com- fortable and her life prolonged if silo were taken away from Portsmouth and the salt air to some inland town, but that she could never recover. Acting on kis advice Mr. Payne had her taken to a small town in Sussex for a few weeks, and here follows a very interesting and most providential circumstance: It seems that the lady to whose house Mrs. Payne was carried had herself been cured of rheumatism in the shoulder by the use of St. Jacobs Oil, and was very urgent in her request for Mrs. Payne to try it. sin less than five minutes after the first application Mrs. Payne began to 'experience Cessation from pain. After the seCond application the pain had almost entirely disappeared, and before the contents of one bottle was exhausted, the pain and swelling had en- tirely gone and, although week and feeble, Mrs. Payne could walk about the house and grounds. From that time on she made a most satisfactory, rapid, and per- manent recovery. Both Mr. Payne and his wife say that she has hot been as well as she is now for fourteen Tears. Mr. and Mrs. Payne are most respected people, both are members of the Wesleyan Chapel in Landport, and Mr. Payne, as above stated has been employed ato Portsmouth Dockyard for fourteen years. They have the names of the medical men who attended her; also the name and address of the lady at whose house she was taken in Sussex. Mrs. Payne will be happy to fur, nigh this lad's address as well as further .particulars of her wonderful cure, to any who may desire to communi- cate with her. The above was such a remarkable case that some of the chemists and dealers in -Landport were called upon with the object in view of obtaining further information respecting this marvellous remedy, among others, Mr. Timothy White, 158 and 160 Commercial Road, Landport, Portsmouth, when interviewed, stated that the demand for this popular remedy was rapidly increasing, that he never buys Ids than sixty dozen at , one order. div.head: CHAPTER IX.
div.p: CHAPTER IX.

AMONG THE ROSES. Dressed in diaphanous blue, her bonnet a wrcailt 1-.4f pale forget-me-nets nestling on cerulean tulle, Irene Stanhope is pirouetting rouffd the Baton-square draw- ing-room, when Lady Fedora enters, looking far niore stately and solemn than she used to look, but still kindly and gentle, especially to Irene. • "My child," she says, as she comes into the room, "you will make yourself very hot and untidy, and not be fit to go to Lady Bertha eumming's party. I ,cannot think what has possessed you of late, your
spirita--se- era ao variable—sOmatimes iremeutiousWome- times at. zero."
"Oh, mother,l don't kitow why,but T feel so happy," and Irene finished a pirouette exactly in front of Lady

Fedois. • • How could any one accuse her for a moment of looking anything but cool and fresh? It was the brightest and sweetest of faces that gazed up into Lady Fedont's, a sunbeam without a cloud on an azure sky' "And What has made you so especially happy to-day

my love?' "I don't loa"Ow, mother'; mere youthful effervea cenoe, I' suppose, and an idea that I shall enjoy thi.;.: garden,paTty at Lady Bertha's—it is a very lovely day, you Icnovi." Lady Fedora shOok her head and smiled, "It is not very diffieult to read between the lines, Irene. You think someone you like will be there." - " Whom do I like ?" asked Irene. "I like so many people, but if you can keep a secret I will shew yon something. mamma."

"A secret?" "Y 631 I mean, you must not say you know, or all the romance will be gone." And from a pocket hidden Somewhere among the azure tulle Irene "produced an envelope. Inside it, wrapped in 'a piece of emblazoned paper, was one single sprig of forget-me-not fastened on to the paper with a silver thread, and no written word save the initials
-Lady Fedora looked at her daughter in some surprise. "This then is the reason ot your blue toilette and __. . _ . . -

the forget-me-nots in your bonnet.. It is foolish; child; very foolish. If I had known you should not hive committed yourself Ans." "Unkind mother," said Irene, pouting. "I would not have told you at all if I had thought you would scold.' "I do not want to scold, Irene, but it is scarcely in keeping with your position in life. to reply in this form to--" • A little reminder that-I was to be sure and go to Lady Bertha Cumming's to-day, in order, to meet Prince Lenskeff, who has been away from town for a day or two. Mother, you haven't got a scrap of poetry about yon. But there's .the carriage." Lady Fedora followed her daughter downstairs, a shade upon her brow. That she wished Irene to make a rich marriage, there was little doubt; that she almost feared, however, the advisability of this one an inward voice seemed to admonish her. In the radiance of Irene's bright spirits the clond cleared before they reached the garden party, which was at Campden Hill, end to which other princes besides those of Russia bad been invited. • It was somewhat late before Lady Fedora and Irene arrived, and the crowd was no insignificant one. As they wended their way through. it towards a, shady spot under a knoll of trees in the centre of the garden,nearly every eye was cast on Irene, whose beauty was such as to render her indisputably one of the bellea: if not the prettiest girl, of the season. She did not, however, need the admiring glances which were cast on her; her eyes were wandering in search ' of 'Lenskoff, who was nowhere to be seen. Already the sunlight was dying out of her eyes ; joy changes to disappointment and back again to joy to easily at seventeen. 'Why was be not there? She had come as promised to the trysting place and he was false. Yes, her mailer had been right; why had she worn the flowers ? And with the impetuosity of her nature she would have taken them from her ' hair and stamped theni under foot if she had only dared. Meanwhile ell her joyousness had depatted ; and giving way to the fitfulness which had charac- ' tensed her ot late, she became so taciturn that she did not speak unless addressed, and then her answers were so tart and snappish as to make several of her acquaintances resolve never again to trouble her with their conversation. Butabont this,' what did Irene care? She had come to-that fate expre,slT to meet Prince Sergius Lenskoff, and since he was not there,' the behaviour of all the rest of the world was absolutely indifferent to her. • Poor child her love for this' stro.nge, almoat un- canny, foreigner Was as overwhelming as it had been sudden, and, see med so thoroughly to usurp her every thought, that it was not surprising it should ,make Phyllis weep and the furrows of care shew themselves on Geoffrey s brow. As for her parents they knew but little of it. Mr. Stanhope Pad looked graver and had scarcely spoken since Sergius Lenskoff °eine among them; while as for Lady Fedora, she had been instructed to find a rich parti for her daughter, and she rejoiced to think that be had been found with so little trouble; and content with the idea that riches would be Irene's in the future, she did unt look below the surface of this man's worldly advantages. That Irene should have loved so passionately and. feveriahlyavould have surprised her had she known it, but she herself, smug in calm affection, micr even guessed at the conflicting feelings that were torturing her child. The change, however, from almost frivolous gaiety to a moi °senses no one could help remarking, did not escape her, though she did not altogether com- prehend its cause : and she was just on the point of telling Irene that in good society people controlled their feelings, and that if she did not know how to behave they had bettor return home et once, when the sparkle came hack to Irene's eyes, and a bright colour to her pale cheeks. Through the entrance gate, whieh she had been watching with no little anxiety, the tall figure of the Russian Prince might he seen advancing. There was something so like a ecowl on his brow, an angry expres- sion in his eyes, wider one wroth' scarcely have thought calculated to clear the clouds from a fair. young beauty's face; hut, airier) the days of the olis fairytale it would seem that ugliness has always had a strong fitecinatian, for beauty—probably owing to the severe contrasts in which nature ever loves to indulge. Prince Sergius went through the usual civil amenities with his hostess, then on no one else did he bestow even a pleasant glance, but strode on to the lawn where the crowd was thickest. Had he not been a prince he would have been called rude and illsbred, but being a prince, his behaviour was merely regarded as "eccentric, and so foreign—you know." One thing Is very certain, he did not care what people thought, and never sought to please anyone but himself. Something pleased him now, for the darkness cleared from his brow; and the smile which- had so much power in fascinating both men and women came to his lips. It we, the sight of the forget-me-note in Irene's bonnet that had wreathed his rough exterior with smiles, and,, whatever the subject for annoyance that he had brought with him to Lady Bertha Cumming's fete, it was banished from hi* mind when he saw Irene Stanhope. Whntanattered it to them that the by- standers, who could not help remarking the change that had come over both their countenances, sneered? "Poor little silly fool, does she think she will marry this big uncouth Russian and be a princess? He'll teach her bow to stiffer as he has taught many a woman before—eldid that she is, she is too fair for such a fate." "Someone should warn Lady. Fedora," suggested a dowager. "Warn a mother who thinks she has caught a prince for a son•in-law ! laugh I the idea is absurd " Meanwhile the lovers—for lovers they already knew themselves to be—had forsaken the knoll of trees where the crowd was seeking shelter from the rays of the scorching sun and had wandered down a path to the rcse garden, a spot they perchance hopec.l would be more or less deserted, Lady Fedora's atxious glances followed them, but she did not attempt to atop them, she only wondered whether it would be settled to-day, and whether her husband would be glad; and then she sought to devote herself to the small talk and interchange of civilities which convenejonsJity exacts. She must look composed and blind to what was going on, and make amends, if possible, for Irene'o fitful behaviour. As for Irene it never occurred to her, as she accom- panied Prince Sergius to the rose garden, to question whether it would be settled to-day or not. There was no thought of doing well for herself mixed up with the sort of worship she had for this foreigner. ' He was there by her side, smiling on her when he' had frowned on others; that was quite enough for her. She was as happy as a bird in the bright sunshine of the present hour ; for the morrow she had neither, thought nor care. It was the simplicity of Irene's childlike joyousness' added to her exquisite beanty that had atta act td Sergius Lenskoff from the first moment he saw her. He revelled in it now As he called her a day-star " and thanked her in glances rather than in, words fOr wearing the

div.p: Bowels that had provoked a reprimand rioo,

Fedora. "You are so late," she said; "why have you comp so late? If they had been real flowers theywould have withered from neglect." "Except for your sweet sake, I should not have come at all." "And why not, pray ? " "-There are difficulties in the life's path of mere human beings like me which, thank ,God, yon cannot undei stand." • r - Irene's brow shadowed over, "I do not like to be told that there are things I' cannot understand. lam not a fool." "A fool I, no,"- mid he laughed. "Of that your worst enemy could not accuse you. But do you think angels know aught of the wickedness and intrigie and. crime that surround mere mortals 1" "And yait are surrounded by wickedness and in• trigne and crime? 'Oh, Prince Sergius, how very dreadful!" "I did not say I was; but if I were would you, deot never to speak to me again?" he asked. She paused for a second or two before she answered him; then she said very seriously, "If you have ever done anything wicked or dread- ful, please do not tell rue. I would rather think of yopt as my imagination has created you,than know.yost are not what I believe you to be." He looked at her earnestly, with something like emotion in his usually atera -face. "As you will," he said; "yes, perhaps it Weie best so, but remember. if rou give me credit for good which does not exist, it id ,rtr fault, not mine." would rather exaggerate the good than the bad,' sue answered' my weakness, you know, is tO exaggerate most things, but you are not so very, veil it to
bad, iire you?" "Y, , have
;t asked
u.

~ave 'just me no. you, - replied, laughing; ,"but I . may go so far as tO observe that but few men are really good, and I ma scarcely one of the few." "After Ferdinand's model. not Geoff's," she replied. "Well, I love dear old Geoa with all my heart, fax more than Ferdinand, It is nice to have a • goOd brother, you know; but if all men were asgood as Geoff the world would be wanting in excitement" "What a very Woman you are"; he said, smiling; "you do not object to wickedness in the abstract, Out you shrink from its contact." "Yes, like a flower that closes its petals in the darin I cannot prevent wickedness from existing; as it doe. exist, I suppose it is for some good reason, but I wish $0 remain in profound ignorance of its details." Beautiful day star! Sin e7its only in a realm 'of darkness on which you will never shine."

He loved her for her purity and her faith in hitu, but was she not of too refined and simple a nature to satisfy Prince Sergius for long 1 If it, should please him to take the girl away, to B aegis as his wife would he for aye, as long as they both should live, keep from her the sin-stained picture of how.low man can fall; and only present himself to her in his meet external form of a powerful, honourable tussian noble Alas alas! Her one chance of escape from entanglement in the meshes of Prince Sergitis' life she herself wad setting aside. He might perchance have judged it honourable to tell ber some portion of his past from which her pure nature would have turned in horror; now, however, she had plosed the book which be would only too gladly have an excuse for sealing.' grad never in any future communications that would 1.,e place between them would she, from his lips, any portion of the truth. In justice to him let it be said that the closing of that book gave him something akin to regret, and for the remainder of his afternoon'S walk with Irene among the Gloires de Dijon in Latlyßertha Oumming's garden he was very thoughtful, and:made love in * subdued tone which unfortunately added not a little to the potencyof its charms. The sun was gone, and had been succeeded by donde from which heat drops were threatening. The sun of their lives, too, seemed for the moment clouded ; 13nt the electricity that was in the air existed none the , less in the relations between them. Of marriage not one word had Prince Sergice spoken. It would almost seem as if he did not dare,lest the mention of such a word might break the electric wire that connected them ; yet he, Prince Serging Lenskoff though he was, had no right to tamper with Henry Stanhope's daughter. This he knew full well, and acting on feelings which circumstances alone con• trolled, he snapped a rosebud from its stem, and pre- senting it to her, said, in a low husky voice, "Will yen keep it, sweet child, and when I come to claim it will you give it to me back" She scarcely knew the meaning of his.words, but she bowed her hcad in acquiescence just as the heat diupe began to fall in earnest, and a voice from behind ale rose trees told her that Lady Fedora was waiting for her. Without another word, only a hand presrare when they parted, Prince Sergius conducted her to her mother, and finally out -of the grounds to the carriage. Then he bowed and left them. He tricked impassable and stern ; she, radient and happy. Itwigh in answer to her mothers 'Well ? " she co,— %live no definite' reply.

AMERICA.—THE TARIFF BILL.—TERRIFIC SNOWSTORM: NEW YORK OUT OFF. A bill of a volnininens character dialing with the American tariff will shortly be introduced in the House of Representatives. The Tariff Rill carries to the free liat numerous articles which now nay duty, and among the items upon which an increased duty is proposed to be established are clothing and wools imported washed, which will pay twice the amount of duty to which they 'Would be subrcted if imported unwashed. It is esti- mated that the reduCtions under the bill will be on internal taxation 70,000,000 dollars, and on the tariff ached tile 25,000.000 dollars. NEW YORK, M0#77)16 Y.—A terrific snowstorm and gale is raging in New York and its vicinity to-day. Business is almost entirely suspended. and traffic' is at a stand- still. Mitny telegraph lines have been blown down, and ell the railroads are blocked. There has been no cora, nannication with Washington since midnight. The storm LS the worst ever known in the city. People living in the suburbs have been unable to reach the city, and even those living in Brooklyn were either delayed for hours or prevented from reachino• their places of busi- ness in New York while' according to some accounts, persons residing in the ets- itself were five hours reach- Mg their destination. Little business was, consequently, done on the -Exchanges. The surface street ears have been abandoned, and the trains on the elevated rail- way run into their sheds. There are no trains leaving New York for the provinces. During the wildest part of the storm a train ran into the rear of another on the Third Avenue elevated line. The excitement thus caused was terrific. The engineer was killed, and a number of Persons hurt. The gale continued unabated throughout the afternoon, the wind shifting, to the west. Navigation la entirely suspended, and the business of the Post-office Paralysed. The storm, which e7.3ended about 60 miles inland, began about midnight with a falling theimo7 Meter, though previously there had been heavy .in. THE DISTRESS AND THE WORKING CLASSRS.—EarcI DR LA WARR moved—" That. in the opinion of this House, considering the depressed condition of agricultural and other industries in this country, and the consequent .di. tress among the working classes, it is incumbent upon her Majesty's Government to take it into their serious eonsideratkin what measures can be adopted to avert the "rave conseauences which must otherwise ensue." He contended that there was much distress among the working classes, and that it was incumbent on the Government to do something towards its alleviation. —Several of their lordships spoke onthe subject.-- Lord Ssusntrny would not admit that the distress V 711,: SO acute as to bring them in presence of a calamity deeply affecting the vast mass of the population; nor did he look upon Protection as a remedy—nay, he utterly disbelieved in their power to introduce Protection, and if it were introduced he thought it you'd lead to a state of division among the classes of the country which would not differ very much from civil war. It was, lie said, to the industry and enterprise for which the nation w‘ei vet conspicuous that we must look for a remedy. —The motion was withdrawn and the House adjourne-1.
