A number of questions were put. as to the sale of con,. Jernned military clothing to volunteer firms not by open contract. and Mr. BRAS!), deeming the answers unsatis- factory, gave notice to cell attention to the matter. Sir MICRIEL RICKS-BEACH pmrnised to" lay before the house the Lords' report of the sweating system, and the PosrmArrau-GENEar, informed Mr. Henniker-Beaton that, a uniform pOstage stamp for Great Britain and her colonies wag not practicable. Colonel Kixo-Flitniku stated that the Goverpnient were considering the advisability of appointing a fresh Land Sob-Commission. in order to _deal more rapidly with the Trish fair-rant cases. At present there were a "'men Sub-Commissioners, and they were disposing of about 2,000 Moen monthly. Mr. liITCWIR said he would bring in the Local Govern- ment Bill next Monday.

Mr. W. TI. Sarrrn said the Budget would be introduced that, day fortniitht.. A nov7 writ was issuod for the Gower division of Gla- noren-ishiro. to fill the vacancy caused by the,death.of Mr. Yeo, M.P.

div.head: NATIONAL DEBT BILL.
div.p: THE NATIONAL DEBT BILL.

On the report of the resolution in connection with the National Debt Bill, Mr. Gnscnsa said, with regard to the time allowed for dissent to the scheme, it wax abso- lutely according to precedent that, dissent should* be required within a reasonable time—only ten 41.ys had 'recently been allowed to holders in France. The House, he hoped, would support him in pushing the bill through by the earliest possible day. Leave was •then given to bring in the bill, and it was brought in by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the inritnation being given that it would be taken lit a morning sitting on Friday. THE NAVX, ESTIMATES. On the motion,to go into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates, • Lord C. BRRYSFORD called attention to the -system of administration at the Admiralty, and moved that the allocation of authority.in the administrative system of the Admiralty requires entire reform. He contended that there was no shred of ci..aystem of organisation able to cope with the requirements for the defence of Vie country in the event of war breaking, out, and it was in consequence of this want of system in the In- telligence Department, and the reduction of the salaries of its officers, that he resigned. ADMIRAL MAywe, in seconding thh motion, endorsed Lord C. Beresford's views, and disclaiming any intentioq or desire to. complain of the First Lord or the'Hdard of Admiralty, remarked that it was the system and not the individuals he attacked.

Lord G. Ilsuir.ToN, who began by denying that any difference of opinion with regard tO the Estimates ex- isted between him§elf.and the Sea Lords, replied to Lord f',l3ereened's charge with regard to the salaries in the Intelligence Department, and said the reduction was not decided upon until it was cone' tiFively shown that the reduced salary was sufficient to secure the best ability and efficiency. In fact, the Admiralty had had no difficulty in obtaining for the Intelligence Department the men they wanted, and in no case had the salary offered been 611;.,:etedto 1- y the officers appointed.; the &hate was continuea by 11fr. r Fitrmerala Mr. Duff.

rx OM Adversely criticised the eonstructiort Of ourl'Aff4 truirefo and Of. V eSsela of the Admiral class. Mr. FOrtwoon took eXteption fo these views, remark- ing that thee vesSelS were pronounced by competent naval authorities to be powerful:and useful ships. The strength of the Navy compared favourably with that of ether nations, and in the estimates for this year a sum was taken fortwo-'vessels which, although commenced last year, m ight beta ken aS additions to the fleet this yerir. Admiral FIELD remarked that an inquiry into the er- ganisatien of the Admiralty would not sufficiently meet te relpiirements Of naval men, who would net be satis- fied with less than a searching inquiry into the state of the Navy generally. He continued to speak until 12 o'clock when. according to the new rules, the debate stood adjourned. MISCELLANEOHS—The Timber Acts (Ireland) Amend- ment Bill and the .Conyright (Musical Compositions) Bill were read a seeond time.—On the motion of Mr: W. H. SMITH It was resolved that a Committee be appointed to join with a Committee of the House of Lords to examine into the present systeth of private Bill legislation, Mr. Seuru stating that the names of the Committee would be announced on Thursday.—Mr. W. H. SMITH brought in a Bill to make further prevision for the restoration and repair of Westminster Abbey.which was read a first time The House adjeUrned at 12-30 a.m.
HOUSE OF LORDS—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 p.m. , THE REF.ORM OF 'PRE HOUSE • OF LORDS.

The Earl of Winwres gave notice that on Monday, on the motion of'EFirl Rosebery for a committee of inquiry into the construction of the House, he would move as an amendment that it would not be a safe thing to plaoe the constitution of this House within the powers of a committee, nor was it-consistent with the dignity of the House, and that ;f any changes were to be made they should be made by the House itself, on the motion of a responSibleMinister of the Crown. '

RAILWAY AND CANAL TRAFFIC BILL. The Muse went into Committee on this Bill. In Clause 12, enabling Commissioners to award dein: ages, including the repayment of overcharge_s, the Ear! ef JERSRY Moved an amendment enabling the Commis- sioners to ,sward damages in respect of matters arisith-: not more than two years before complaint made, instead af one year as provided by the bill.—Lord STANIAY of PRESTON accepted the amendment.--Lood BRAMWELL contended for six years, to which a person was entitled at common law. On Clause 25, relating to preferential rates In favour of foreign merchandise, the Earl of TEnsur moved a series of amendments with the view of securing equai treatment for the carriage of the goods of home and foreign producers.—. Lord WALSINOTIAM. in the inter. ests of agriculture, urged the Government to accent the amendment, which would have the effect of abolishing the bounties given to foreign over home produoers. The House divided on the first amendment— For the amendment 69 Against ' 63

Deajority against the Government.— —6 The amendment was then carried, arid the others. aftcr a brief discussion, were withdrawn. Several verbal amendments were agreed to, and the bill passed through Committee. The remaining orders of the day were disposed of, and the House adjourned at 7 30. •

HOUSE OF COMMONS.I-I.FinesisAy. The Speaker took the chair it 35 p.m. QUESTIONS. The UNDED-SECRF,TAITY for FOREOGN AFFAIRS, is answer to Mr. Dillon, disclaimed all , knowledge that let- ters to and from the Red Sea were opened by the officials at Suakin'. The. SOLICiTOR-GENARAL for IRELAND stated that 22,728 leaseholders had entered the Irish Land Courts up to February 29th last, under the provisions of the Land Law (Ireland) Act, 1887.. The CHANCILLOR of the Excinsauxn told Sir John Lubback that the bonus to holders of Consols and Reduced, who accepted the new stock, would be treated as interest. Sir J. FERGITSSON informed Mr., Caine that the total revenue derived irons intoxicating liquors in British India during the year 1885-80 was 3,340,000 taels of rupees'. The Pinar LORD of the TREASURY said he was not yet prepared to stet& the views of the Government. relative to the renewal of the powers of am Land Commission, which will expire in August next. in -reply to. Mr. W. Me.Laren, Mr. NV :Lola; said the attention of -the Agricultural Denartinent had- called to the large admixture of animal fat in the manu- facture of American cheesel, which enabled the latter to be sold in this country as pure cheese at prices injurious to the manufacture of pure cheese, and the Foreign Office had been asked to obtain reports from our consuls in the United States as to the prevalence of this adulteration.. , The licutx. SECRETARY' informed Mr. Bradlaugh that he ' had called the attention of the Public Prosecutor to the notices of a lottery, to be held on Primrose Day, at the Church Conservative Club, and, as some of the prizes were cigars, he had also directed the attention of the I Inland Revenue authorities to the subject.
NEW BILLS.

Mr. ADDISO_N brought in two bills, one to rialeve the Courts of gsizes from the trial of offenders committed to the Quarter Sessions, and one to amend the vexatious Indictments Bill. Mr. Cancan gave notice of his intention to bring in Parliamentary Registration Amendment BilL

THE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA. Considerable attention was aroused when Mr. Sr-Loci rose to propose his motion, which characterised the frontier policy of the Government of India as unwise and productive of grave financial difficulties, leading, as itdid,to increased burdens of taxation,to theextension of the sale of intoxicating drink for the sake of revenue, arid to neither the moral nor material welfare of the people. In an effective speech he said it was a disheartening task to try and make head or tail of the Indian accounts ; but their extreme complication, he added amid laughter, lent itself to a plan often adopted of throwing a barrow- ful of figures on thelloor of the House towards the end of a debate. The question he asked was, "Has the money been wisely spent, and have we gotvalue for it ?" His contention was that value had by no means been re- ceived for the money; that not one single department of business conducted by the Indian Government made any profit whatever; the last year there was a loss of 2i millions on its business efkrts. The taxation of the people, he pointed out, was' heavier than they could bear ; and he asked who was responsible for the policy of defence on the confines of Afghanistan—was it actuated by irresponsible Russophobism or wild Jingoism in mad career after decorations and K.C.B.'s ? It had cost fifty millions to establish us in one corner of Afghanistan, and that was a mere fleabite to what would have to be spent if the present policy were continued. The natives of India, he said, spoke in terms almost of execration of the enhancement of the salt duty: but there was some- thing more ominous in the thatements of the native news- papers for his manufacturing friends, especially in Lan- cashire' for many of them strongly recommended a re. turn to those obnoxious duties on the import of cotton goods in India which were removed some years ago. Sorry indeed should he be to see a reversion to• such a policy. With all our resources, and wealth, we ought to hold our magnificent Empire in India ' • but we should govern with prudence, economy, and justice. Mr. CAINE seconded the motion, contending that if the policy of doubling the revenue every ten years by the sale of intoxicating drinks were , continued India would become one of the most drunken countries in the world. Lord Rminomm Clumenitt, who said Mr. Slagg had imported into his speech a great deal of partisan ferocity, maintained that a more complete defence of the frontier was absolutely necessary at the time it was menaced by Russia, nor could the outlay be regarded as unproduc- tive expenditure, But he emphatically urged economy and retrenchirlent, saying that If this course were not adopted the Indian Government would be approaching a financial position not far removed from actual in- solvency. , Sir Rum GOMM replied on behalf of the Government. Other hon- members having spoken there were at mid- night cries of "Divide," and the House divided, the figures being—For Mr. Slagg's motion, 72; against, 122; majority, 50. Select Committees yere appointed to examine into the Army-Estimates, the Navy Estimates, and the Revenue Departments Estimates. The House adjourned at ten minutes after twelve. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNFSDAY. _ - .

The Speaker took the chair at 15 minutes past twelve o'clock. PrrrrioNs.—Petitions• were presented in favour of granting the franchise to women legally qualified, by Mr Sidebotham, from the Hyde Women's Liberal Association; and for the repeal of the blasphemy laws, by Mr. Cod- dington, from Blackburn. • DEBATE ON THE OATHS BILL. The chief interest of the House of Commons was con- centrated upon the Oaths Bill, Mr. Basial-suon moving its second reading in a speech in which he said Abe measure consisted of only two clauses, and followed pre- cisely the words of the Affirmation Act which applied to members of the Society of Friends. To meet the wishes 1 of those who desired the opportunity of affirming, he had introduced in the first line of the first clause the words "on objecting to being sworn." The bill, he showed, would apply to members of Parliamegt, Imagiatrates, banisters; jivers, policemen, the rank and file of the army, and many others; it was no longer a party measure, had been en- dorsed by men on both sides of the House, and was oon- sidered by a large number of Ministerialists to be a fair and proper solution of an extremely difficult pro- bleni: But he was not asking. the House to abolish oaths altogether, because there were many conscientious men who thought they ought to be permitted to swear their allegiance and to make the appeal which they considered was now contained in the oath. He only asked that there might be an option for those who were disabled by law at present or who desired to relieve themselves from a position that often became intolerable. Mr. Stanley LEIGHTON moved an amendment that as the Oaths Bill involved grave questions of constitutional usage affect- ing every class of the community, the House should not alter the law until the question had been investigated by a Royal commission. Mr. De Linz seconded the arnehdment, and a long debate followed. It was con- tended that if thwoath were abolished the foundations of society would be sapped and England's downfall be im- minent; that oath-taking was really no prevention of untruth or perjury; that the oath was necessary in courts of justice, the humbler classes not being afraid of prosecutions but "afraid of being damned." It was Mr. (ledge who made the latter assertion; and he added amid laughter, that it was a great advantage that that fear should keep theni straight. Cries of "No. no" and interruption greeted hkm when he took it for granted that hon. members believed an Atheist was a man upon whom conscience had no binding effect. Sir J. PEASE spoke in favour of affirmatiOn, and said those who op- posed the bill were setting up a double standard of truth, -winch would be detrimental to all true moral- ity. The Arronsiny GENERAL was against the bill, which, he held, would enable people who intended to lie to do so with impunity so far as their consciences were concerned. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT took exception to the Attorney-General's contention that a man profes- sing atheism should declare himself an atheist, and asked Mr. Bradlaugh to accept Mr. Darling's proposal, ,so as to make the bill apply only to persons who had a Conscien- tious objection to take the oath. Mr. BRADLAtron ex- pressed his willingness to amend the bill in the manner suggested. The •SOLICITOR-GENERAL spoke amid cries of divide," and soon afterwards the House divided, there being for Mr. Stanley Leighton's amendment i 37, against 247; majority, against, 110. The announcement was loudly cheered by the Opposition. Mr. Nomus was ruled out of order in moving that the bill be read that day six months, and for some time the House was in a state of excitement. Mr. Tpm-usisoN, unheeding the cries of " divide," moved thesadjournment of the debate. The motion was seconded by Mr.'MAint STEWART amid renewed cries for a division; but Mr. BRADLAUGH, spring- ing up adroitly, moved that the question be now put. After the loud Opposition cheers had died away, the SPEAKER gravely said, "The question is that the,ques- tion be now put." "No," shouted Mr. CuArrix, his vehemence causing much amusement. Ignoring the laughter, he challenged a division, and it was taken, the result being—for the motion, closure 334; against, 50 majority for, 284. Againthe House divid'ed, and Mr.lirad- laugh's motion for the second reading was carried by 250 votes to 150, the announcement being received with cheers. . The House adjourned at 20 minutes to six o'clock. • HOUSE OF LORDS.--TRURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter past four o'clock. Miscrwassous. The Archbishop of CANTERBURY moved the second reading of the Church Discipline Bill. which was agreed t.—Lord HERSCHELL cabled attention to the woriring of the Merchandise Marks Act, with a view to render it effectual in India, the colonies, and foreign countries. Pressure, he thought, should be put on the Indian Government to induce them to prevent the importationtf falsely marked goods.—Lord Cnoss and Lord Einnsrosin having explained that the Indian Government and the colonies had been urged to adopt similar measures, Lord SALISBURY said he did not know what steps could be taken to induce the observance of the Act in foreign countries, but the Government would be glad to consider any practical suggestion.—Several bills were real. a second time and their lordships ad- journed at twenty-five minutes to seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tirunsmy. ' . .

%.• v .4 v. v The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QuasrioNs.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said the bonus of 5s per cent payable under the Conversion scheme to stockholders would not be charged to the revenue of the forthcoming financial, year. Replying to Air.Maclure, he said, with regard to the protection of trustees, that he was considering how to make their position absolutely sure. Sir W. Houlds- Worth ascertained that the Government bill for remedying abuses in the formation of limited liability companies would be introduced in the House of Lordsloy the Lord Chancellor —Mr. Healey and Mr. Dillon put several perplexing questions to Mr. Smith as. to the fiolitical ardour of Civil servants, Mr. DILLow re- marking that it was most important the Irish people should not be led to believe that a man might take a side with the Unionists with impunity ,'while the slightest ex- pression of opinion on the other side would lead to dis- missal.—The FIRST Loan of the TREASURY asked that no- tice of the questions might be given.—Asked about the Easter holidays, Mr. SMITH expected that the House would adjourn after a morning sitting on Tuesday, the 27th inst., until Thursday in the• following week.—Mr. Chamberlain entered the House amid cheers; and Lord W., Gordon Lennox took his seat for Chichester, recently relinquished by the Earl of March. NAVY ESTIMATES. &C.—The debate on the motion to go into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates was I resumed. by Admiral FIELD. Many suggestions were made, some in favour of strengthening the navy, others for retrenchment and the dirninutien of work in ttje dockyards.—Lord GEORGE Ethan:roil replied, and refer- I ring to the complaints that the navy was inadequate to the requirements of the nation, maintained that it was important to secure a careful but continuous expenditure in shipbuilding. The House having gone into Committee of Supply, Lord Citannfis BmnsFonn, on the vote for £3,112,100 for wages for officers and seamen, urged that the number of non-combatants on board ship should be reduced. The vote was agreed to. On the vote of £3,614,903 on account of the Civil Service, the action of the Government towards Ireland was strongly criticised; and described As mean and contemptible. At five-and-twenty minutes to twelve Mr. SMITH moved that the question be now put. There were cries of "Half- an-hour yet" and "Shame." Mr. Slurs pressed his

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

At the Shropshire Assizes, on Saturday, Elijah Bowers, farmer, who had been found guilty of killing William Powell, another farmer, was sentenced to 15 years' penal servitude. FATAL TOBOGittNING ACCIDENT.—A fatal tobogannirg ease is reported from Dover, a young gentleman named Ileauntont having succumbed to the injuries he sustained while tobtaranning on a local slide. He was thrown out of the car and dashed against a post. Osborne Mill, Chadderton, Oldham, was almost totally destroyed by fire on Saturday. The outbreak occurred , while the mill was being lighted, and spread rapidly. The roof fell, and the spinning rooms were destroyed. The earding room was saved. The. damage is estimated at £lO,OOO, Mr. Burt, M.P., has issued a circular to the Northum- berland Miners' Union, in which. referring to the recent vote on the subject Of salary, he says he has felt that the payment of members is only a true and just prin- ciple, and that if the system breaks down in Northum- berland, it will probably be shaken, if not destroyed, elsewhere.

THE MI7RMIR OF A SIFRETHRART.—At Barnet, on Mon- day. Henry Cullum, 24, was charged on remand with the wilful murder, of Emma Bignall, his sweetheart, whom he shot on Vlfednesday, at Shenley, near Barnet. Some time ago the, prisoner's father sought to have him con- fined in a lunatic, asylum, but failed to obtain a certifif cite as to his insanity. The prisoner, who seemed to take little interest in the proceedings, was committed for trial. • Loss OF A SCHOON7O2 AND FOUR tlVßA.—lntelligence has been received at Queenstown that the three-masted .chooner Nellie Bowers was wrecked on the 26th ult. on Richmond Island, Coast of Main, during a heavy snow- storm. Captain Spear, first mate Robinson, second mate Gardiner, and the cook, Charles Higgins, were drowned, The remainder of the crew were landed with difficulty on the i.dand. The vessel was on a voyage from Port- land to X....

TEI MtITHDRH OF • GAlinrinrrint : RVSPITIS FOR THF CuLrarr.—On Monday, the Governor of Armley Gaol re- ceived a communication from the Home Office granting a respite La the case of David Pilniore, who was sentenced to death at the Leeds Assizes for the murder of a game- keeper, named Oopley, near Pontefract. The execution had been fixed for yesterday. The petitions asking for a commutation of the sentence received 70,000 Signa- I-urea—The culprit is to be kept in penal sarvitude for life.

DIVORCX AND kfannuan IN AMEETCA.—In the Divorce Court, on Monday. Captain M'Mahon; of the Royal Artil- lery, obtained a decree nisi against his 'wife for inter- marrying in America with a Mr. Beevor. The latter was made co-respondent, but had to be dismissed from the suit as being beyond the jurisdiction of the court. • Mrs. M'Mahon, the daughter of an American, was stay- ing in America with her mother, when she got a divorce Nom her husband in a Colorado 'court, and married Mr. Beevor. MANSLAUGHTER OF A. FAMINE. At. the Shropshire Assizes, on Saturday, Elijah Bowers Forester, a farmer, of Whiztall, Salop, was brought up for sentenee, having been found guNtv on Friday of the minslaughter of his brother-in-law, Vihiam ?cwt.!): another farmer, by shooting him. The defence was that the prisoner and the deceased had a struggle for the possession of &loaded rrun, which Went'off aecidentally, killMg Powell. Mr. Justice A. L. Smith on Saturday sentenced the prisoner to fifteen years' penal servitude.

Surma or A CLIMATILO7.—The South Staffordshire coronet held an inquest on Saturday, at Tipton, respect- ing the death of the Rev. Angelo Solari, vicar of Ocker Hill, who committed suicide. The deceased had lately complained of being distracted in consequenee of the im- poverished condition of many of his parishioners. The applicants for relict had been very numerous, but each one he supplied with a loaf. On Thursday morning he cut his throat, .severing his windpipe and died almost immediately afterwards. A verdict of "Suicide during , temporary insanity" was returned.

FIRE IN LONDON : Savage'. Fievans Isrtrasn.—A fire broke out at half-past one on Satarday morning, in a four-storeyed building, used as a seed warehouse, Parker-street, Drury-lane, belonging to Mr. Gay, Covent Garden. The neighbourhood Is thickly populated. The engines were soon on the spot, and while playing on the flames the wall of the bulling in Parker-street gave my, a mass of brick falling into the street,. Four fire- n Were wounded by stones. and two buried beneath the ruins. One was extricated, but little hope of..rescu- ing the other is entertained. ATTEMPT TO MURDER A SON.—Thomas Simmons, formerly a colliery proprietor at Broadstone, was charged at Walsall, on Monday, with attempting . to murder his son Joqeph. On Saturday morningi by threats, he drove his wife and family from home, but. on. Sunday night the eldest son entered, and the prisoner. who had threatened to murder anyone who came pear. pointed a double barrelled gun ,at him and discharged both barrels just as the eon struck the gun downwards. A fierce struggle followed before the prisoner was secured. fie was remanded with a view to committal to the assizes. _

EXECLITION OF A HIGHWAY MIIRDERER.—David Rees, 26, was executed at Oarma.rthen Gaol at eight o'clock yesterday morning for tile murder of Thos. Davies. at Lianally, on the 12th November, when the latter was carrying a bag, containing-the wages of work- men, from Llanelly to the Dafen Tinplate Work,' An accomplice of Rest has not been found. Rees refused to reveal his identity. Berry, the executioner, allowed a drop of six feet, and death resulted immediately. At the inquest subsequently, a statement by the cul- prit was read, in which he confessed the murder, and said he hid the money which he had stolen in some hedges. He attributed the act to the fact that he had been drinking heavily. FIVE MONTHS ON A DESERT IstAND.:—/VireJanaesi WOhle, of Limerick, one of the survivors of the barque Derry Castle, of Limerick. which, while on a voyage from New Zealand for Queenstown or Falmouth for orders, was wrecked on March 26th last on one of the Auckland ' Islands, came home in the Orient Company's steamer Orizaba, which arrived at Plymouth on Friday evening from Australia. Mr. M'Ohie was the only passenger on board, and, with seven of the sailors, succeeded in swimming ashore. The captain, officers, and remainder of the crew, 15 in all, were drowned. The survivors lived on a desolate island for 154 days. their priocipal food being the seals which they caught. Mr. M`Bilde, who proceeded in the ship to London, still feels the effects of his long auffering.and terrible exposure. . .

Tne ARISTOCRATIC Ass Arm. Casa.—Tbe hearing of the charge against Major Kildare Burrows of assaulting Lord Howard tie Walden was resumed, at Middlesex Session.% on Saturday. The Judge refused to allow Mr. Lockwood to call evidence in justification of the assault, or to allow Major Burrows to Tooke a statement before his counsel. 'Mr. LoCktbood then addressed the jury, and Said if Lord lieward. had taken his proper place on re• turning' home' he would have been allowed to do so. ' The jury found the defendant guilty of assault and cßueing actual bodily harm. Upon the other counts they returned a verdict of not guilty.—Mr. Edtin„ Assistant Judge, ordered defendant to pay a fine of £4OO and costs, and to enter into recognisances in the sum of £5OO, and; two sureties in £250 each to keep the peace for twelve inonths.-Major Burrowes was admitted to bail pending payment of the fine. ron.kcco-onowngo IN ENcirANP.—A .deputation from the British Tobacco Growers' Association waited on the Chancellor of the Exchequer, at Whitehall; on Saturday. The object of the deputation, as expressed by Lord Harris, Sir E. Birkbeck, and other gentlemen, was to in- duce the Chancellor to support •a hundred experiments in tobacco-greeting in different parts of the country, by taxing them at the reduced rate of £25 per acre. Mr. Goschen, in rely, said he thought the proposal was a rather extravagant one if it was intended to place the tobacco raised upon the market. lf, however, it *as for experiment only, and the tobacco was not sold, then perhaps the duty might be waived. Lord Harris bald it certainly was intended to sell, the tobacco if a market could he found. Mr. Goschen said that in that case he could not see his way to assist the deputation, but, he would further consider their views.-

A TROVGIITFUL EXPLOYRR.—.I FORTIINT OUT OF To- isAcco.—lt is announced that the servants of all descrip- tions, including gardeners, coachman, etc., of the late Mr. George Cope. of the well-known Liverpool firm of cigar manufacturers, have been informed that the deceased had willed that each of them should receive 20 for every year which they had been in-his employ, As some of the servants had been with Mr. Cope for a long time, they were recipients of handsome amounts. For instance, the coachman was entitled to £350, George Mainwaring received £2BO, and thb others sums of varying amount according to their years of service. It was intimated that they would each have the privilege of investing the money in the tobacco concern, the necessary legal formalities connected with which would cost them laothing. Dir. Cope has also made bequests of £2OO each to six or eight of the heads of departmentaatthe factary in Lord Nelson-street, and £l,OOO to the benevolent fund in connection with the factory.

MRS. GORDON BAILLIE ALLEGED FRADD.—Mr. E. NATION _MOURNING.

BERLIN, SATURDAY.—The body of rhe late Emperor has. been embalmed, and is now lying in state in the hall of the Royal castle, where the arms of the Imperial family are hung. A large number of privileged visitors win.oe the remains to-day. The features of the deceased are placid, and show no trace of pain. A funeral service was held yesterday evening in the Mortuary Chamber. hie Emperor lying with a crucifix on his breast, and holding an ivory cross in his right hand. After the ser- vice the remains were provisionally placed upon the bier in the Palace Armours', surrounded by flags of all the Berlin regiments. The Imperial slecree regarding the national mourning meets with universal approval, The Berlin Town Council have decided to wear mourn- ing for six weeks at their sittings.

Beetle, MONDAY Nezzrr.—Te the trials through which Germany is now passing must he added the Hitless of Prince Bismarck. Happily the Prince is not very ill, and perhaps it is only a cold caught during yesterday's journey to Leipzig. It is said, however to have pro- duced the Chancellor's old affection of varicose veins. and at his age such shocks to the system sometimes lead to unexpected results. The remains of the late Emperor were transferred to-day from the mortuary chamber of the Palace to the Cathedral. The coffin was covered with a black pall and borne by soldiers of the Imperial Body Guard. The Crown Prince, Prince Henry, and. the other princes of the Imperial family, as well as a number of distinguished officers, walked immediately behind, the corfroe being closed by a de- tachment of cavalry. The Cathedral was thrown open , to the public, and was thronged by a constant succes- sion of visitors. The coffin containing the remains was richly ornamented, and the catafalque was brilliantly lighted. It was observed that the Emperor's head was I covered with his military cap, and the body was clad in the uniferm of the First Regiment of 'Guards, and wrapped in the gray military cloak worn by the deceased Monarch. Around the coffin stood like living statues' representative ,non-commissioned officers froni the regi- ments of the Berlin garrison. By one o'clock the crowd was massed in a dense column, the five alleys of the Lustgarten being also filled. All these columns were made to converge upon one opening into the , cathedral, through which only Ra people at a time were , admitted; in other words 40,000 people were directed + on, to one narrow point. During the first hour tle sufferings of the crowd emits very great, but were borne patiently enough. AS fdrther thousands fell in the pressure was greatly.increaSed, and soon became unen- durable. Women shrieked and fainted, but it was impossible to get them out of the crowd. In the course of the next hour upwards of 100 women fainted, and hundreds more told by their blanched cheeks how intense were their sufferings from the crush. One fainting woman fell and was trampled on in the mad heedlessness of the crowd, her blood,atainine the ground. Probably many of those present have been Injured for life.
FREDERICK UT. AND TB E EMPRESS VICTORTA.- TRE JOURNEY FROM SAN REMO.

The new German Emperor and Empress started from San Bono for Berlin it nine o'clock on Saturday morn- ing, accompanied by Sir Morell Mackenzie. Except for n somewhat yellow complexion, his Majesty looked well. On arriving at the station of Sampierdarena the Emperor was met by Ring Humbert, who entered the Imperial saloon, remaining ten minutes. Conversation was carried on by means of little slips of paper, upon one of which the Emperor Frederick said he desired to thank the Italian Parliament for its expressions of sympathy during his present trials. Signor Crispi and the other officers of the King's honsehold were also admitted to the saloon carriage to pay,,their respects to the Emperor. On the arrival of the frain at Milan the Imperial party were silently saluted by a large number of persons, among whom were the Duke of Aosta, a number of general officers, the Prefect of Milan, and the principal German residents. CHARLOTTENItOI2O, BtrtiDAT NIIGHT.—At 11 10 to-night, the Emperor Frederick arrived at this station, the train being only half an hour behind its time. Although the station was kept clear, and Charlottenburg is three miles from Berlin, and in spite of a terrible snowstorm which commenced about el ht o'clock, many thousand persons stood in a dense line which stretched from the station to ,the castle. The weather was terrible. A whirlwind of snow enveloped everything, and in an hour it lay several inches deep. At last the imperial train steamed slowly info the station. It consisted of sixteen carriages. The first to step on to the platform was the Empress Victoria, assisted by Prince William, and they'drove away together. The crowd seemed to see that the car- riage did not contain the Emperor, and there was not much cheering. The next carriage followed with Princess William and her sister-in-law, and. as the third, which contaistedthe Emperor, drove through the gate of thc station, cheers of the wildest and most enthusiastic description broke out, and were continued till long after the carriage was out of sight. The Emperor held himself erect, with his old military bearing, and raised his plumed hat he drove away. Though a squadron. of Gerdes du Corps were in attendance to escort the new Emperor to the suburban palace of his father, his Majesty dispensed wittrthe pomp of their clmapittiv, and drcrve 'rapidly home. The Emperor stepped lightly out of his carriage, holding a handkerchief before his lips, and as soon as he was indoors his Majesty threw open his military mantle, and holding himself erect and firm, to the joy of those who saw him, wullred upstairs with his usual command- ing mien. Sir Award Malet was present, and an efficer who was also present spoke with almost glowing enthu- siasm of the astonishing appearance and deportment of the Emperor. BERLIN, TUESDAY.—The Emperor Frederick rerhains at Charlottenburg. He shows no signs of weakness, and is engaged writing throughout the greater part of the day. His voice is hoarse, but audible. The Emperor this morning received a visit from Major-General Von 'Winterteld, and Afterwards gave audiences to Prince Bismarck and Count Yon Moltke." The Emperor has charged he Crown Prince to represent him in the event of hie being incapacitated.

THE TITLE. OF THE NEW EMPEROR. The title of the new Emperor is a matter of consider- able dispute. Prince Bismarck, in his address to the German Reichstag, on Friday, appears to 'have, set the matter at rest,. He announced Una the Prussian Crown, together wirb The Imperial dignity referred to in Article 11 of the Reich Constitution, had passed to his Majeiity Frederick 111., King of Prussia. T4.le report adds that murmur of pleased surprise rippled over the House at this revelation that the Crown Prince had resolved to rule as the namesake of the hero of the Seven Years' War instead of his uncle Frederick William W., by whose name be has hitherto generally called himself.

PROCLAMATION OF THE NEW EMPEROR. Beaux, MONDAY.—The new Emperor has issued a proclamation, which is printed in an extraordinary edition of the Oficial Gazette to-night. It bears to-day's date, and runs as follows To My People. • The Emperor has departed his glorious life, in the much loved father whom I bewail and whom my Royal house with me laments in deepest sorrow. Faithful Prussian people have lost their fame-crowned King; the Ger- man nation the founder ,of its unity; the newly-risen empire its first ,German Emperor. His illustrious name will remain Inseparably bound up with all the greatness of the German Fatherland, in whose new creation the strenuous labour of the Prussian people and Princes has met with its most splendid reward. While King William raised the Prussian army to the height of its earnest vocation by the never-tiring care of a nation's father, he laid a sure foundation for the victories which were gained by German arms under his leadership, and out of which sprang the national unity. He thereby sebured to the Empire a position of power such as up to that time any German heart lied yearned for, but had scarcely dared to hope for, and that which he won for his people in the hot, death-bringing fight, it was appointed for him to strengthen end beneficently to increase by the long peaceful toil of his laborious years of , government. Safely resting on her own strength, Germany stands forth esteemed in the council of nations, and desires only to enjoy in peaceful progress that which she has won. That this is so we have to thank the Emperor William. His never-wavering devotion to duty, and his indefatigable activity, consecrated to the welfare of Fatherland. supported by his reliance on the self- sacrificing devotion of which the Prussian people had :riven unvarying proofs, and, in which all the Ger- man races shared. All rights and duties which are connected with the Crown of my house.. and which for the time which, acceding re. God's will, may be allotted to my rule, I am resolved faithfully to pre- serve, have now passed to me. Imbued with the great- ness of my roission I shall make it my whole endeavour to continue the fabric in the spirit in which it was fotinded —to make Germany a centre of peace, and to foster the welfare of Germany in agreement with the Federal Government as well as with the constitutional organs of the empire, as also of Prussia. To my faithful people who have stood by my house throughout the history of a whole century in good as in evil days, I offer my unbounded confidence, for I am convinced , that on the basis of an unbreakable bond between sovereign and people, which, independently of every change in the life of the State, forms the unalterable inheritance of the House of Hohenzollern, my crown rests henceforward as securely as the devotion of the country to the Government of which I am now called and of which I solemnly promise to be the faithful King, both in happiness and sorrow. God grant me this blessing and strength to carry out this work to which my life shall henceforth be devoted.—(Signed), Berlin, March 12, 1888. FREDERICK.

VIOLENT GA.L.E.;--al-11.1"1"ING DISASTERS AND LOSS OF LIFE. Early on Stenda.y morning, sherry gale from the west sprang tin at Liverpool, accompanied by showers of rain. and lasted some hours. Towards night, however, the wind dropped and shifted round to east-north-east. During the gale a coasting vessel was sunk off the East Hoyle Bank, but it is not known at what time the wreck occurred, nor is the name of the vessel known. The fate of the crew is uncertain. The Lake district was visited by a severe snow storm, on Sunday. Snow fell without intermission for several hours, and continued on Monday. In the Fell district, the weather for the past three days has been extremely wild, the drifts from the last storm have not disappeared. Several inches of snow fell on Sunday night. In Plymouth, on Sundkv, a large ,chimney stack VW ' blown down, and crashed through the roof of a cottage to the ground floor. There were 13 people in the house, the majority of whom were buried in the debris, which to blocked the doorway that it had to be burst in before any rescue could be effected: All escaped unhurt. The houseis completely wrecked. Throughout Sunday nicht a terrific gale from the east- ward raged in the neighbourhood of Barrow. The full- rigged ship, Queen of Scots, Captain Nichols. from Calcutta to Barrow, with a cargo of jute for the Barrow Flax and Tute Company, was being towed into Barrow Harbour on Sunday midnight, when she struck on Peel Island in a. most dangerous position. Efforts were made to get her eff, but without avail. She will probably became a total wreck. In that event most of her cargo could be saved. A collision occurred in the Downs, on Monday, between the brig Kate, of Guernsey, and the steamer Castlemarne, of London. The former had her bows smashed, and was towed into Dover in a crippled state. A Norwegian brig, name unknown, passed up the Channel, on Sunday. with mainmast and yards carried away,. sails tern to shreds, and a distress -flag flying at half-mast. The gale AIM terribly severe in the Channel. A Lowestoft fishing boat, arrived at Plymouth. re- ports that she saw a large Lowestoft fishing sloop founder in the Channel on *unday. The crew of ni,e hands were drowned. NRNV Thax, TUF.131)4 Noow.—The snowfall has ceased. The North and East Rivers are blocked with ice between New York and Brooklyn. Business on to-day's Stock Market was again suspended, owing to the storm. ANOTHER LIFEBOAT DISASTER. Lloyd's agent at Niton, Isle of Wight,. telegraphed on 8 :turay :—The ship Siren* which went ashore on Mon- day at. Atherfield, lies rieht abreast of the coastguard station. The captain's wife and family were landed by the lifeboat at Atherflehl, where they still remain. The master and crew remained on bard the vessel, and the masts were still standing. An attempt was Mdde early on Tuesday morning by the Brixton life boat to reach the stranded vessel, but in the attempt the lifeboat capsized, and several of the crew of the ship and lifeboat were drowned. Twelve of the crew of the Sirenia have been landed at Niton. Angther lifeboat has gone off to the rescue of the others still on board. TWENTY-EIGHT LIVES LOST. 'According to statements of the two survivors from the City of COrinth, who were brought to Dover, on Saturday, 28 lives were lost when that vessel went down on .Friday. Miller, who was the chief mate, states that he has no recollection of how he was saved. He was in his bunk at the time of the collision. A large breach was made in the starboard side of the City of Corinth, and the vessel went down in two minutes. He heard shout- ing on deck, and ran un with no clothing but his shirt. He himself sank with the vessel, but rose to the surface, and swam to the Tasmania, climbing on deck by her chains. The rest of the crew went down in their bunks, with the exception of two or three, who were killed on deck by falling spars. The Tasmania herself was only kept up by her watertight compartments. GALLANT RESCUE BY LIGHTHOUSE-KEEPERS. Point of Ayr, the extreme north of the Isle of Man, was the scene of a heroic rescue of a shipwrecked crew on Sunday. The schooner Burns and Bessie, from Port' Glasgow to Duddon; with coal, was driven ashore dur- ing the strong eesterly gale, and immediately heeled sea- ward. William Wallace' and wife, John Christian, and Mary Blythe, daughter ef the head keeper, rushed from the lighthouse with rope,. and whilst the women stood on the shingle beach, which is precipitous, afyording treacherous footing, Wallace and Christian entered the water beyond their depth, rescuing three men from the bowsprit, and Captain Mae.Phearson from the rigging, after great and perilous exertions. The vessel became a total wreak, •

Itobert Barr, living. at Ballynahinch, County Down, was found dead in his bedroorn.on Sunday morning, with one of his arms and part of his head burned to a cinder. It appears that the man went to bed intoxicated, and that he set fire to the bed with a lighted candle. -

On Monday,; woman, named t,elia Lawlor, aged 23, was found in Wood-street, Dublin, in a dying state, bleeding from severe wounds in the face and neck, a shoemaker's knife lying beside her. She expired while being removed to Meath Hospital. Her features were Almost utnmognisable, through the number of wounds, an4seVeral important vessels were severed. It was as- certained that she had quarreNed with her husband at a friend's house, and on his being apprehended he ad- mitted having attacked her in a fit of passion. Mr. Justiee Gibson. in opening the Cork Assizes, on Monday, commented upon the:fact that the number of nffences committed in both ridings of the County during the past six months differed little from the correspond- ing period of. last year. He found, however, that boy- cotting was on a decline; and there WAS now less die. position on the part of attarieved persons to prosecute offenders. The returns presented evidence of improve- Tent, anti left no grounds for discouragement as regards

future peace. - On lilondayMr. Bourke and Mr. Harvey, resident re agi s- tratee, held a Crimes Act court at Bunber. Three were simtenced to nine months' imprisonment, and the others to six months' imprisonment; but they all appealed, and were released on bail. Considerable excitement prevails in rho district, order being kept by police and the Tenth Hussars. At Sixmilebridge, county Limerick, yesterday, Mr. Percy Snelling, delegate of the London Anti-Coercion Committee, was sentenced to one month and six weeks' imprisonment respectively, for having upon two ocm- sions advocated the plan of campaign. The magistrates said they would put a stop to .itinerant politicians com- ing over to Ireland from England. The prisoner exckiintei that there would be plenty of others to take his place.

! Ma. ChAmeEeLAlN's Re'renx. Mr. Chamberlain landed at Liverpool by tender from the Umbria on Sat- urday evening. He was received by the Mayor and Mr. Jessie Collings, M.P. Having driven in the Mayorl carriage to the North-Western Hotel, the right honour able gentleman received an address from the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce and other bodies, and in reply i ' said that the success of the negotiations n which he had, been engaged was largely due to his colleagues, Sir Lionel West and Sir Charles Tupper. The settlement was one the Commission believed to be fair and honourable. lie had the best reason to believe the result would be are ! proved by the Canadian Legislature. Nor could he : doubt that the American Senate would rise superior to party considerations in dealing with the matter. Mr. ' Chamberlain left Liverpool shortly after seven and ar- rived at New-street Station, Birmingham, shohly before nine. There was a large assembly of nearly all the lead- ing men of the town on the platform. Replying to ad- dresses, Mr. Chamberlain said that when he departed 1 four months ago on his mission, many thought it was a forlorn hope, but he was glad that so far as his reponsi- bility was concerned that mission had been brought to a successful issue. The treaty made involved no surren- der of rights, and was an honourable settlement. Mr. Chamberlain was enthusiastically cheered. NATIODULL RIFORAI UNION —The annual meeting of the National Reform Union was held on Wednesday after- noon in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester. Mr. R. Bar- low (ohairman of the Executive Committee) presiding. The report was read by Mr. A. G. Symonds and adopted. Mr. C. E. Schwann, M.P. (preoident of the Union) and Mr. J.. T. Brunner, M.P., addressed the meeting on the , various branches of work with which the Union lad been concerned during the year. Mr. Selpvann was of opinion that the defeat of Mr. Gladstone's measures had not been without its good results, inasmuch as ,it had given , the Irish and English people a better opportunity of knowing each other. Mr. Brunner advised the Irish members to , rise lies violent language than was sometimes the case- Mr. Cox, M.P., said the Irish cause of legislative hide • pendence would continue in the forefront of English politics. He denied that the Irish wanted separation: ,on the contrary, they desired a closer and more real union. Mr. C. E. Schwalnn was elected president of the Union, afid the other officers were appointed. In the evening the Union entertained several members of Par- liament who have been imprisoned under the Crimes Act • at a hatquet in the Free Trade Hall. AbOut 500 sat down to dinner, over which Mr. C. E. Schwalm, M.P., presided, and afterwards the galleries were crowded with • delegates froit various towns: Speechea were delivered by the Chairman, Mr. William O'Brien, Mr. Wilfrid . Bllint, Mr. T. D. Sullivan, the Hon. J. Stansfel, and the Earl of Cavan. Tho proceedings throughout were higbsY enthusiastic.

Mr. LABOUCHERE'S motion in the House of Commons, the other evening :—" That, in the Opinion of this House, it is contrary to the true Principles of representative Government, and in- jurious to their efficiency, that any person should , be a member of one House of the Legislature by right of birth, and it is therefore desirable to put an end to any such existing rights" was supported by no less than 162 members, the Government raaiority being reduced on this occasion to 61. The fact is a significant one; for it may be taken as an intimation to the members of the UPper House that their feeble and peddling at- tempts at reforming themselves will be of no avail. Lord HARTINGTON was almost angry to find . that the motion was supported by Mr. JOHN MORLEY as the leader of the Liberals in ' the absence of Mr. GLADSTONE. He reminded the souse that this was a distinct change of attitude from that taken up by Mr. GLADSTONE two years agn. This, in its turn, brought up Sir WILLIAM • 11AECOLTRT who, amisl the cheers of the Opposi- tion, described Lord lIARTINGTON as a politician whoa° "progress was always backward." This epigram will be likely to stick to the member for Rossendale ; it hits him off to a nicety. The least satisfactory element in the debate,, from a Liberal point of view, was to observe a member • like Mr. RATHBONE intervening with an amend- Ment to the effect that it was desirable that the - }louse of Lords should not rest solely on right of birth, as if the hereditary principle were in some degree admissable. Surely'if a change has to be naade--if there is to be a second House of Legis- lature—it must be put on a basis that will be likely to be workable and permanent. The here- ditary principle is bad because it is found to ob- tain no support either from nature or experience. Given any number of wise and goOd men, be they Peers or peasants, it is certain that there will be a ' percentage of fools and knaves amongst their des- cendants. It is to the interest of the community that these classes should be weeded out, or that 'the 9 should find their way to the bottom, where they will be least harmful. But the House of :Lords disregards the law of the survival of the fit- -144 • the born lord is a born legislator, although Ile May be a born fool; and it thus happens that the Upper House is the incarnation of all that is foolish and mischievous in legis- lation. Granted that the peers are no \verse than so many tinkers or tailors would be tinder similar circumstances, the question is— Why should the evil be allowed to exist when there a possibility of getting rid of it? We do not insist on hereditary musicians, or artists, °eon- gineers ; and why should we have hereditary legis- lators.? If the principle was worth anytling, where could it be more fittingly applied than in the House °I Commons—which accomplishes nine-tenths of the law-making of the country? But let Mr. ItarnnoNE, or any other Liberal with a loose grip " of his creed, propose to introduce the principle of hereditary wisdom into that House, and he will f Lnd that Tories even will laugh at him for his _ . . .

The House of Lords is an old and bad survival of feudalism, and like other survivals—such as that of the law of primogeniture—it will die hard. But it will die; it is decrepit and powerless except as a Stumbling-block; and it is the dUty of Liberals to see to it, when it is finally dealt with, that nothing is set up in its place which favours in the remotest degree irresponsibility and the hereditary Principle. Lord SALISBURY seemed to think he Was saying a significant thing two or three years ago when he observed—" If the House of Lords is to be the mere echo of the will of the House of Commons, I for one say the sooner the House of Lords is abolished the better." Unfortunately for his lordship, the people echo his sentiment in a Way he little anticipated. The House of Commons is elected to represent the will of the nation, and as the House of Lords takes upon itself to oppose the will of the nation, it is a matter of course to say the sooner the House of Lords is abolished the better. Lord SAusarrav would doubtless Plead that the peers would save the peo- ple from themselves. But they do not 'stand in neql of such salvation. They require rather to be saved from those out-door and whole- sale paupers—the members of the House of Lords; the 4, Noblesse Oblige who declaim against paid embers, and pay themselves in one form or another an average of £B2O each per year; the considerate gentlemen who have made the railway companies pay £50,000,000 more for their land 'than it was worth; the kindly fellows who have

taken to themselves 16,000,000 acres of the best land ' of the country, and who, in return for the booty ,• they have secured, have shifted the burden of taxation from tbeirown shoulders to the shoulders of the workers, helping meanwhile to run up d• national Debt of eight hundred millions I ipur here- ditary legislators are, of course, backed up by the bench of bishops ; for, as Sir JOHN BENNEtT aptly remarks, when anything particularly bad was to ,1;!? done—" The Church was to Sanctify the deed, . and the two together were to share the plunder." There was a time when the Barons were useful, "when they made a stand against the tyranny of kings, and laid the foundation of the liberties of the people. But their day of usefulness is past; they have themselves become tyrannical ; they now stand between the people and good gov- ernment ; they are an anachronism, an absurdity, and 40 far as legislation is concerned, the nation Would be the gainer if they were reforme'd out of existlnce. •

I WE publish in another column a letter from San Fransisco written by Mr. H. WHITHAM, who deals with the Fair Trade question from an American point of view, and furnishes facts and figures which are calculated to startle those on this side of the Atlantic who have cherished the delusion that Pro- tection is beneficial to the people of the United States. Mr. WHITHAM'S statements areacuriously confirmed by the Consular Report upon the Trade and Commerce of Texas wllich has just been issued by our own Foreign Office. Speaking of the costs of living in Texas, Consul LYALI: says the expenses of a working-man with a wife and six children would be not less than £lBO per year, of which money one-third goes into the pockets of the Pro- tected manufacturers. The average taxation on "actual necessities" is close on 50 per cent., and the tariff makes everything so dear that the working classes "cannot afford to buy decent clothing, and are almoit to a man ragged and meanly dressed." Can we wonder, in view of his special experience, that Consul LYALL speaks of the ' Protective system as the greatest enemy of the workmen of Texas? Lord SALISBURY has of codi•se read this report, and it is not unlikely that it had ' something to do with the reply which he gave the Protectionists, in the House of Lords, on Monday evening. Dealing with the motion of Earl DELA- WARR, in which, while referring to agricultural de- pre,ssion, he sought to insert the thin end of the Fair Trade wedge, the PRIME MINISTER said With regard to the suggested remedy of Protection, the noble marquis had simply to say that the coun- try had adopted the oppOsite system, after a contro- versy unexampled in its length, in its earnestness, and in the decision with which the ultimate issue was arrived at. If they were to undertake the re- examination of that question it must not be done incidentally, by insinuations, allusions, and hints. If the noble earl really wished this country to re- trace its steps in respect of Free Trade, he must bring forward a definite motion, state the arguments in its favour, and let them besdiscussed with a care suited to the gravity of the subject. Then he (Lord Salisbury) would be quite prepared to set forth at length the reasons which utterly disabled him from agreeing, with any such proposal. In his belief the economical arguments against Free Trade were very strong; but they were not the only ones to be' dealt with. It was apparent from the speech of Sir Robert Peel when he proposed Free Trade that'the political argument weighed even more heavily than the economical with him. The political argument had lost none of its force; and the noble marquis utterly disbelieved that it vvfo in anybody's power to introduce Protection. If, however, that were done it would create among theclasses of this coun- try a state of division differing very little from civil war. For these reasons, he could not accept the remedy of Protection. .They must look instead to the ordinary working of the economic laws, to a re- turn to more healthy conditions which in the past had always followed periods of depression, and to the combined working crf the industry and enter- prise of the nation which had lost in no degree those qualities that had led it to its high position. We are not in accord with Lord SALISBURY when he expresses the opinion that the economical argu- ments against Free Trade are very strong; but we agree with him in saying Slat it is not in any- body's power to introduce Proteition. If his lord- 'ship is not consistent in his reasoning, he is at least consistent in declaring that Fair Trade does not come within the region of practical politics. It is to be hoped the Fair Traders will take the hint and ceast their fooling.

AN inquiry at Pendleton, or 'Monday, into the circumstances of the death of a factory lad named SEDDON brought to light an extraordinary amount of overwork on the part of the boy, nothwithstand- lug the provisions of the Factory Acts. It seems that SEDDON, who was fifteen years of age, had been struck behind the left ear by his Sunday School teacher for unruly conduct. Inflammation of the brain ensued, and the lad died on Saturday last. The medical evidence showed that SEDDON was suffering from tubercular disease of the lungs and was, besides, so emaciated that he was predis- posed to inflammatipn of the brain. It transpired that the lad had been terribly overworked. Owing to his father being ill, he had taken iis place as "knocker-up," getting up to execute his task at four o'clock in the morning, and then going to the factory at six o'clock. After finishing his day's toil in the mill, he was in the habit of selling even- ing papers. Can it be *ondered at that the little fellow was emaciated? At a time of life when he required light work and plenty of sleep, he was called upon to do double duty. What a cruelty to turn a lad out at four o'clock in the morning during such weather as we have had, with the prospect before him of having no real break in his toil till seven o'clock in the evening! One juror remarked that the victim of this white slavery had been over- worked in order that his parents might put money in the savings bank. If this was so, the mother deserved a censure even more severe than that which she received from the coroner at the direc- tion of the jury. It seems that'the parents were warned twelve months; since by the proprietors of the mill that the lad was being overtaxed, but no notice was taken of the warning. A verdict of "death from natural causes" is a mockery in such a case. It might just as well be said that natural causes were in operation if the lad had been starved to death. Let parents see to it that they give their children a fair chance—that they do not stunt body and soul eitter to put money in the savings bank or anywhere else. We cannot but express our surprise that the Sunday school teacher was not told that he has himself a great deal to learn if he does not know better than to punish a scholar by striking him behind the ear. Unruly conduct is not to be amended by brutality of this kind, which, when it does not result in inflamma- tion of the brain, may cause permanent injury to a most delicate organ. Altogether the report ef the proceedings at this coroner's inquest is one of the saddest things we have read for a long time.,

WARRINGTON INCOME-TAX COMMISSIONERS.—In the House of Commons on Tuesday, Mr. Caleb Wright asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether any portion of the £2OO in the iteni of £3,650 mentioned in the estimates of the Inland Re- venue Department had been incurred by the War- rington Commissioners of Income-tax in providing an additional place- in the Leigh Parliamentary' Division; if not, would a placebo provided in Leigh Division, where there is a population of 54,000 with- i in a radius of three and a NW miles from Leigh mar- ket-place and whether all appeals at present had to be beard at Newton, a distance of ten miles, or at _Warrington, a distance of fourteen Miles. Mr. W. L. Jackson said Leigh was one of the places at which the expense could be defrayed under the item re- ferred to. It was the duty of the district commis- sioners to find places in their division where appeals could most conveniently be heard, and her Majesty's Government would not be justified in dictating to the district commissioners in such matters. Ile understood, however, that the Warrington Commis- sioners decided at their last meeting to holu the meeting at Leigh, under the new assessment in which schedules A and B were made, which woul4 be the case next year.
