Sr. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES. On Tuesday, the Bishop of Liverpool licensed the Rev. George Antonius Le Bert to the perpetual curacy of the church and parish of St. Ambrose! Widnes. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—Major Hazlehurst yesterday sentenced Henry Penketh 'Mather, an elderly man, to seven days' hard labour for being drunk in Bridge-street on the previous day. Police-constable Sutherland proved the case. RUNCORN STARR-BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.—An ape propriation in connection with the first Runcorn society took place at the office in Bridge-street, ozi Monday last. M. J. Gayton, niece of Mr. D. Bisbrown, of Church-street, was the lucky member, and she is entitled to the loan of £lOO for 14 years free of interest. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF ROPE, WIDNES.—A 'public meeting in connection with this society was held in Hutchinson-street Chapel, on Wednesday evening. , There was a good attendance, and Mr. J. H. Lee occu- pied the chair. The customary entertainment of songs, recitations, &c., was given by the children. THE VVgsT LANCASHIRE CUP TIE.—In the semi-final tie for this cup the Widnes team meet Litherland to-day (Saturday.) The match will be played at St. Helens, and the following, team will represent Widnes :—Full back, S. Bingham ; three-quarter backs, E. Farrell, J. Parkin- son, and F. Plumpton ; half-backs, R. Barker and J. Wilkinson ; forwards W. Kiddie, T. Hughes, J, Bing- ham, J. Hardman, J. 'Gandy, T. Pennington, G. Woods, W Barber, and J. H. Smith. MASQUERADE BALL AT WIDNES.—What was described as the " Tradesmen's " Masquerade Ball was held in the Baths Assembly-room on Tuesday evening. The scene was a very gay one. The room was profusely decorated with pictures, &c., and was brilliantly lighted by the limelight, whilst the costumes worn by the forty couple who were present were of the most bright and varied description. Mephistopheles (Mr. J. G. Kiddie) was the M.C. Mr. C. Powell's band supplied the music. The balcony was crowded with spectators. A SAILOR'S AMUSEMENT AT RUNCORN.—On Wednesday a seamen, named George Ennis, was brought before Mr. Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, to answer a charge of being drunk in Regent-street early that morning. A constable found the man, who was very drunk, knock- ing at the doors in Regent-street. He said he was want- ing a night'eflodgings, and he was accommodated with a cell at the Police Station. He was in possession of a, money order for £lO, and had also us in his pocket.— Mr. Brundrit said it was fortunate for him thepolice took care of him. It was a pity he could not amuse himself in a better manner than getting • drunk. A fine of 2s 6d and costs was imposed. WIDNE,S SCHOOL BOARD.—Mr. G. H. Denby, the clerk, on Thursday, summoned the following persons before the magistrates for breaches of the Education Act : James Murphy, 7, Peel-street; J. P. Davies 73, Beau- mont-et. ; John'Clegg, James-street, West liaqk ; Henry Mizen, 10. Beaumont-Street; William Carter, 19, Pear- , street ; Peter McLochlin, 18, Catherine-street • Thos. McAuley, 12, Caroline-street; Maurice Leary, 38, Catherine-street': Charles McKenna (two cases). 14, Elizabeth-street; James Handy, Oxfetd-street • James Welt, 2, Lee-street ; and Michael McPartland, Pleas-' Ant-street. The usual fine of 58 was imposed in each case. ROBBERY WITH VIOLENCE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, James Daniels, a young man, was charged with stealing two shawLs, valued at 16s, from the person of Mary McGuire, aged 17, who resides in Margaret-street. On Saturday night the girl was walking across Lugsdale Bridge„when she met the pri- soner; who seized hold of her, and putting his arm round her neck kissed her. She screamed, and he released her, but as ,the was making her escape the prisoner tore from her shoulders two shawls that she was wearing. She gave information to the police, and from the des- cription given of the robber, P.C. Thonlpson at once went to the house where the prisoner lodged. The girl at once recogildged her assailant, The prisoner was re- manded for a week. THREATENING A EU.= AT RuNcoux.—At Runcorn Petty Session on Monday, Mary Clark was eunimoned for neing threatening language towards Sarah Eyres. ' The comialainanfeeid the defendant was her sister, and they lived near each other in Zion piece. About half- past six o'clock on Tuesday morning the defendant kicked at the door of her house and shouted "Are you getting up?" She returned no answer, and the defendant then said that if she did not bring back a table and bed that she had lent to her she would run a knife thronah hJ heart, She tIIM ;Mashed a winclsw, and thITTO into the house a bncketful of water. in reply to the Bench, the complainant said she was not now afraid of the defend- ant, and the summons was dismissed, Mr. Brundrit remarking that it was a pity two sisters could s not agree'. TEMPERANCE CAMPAIGN AT RUNCOML—Under the aus- pices of the Church Temperance Society a vigorous cam- paign has been conducted in Runcorn during the past week. Meetings have been held in schoolrooms in various parts of the town on each evening, and the at- tendance of the public has been gratifying to the pro- moters. Each day at noon a meeting has heed held at one or other of the works in the neighbourhood, and also at the docks, and working-men have attended in large numbers. The chief of the campaign is Mr. T. Miller, of Chester. who has delivered a stirring and convincing ad- dress on each occasion, and many have been induced to sign the pledge. The Vicar, the Revs. A. Maitland Wood, ALA., has taken an active and earnest interest in the work, and it is through his instrumentality that the campaign was undertaken. TEARS AvAILIID Ilen NOT.—Mary Ann Moran, an eld- erly woman was brought before the Runcorn magis- trates, on woman, a charge of stealing a pair of boots from the shop of Andrew McQuinn, shoemaker, Top Locke. It appeared that on Saturday, the 3rd inst., In- , specter Millington saw the prisoner and another woman acting in a suspicious manner In Bridge-street. Re watched them, and followed them into Mersey-streets where he found the pair of boots produced concealed under her shawl. She admitted that she had stolen the boots from a shop near the canal side.—Andrew Mc- , Quiinn identified the boots, which were an odd pair.--The prisoner said that if it had not been for drink she would not have stolen the boots. She hoped the magistrates would 'give her "her time" that day. She pleaded hard not to be consmitted for trial, and cried bitterly-. She was, however, committed to the Quarter Sessiens for trial, as she was a very old offender. PROTECTING THE PUBLICANS AT RUNCORN.--,John Mc- Comb, a Young man, Who earned his living as a pedlar,' was charged with having, on the 12th July, unlawfully assaulted David Snell, landlord of the Blue isall Inn, Fryer-street. The prosecutor said for three or our days together the prisoner created a great disturbance in his house, until at last he had to fasten up the premises in order to keep him out. On the 12th July he tent for a Iconstable, and when he saw the officer corning the pri- soner kicked the prosecutor on the leg. a Afterwards, , whilst the prosecutor was away taking oda summons, the prisoner again went to the houses and attempted to kick his wife. He struck with such force that when his foot missed itsaim, he fell upon his back.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and Mr. Brundrit said such men as he could not be allowed to do as they thought proper. When' a man tried to keep his public-house respectable, the Bench would protect him, and the prisoner was fined 40s and costs, 8s 6d, or in default a month.—Superin- tendent Hollingworth applied that the pedlar's certificate held by the prisoner should be cancelled, but the magis- trates, after due consideration, decided to give the pri- soner another chance.—The prisoner went to gaol. ! WATCH ROBBERY AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. Thinnis, at Widhes Police Court, on Monday, Rebert Beckett. a young man from Sheffield, was charged with stealing a silver lever watch, worth £7 10s, the property of James Pilkington. it appeared that the men had lodged at the I "Manchester House," in Wellington, and had occupied thesame bedroom. On the night of the 7th inst Ming- , ton placed the swatch in his box, and next day the land- ' lady, Mrs Gill, hearing a noise in the bedroom, went to ascertain the cause. The prisoner, who wa.s in the room, , said he was ovily looking after his knife,-and after bor- rowing is from her he left the 'house to look for work at the new theatre. Mrs Gill afterwards discovered that Pilkington's hex had been opened and the watch stolen. Information was, given to the police -and P.C. Worsfold on the 9th best., travellorto Sheffield, and arrested the prisoner as he was leaving Victoria Station. He ascer- tained that the prisoner had left the watch at Godley Junction in Hereof his fare, and he Afterwards received it from the parcels clerk at Sheffield. •The prisoner said he was anxious to return to Sheffield as he could not get work in Widnes, and he had taken the watch to pay his railway fare. Ife intended to return it. The prisoner was committed to the quarter sessions for trial. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Office, on Wednesday, Mr. W. Littler presided, and there were present :—/ilecsra J. Handley, J.P., ii. Coleburn, W. Whittaker, and W. F. Salkeld (Secretary). The secretary reparted that the interments for the eleven months ending February 25th, amounted to 330, an increase of 30 on the, corresponding period last year. The fees received during the same pelied amounted to £344 13s. 10d., an increase of £46 Ills. Bd. on the corresponding period last year. The Finance Committee reported that they had examined the month's cash account. The receipts amounted to £33 55., and after paying wages £2l 16s. was paid into bank. Accounts amounting to £23 3s. sd. were recom- mended for payment; also interest on loans .arnountiag to £5B Ws. 2d. The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Whittaker.—Com- plaints having been ,made on several occasions of James Wright, the sexton, filling graves in the preseac,e of the friends and relatives of the deceased, it was unanimously resolved that the secretary should inform the sexton that he must discontinue this objectional practice, or he would be dismissed from the service of the Board. It was resolved to serke a notice upon the overseers asking them to call a meeting of ratepayers for the purpose of appointing two Orsons to audit the accounts of. the Beard to the 25th March, and to fix other meetings with regard to the same. Mr. Handley said the Finance Committee, in looking over the banking actount, Over One Thousand Testimonials have been received from that afternoon, found that there would be sufficient Medical Men for `, Coleman's* Liebig's Extract of Meat and moneyin hand to meet current expenses for the next six Malt Wine 's which is the finest Tonic in the world. Sold in months. The committee, therefore, only purposed to 2/9 and 4/6 bottles by all, Chemists, Wine Merchants, and make a call upon the overseers for the usual instalment at the principal Stores. Write for , price list to the Sole Manufacturers, Coleman and CO:, Norwich, who pay -ear_ of £6O for the Sinking Fund Account, to be paid in riage on any quantity to any part of the United Kingdom.— June. The members expressed pleasure at this satisfac- Ay. tory state of the finances.

The dinner to Warrinton cabmen has been a sw•cess. There is great satisfaction in preparing a dinner in knowing that it will be eaten. What a ready respond there was to "the whip!" "Full inside" was the order of the evening ; and quite early on there wasn't "a growler" to be found.

Mr. Stuart Wortley has been presenting a peti- tion to the House of Commons in favour of a close time for hares. He said it was signed by a num- ber of farmers, and by working-men. They must be curious farmers who want to increase hares which reduce crops. The working-mOn who take so much interest in hares are probably poachers.

If the "Morning Post • is to be regarded as an authority, the new Local Government Bill will go the full length Of the principle of "one man one vote," and will make no provision for ex-officio members. Otherwise, it does not seem that any radical change will be made. But we shall see what we shall see on Tuesday; for the bill is to be introduced on Mondu next, not Thursday, as was' understood last week.

A labourer named Greenwood, in applying for an administration order at the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, stated that he was married, had eight children, and eighteen shillings a week. No wonder he is in debt. Will the time ever come when working-men will direct their attention to the advantage of reversing these conditions—that is, having a large wage and a small family? It is a difficult problem, but surely it is not beyond solution.

Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., has a brother, Mr. W. R. Bradlaugh. He is connected with the London Evangelisation Society, and has been conducting a series of mission services in the Methodist Free Church, Russell-street, Liverpool. He is twelve years younger than the Secularist lecturer; like, and yet how unlike; for, as Waugh has it in " Eawr Folk"— When t'one's bin strivin' o' he con To awter wicked men, Then t'other mays some marlocks an Convarts 'em o'er again.

The presentation to Mr. atid Mrs. Monks is a pleasant feature in these days of hard 'driving be- tween employer and employed. One of the work- men who spoke at the Drill Hall, on Saturday, put the whole matter in a nutshell when he said Mr. Monks had shown respect for his workmen, and now they had joined to show respect for him. The portrait of Mr. Monks by Mr. Charles is a striking likeness; it is a credit to this rising artist. But is it not too high in colour ? Mr. Monks does not usually look as if he might have been having "a drop too much."

The Emperor Frederick has begun well. The proclamation to his people, and the letter to Prince Bismarck, show that he has at heart the welfare of the nation, and that, in his judgment, the greatest of German interests is peace. What could be finer than the last sentence in the letter to the Chancellor Regardless of the lustre of deeds that have 0p).7 a transient glory, I shall be eatisfied if in the Pules to come it will be said of my reign that it was beneficial to ray pecple, useful to my country, and a blessing to my realm." May he, too, live to be ninety and one!

The late Emperor of Germany seems to have made " &good end on't." He had his wits she'd him to the last, judging .from the following inci- dent, which is thus officially narrated :—" Up to his last hours the Emperor conversed freely, and even frequently tried to express himself jocosely, as of old. When, for example, he was asked if a glass of champagne was to his liking, he replied, Well, yes, but there have been times when it has tasted better." The quiet humour of this remark suggests a story which is told of Hood's last illness. Some friend recommended him to try an orange. "No," Hood said, "I will not try an orange—l might roll off." a

The attitude of the 'English Church on the tithes question is not unlike that of the French Church as described by Carlyle in his History of the French Revolution. He says—" Our church stands haltered, dumb, like a dumb ox; lowing only for provender (of tithes) ; content if it can have that; or dumbly, dully expecting its further doom." Again, when the Archbishop of Aix spoke of tithe as that free-will offering Of the piety of Christians," the Duke la Rouchefoucault drily said—" It is a free-will offering on which there are i now forty thousand law suits n this realm:' We are not without tithe disputes to-day, for history repeats itself. -

It is not often that a Tory Government is de- feated in the House of Lords; but this phenome- non occurred on Tuesday. There seems to he some doubt as to whether, in the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill, opportunity is not affiorded, English railway companies to give undue preference to foreign traders; so Loot-Jersey moved an amendment to absolutely prohibit un- due ;Reference. This the Government resisted, on the ground that the law already put its foot on undue preference. Lord Salisbury sought to dis- pose of the amendment in a very summary fashion, but, on a division, it was carried, the Govern- ment, for once, finding themselves in a minority of six.

In the House of Commons, on Tuesday, the Home Secretary, replying to Mr. Brad laugh, said his attention had been called ti; the fact that the Church Conservative Club proposed torsise money by lottery to reduce the debt on the club premi- ses, and that the drawing was announced to take Owe on the 19th April—Primrose Day. It ap- peared from the notice issued by the club that tie primes included cigars. He had called the atten- tion of the Public Prosecutor and of the Board of Inland Revenue to the matter. It is interesting to see how these Constitutionalists propose to 4' honour" the late Lord Beaconsfield by breaking the law. Perhaps it is to be regarded as further evidence that, as his lordship once said, the Tory party is an organised hypocrisy?

Mr. W. H. Smith was caught tripping in the House of Commons, on Tuesday. In answer to a question put by Mr. A. O'Connor, be said it was a well understood rule in the Ireland Re.venue ser- vice that civil service officers were bound to abstain from taking part in plitical matters. 'Questioned further, as to why General Sankey, Chief Com- missioner of Works • Mr. Roberts, Junior Com- missioner; and Mr. Works; Secretary to the Board of Works, were permitted to take part in the Dub- lin welcome to Lord Hartington, Mr. Smith said these gentlemen did attend the meeting, but it was 'in their private capacity." What a shuffle Henceforth Civil Service officers may break the yule every night "in their private capacity " ; but woe unto them if their venture "in their private capacity" to attend a Liberal demonstration.

The letter of Mr. Burt, M.P., to the Northum- berland miners, whom he represents, is a clear and dignified statement of his position. They are fortunate in having such a leader, and ought to make further sacrifice to keep him in the House. Touching the sug-gestion that a labour representa- tive should hold aloof as to general questions, he remarks :—" It is saying in the most practical way that the worker is something loss than a man and a citizen; it is asserting that he is a mere wealth- orodncing tool, that he should separate himself from humanity, ftom great questions of justice between individuals and between one nation and another, and should concentrate all his energies upon mtttters that affect him as a manual labourer. Our aim should be to unite men, not to divide them to break down, and .not to intensify and accentuate class distinction."

UETHRSDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RDNOORN.— The Rev. R. G. Hughes, of Widnes, on Wednesday gave a lecture on "Dramatic power" to the members of this society. There was a good attendance, and the Rev. J. D. Thomas presided. In the course of his remarks Mr. Hughes recited portions of Shakespere's works. DAMAGE TO STREET LAMPS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Jades Weir, of Warring- ton-road, was summoned by the Lool Nard for having wilfully broken a street lamp.—Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the Local Board, said that during the last six months there had been 72 lamps broken, but the Board had failed toSrace the offenders, but in this case a boy named Chadwick, o 26, Charles-street, who had been in the employment of the Local Board, had seen the damage slow by the defendant throwing a stone.—The Bench in- flicted a fine of fis and costs, altogether 14s .6d. VIOLEVT W/DNES WOMAN.—At Widnes Court, on Tuea- day. Catherine Lynch, a middle-aged woman, of Mar- garet-street, was charged with having caused grievious bodily harm to Rose Kelly, of Edmund-street. On Friday night last the women were fighting together in the street, when the prisoner got Kelly's finger in her mouth aid almost bit the end off. The doctor considered the wound inflicted of so serious a nature that he oldered the woman to the Hospital.—ln her defence, the prisoner produced a bunch of hair, which she allege& that Lynch had pulled from her head. She said she had simply acted in self-defence The magistrates remanded the prisoner for a week in order to see how the wound pro- gressed. THE DEATH or THE EMPEROR OF GERMANY.— In the several churches inEuncorn and Widnes on Sunday the preachers referred to the momentous event of. the death .of the Emperor of Germany. His wonderful career was sketched, and appropriate lessons deduced from his fife. . IMPUDENT THEFT BY BOYS AT WIDNES.—Alfred Williams; aged 14, and John Walsb, aged 10, were brought before the Widnes magistrates on Tuesday with stealina V. 3s Gd from the shop of Mrs. Ham- lin, grocer, Major Cross-street. At half-past three on Monday afternoou the money was safe in a box under the counter.. At that time the prisoners were at the shop window, and Mrs. Hamlin told them they were there for no good purpose, and sent them away. She then went into the kitchen, and on re- turning found the box on the door mat, but the money had gone. Later P.C. Holbrook apprehended 1 the prisoners, who admitted their . guilt, gad took ' him to some vacant land near St. Paul's Church, where he found .E 1 188 2d hidden. The boys said they had spent the remainder of the money in whis- key, pipes, tobacco, scones, and also on an auto- matic machine at the railway station. The boys also admitted having stolen 5s from the same shop on the Thursday previous. Each prisoner was fined Ds.

AN IstretovolcatsT AT RUNCORN.—A much-needed improvement his been made in the street running alongside Ferry-lane, and in front of houses named "Mersey-view." It will be remembeted that several serious accidents have occurred at this spot, to per- sons who, in the dark, had fallen from the street into the lane, a distance of about 12 feet. A sub- stantial wooden rail has now been erected, and it is t 0 be hoped will prove a protection against acci- dents in the future. CO-OPERATION AT WlDNEl3.—Under the auspices of the Runcorn Co-operative Society a lecture on the principles of Co-operation was given in Widnes Baths Assembly-room, last evening, by Mr. William Bates, of the Wholesale Co-operative Society, Man- chester. There was a fair attendance of the public. Dr. Hurter occupied the chair, and he was sup- ported on the platform by the directors of the local society. In introducing the lecturer, Dr. Hurter remarked that God did not help the careless man. God helped them that helped themselves, and Mr. Bate had come to teach them how to help them- selves to cheap provisions, clothing, boots, and the rest of the many things they daily needed; and also how to lay by for a rainy day. Mr. Upton, secretary of the society, stated that the trade of the society in 1886 'amounted to £64,804 193 Id, and in 1887 to £77,050 3s 4d, an increase in twelve months of £12,245 4s 3d. Then as to capital the members had invested in the society no less' than £27,494 5s Bd, an increase over the year of 1886 of £3,709 13s sd. Mr. Bates atterwards delivered

his lecture. The proceedings were enlivened .by glees by the Good Templar choir, and recitations. The Soap Work. Brass Band also gave a selection. STORK AND SHIPWRECIC—The coasting steamer Galgorm Castle, which left Garston on Monday with a cargo of coal for Sligo,was wrecked near Drummore during the snowstorm of Tuesday night,and 5 of her crew of seven men were drowned. The snowstorm of Tuesday night and on Wednesday ' morning ap- pears to have extended over the greater part of the country. It was accompanied by a gale of wind which has caused deep drifts in some parts. In the north of Scotland the storm continued all through Wednesday. A Fileshire farmer named Forfor got lost in the snow on Tuesday night, and perished ot cold. _ _ _

• TERRIBLE FALL.—Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the St. Helens Town Hall, go Satur- day, touching the death of William Moore, 26, Wright-street, 'Eccieston, who died in the Provi- dence Hospital, on the previous Thursday. It ap- peared that the deceased was a bricklayers !labourer in the employ of Mr. James Penketh, con- tractor. He and some other men were on Wednes- day engaged in taking down some old spouts from some cottages at Blackbrook, and a portion knocked him Off, a ladder, upon which he was standing, t 14 feet from the ground. He alighted on some rail- ings which penetrated his abdomen and ruptured .his bowels. He was removed to the hospital where he was attended by Dr. Donnellan. The jury re- turned &verdict of accidental death. WARRINGTON AND WIGAN. —The "Wigan Ex- aminer," commenting on the proposal to erect an hospital for infectious diseases at Wigan, says:— " The minutes of the Sanitary Committee were I unanimously passed, and thus the Council are com- mitted'to the erection of an infectious hospital at a cost of .£7,000. The sub-cominittee who visited the sanitoriums at Bolton and Warrington, *recommend for Wigan a building similar to the one at Warring- ton, both in arrangement and accommodation,. and ! they think it may be provided for the sum of £7,000. The Borough Surveyor has been instructed to pcepare the necessary plans and drawings. Mr. Alderman J. Smith paid a well deserved tribute to the efficiency of. such institutions when he re- ! marked that he had sent a child of his own to the , Warrington sanitorinin, and had found the atten-' lion given to it everything that could be desired. When we have the hospital in full swing, and the enipulsoryanotifiCaition of infectious diseases in operatloll' we may' with certainty look for an hn- provement in the public health, which will far more than compensate for the expense." A CLERICAL SCANDAL.—A Farnworth correspon- -o.eat is informed that a commission, consisting of ! the Archdeacon of Warrington, the Rector of Liver- pool, the Rev. Canon Warr, Messrs. John Brancker, and Robert Gladstone, has been appointed to inves- tigate several 'acts of intemperance which have been charged against the Rev. G. Bond, vicar of Farm- worth, and that the preliminary Meetin,g will be held on the 21st instant. Mr. Bond is a graduate of Lincoln College, Oxford, where, he took his degrees, B.A. in 1842, and :M.A. in 1857. He was ordained deacon in 1853 and priest 1854 by the late Bishop of Ripon. Previous to his preferment to the vicarage of Farnworth in 1881, Mr. Bond held the following appointments in succession: Curate, St. John, Bowling, Bradford, 1853 'to 1856; St. Matthew, Ipswich, 1856 to 1861; Fakenham, Nor- folk, 1861 to 1862; Rector of Baylield, Norfolk, 1862; Reetor of Sutton, 1862 to'lBBl. The parish of Pam- worth contains a gross population of about 6,000, and the church has accommodation for 1,060. The living, which is valued at .f.. 364 with residence, is ,in the gift of the Vicar of Prescot. Mr. Bond was this week wanted on a writ, but he was not to be found, and it is suggested 'that he has gone from the neighbourhood.

-- YOUNG SHOPBREAKERS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. W. Deacon, Martin Kelly, Win. Fallow, and Anthony Burke, boys, were charged with hav- ing, on Saturday night, burglariously entered the shop of Peter M'Kinley, smallware dealer, Ann- street West, and stolen a Cash box, a purse, lead pencils, one dozen boxes of dominoes, a black lead brush, and other articles, altogether of the value of 255. Margaret Kelly, mother of the prisemer of that name, was charged with receiving the articles, knowing them to have been stolen. The shop was securely locked up on Saturday. On Monday morn- ing Miss 111•Kinley found that the back door had been broken to pieces and the ceiling of the back kitchen looked as through it. The boys Kelly and Burke were con- tinually annoying her. Mrs. Kelly on Monday offered one of the stolen rings in pledge at the shop of Mr. Neil, and she was placed in the custody of F.O. Porter. who afterwards found a number of the missing articles at her house, and another part he discovered in an empty house in Penn-street that the boys bad pointed out. The prisoners were com- mitted to take their trial at the next Quarter -Ses- sions, bail being refused. SUDDEN DEATH OF A NAVVY AT RUNCORN.— Mr. J. E. INorsley, the coroner, yestatly held an inquest at the Burial Board Office, Runcorn, Ott he I body of ,TOLn Carter, a navvy, aged about 45 vtan, w hi, died suddenly on Thursday morning. It ap- peared that the man had been employed on the Ship Canal for three days, and for two days and nights had lodged with Mrs. Higgins, of Regent- street. During this time he had been unwell, and had consulted a doctor. On Thursday morning" Sergeant Woolley found the man leaning against the old pump in Mersey-street. He was then in a dying state, and although the man evinced great reluctance to go back to his lodgings, the sergeant ' took him there. He also had Dr. McDougall quickly in attendance, but on the arrival of that gentleman life was extinct. Dr.-McDougall, who had made a post-mortem examination, deposed that one of the - lungs of the decease 4 was entirely gone, and he had also enlargement of the heart. These facts would account for the death. Mrs. Higgins wag called, and stated that, although the deceased had not paid for his lodgings, he had had no lack of good food, and she had not turned him out.—A verdict of natural causes was returned, and Mrs. Higgins was advised to look better after her lodgers. div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOXRD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOXRD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall,' on Tuesday. Mr. F. .11. Gossage presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley, D. Wright, R. Cook. F. byes, J. Taylor, J. Houghton. S. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr /engineer), T. Higginson (surveyor), and J. Dickson (nuisance inspector). CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION. .

Mr. William Cooper, of Springfield, wrote that owing to the basement of his residence having been flooded by surface water in November, 1886, great damage was done to his furniture, Sze., and also to the walls of the building, and he asked the, Board to compensate him in some way.—The letter was referred to the Highway Committee.

• On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £11,699 12s 8d were passed for payment.
nut ALKALI WASTE.

The General Purposes Committee reported theappoint- ment of Mr. Walter Lowe as inspector of alkali waste de- posits at a salary of £2 per week and he had made a report. Fever hospital—Pauper cases: Letter, Ist March, 'from S. H. Hartley, stating that the Guardians are will- ing to pay 35 per day for pauper patients, and that "The Guardians define a pauper 'to be a person actually in receipt of relief in money at the time of removal to hos- pital." Instructions given to inquire whether the Guar- dians undertake to provide medical attendance in addi- tion to paving the 3s per day, also to Inggest the desira- bility of a conference with the deputation recently appointed by the Guardians to meet this Board respecting the admissioq of pauper cases to the hospital.—Mr. Carey, in mobing the adoption of these minutes, said the inspector's report was a satisfactory one, and the ap- pointment had done good. Dr. O'Keeffe seconded the motion, and the minute 3 were unanimously approved. •

RECEPTION AT WIDNES PUBLIC OFFICES. An important event in the municipal annals of the town took place in Widnes Public Offices on Thursday -evening. In his capacity as chairman of the Free Library Committee, Mr. H. Wade Deacon, of Appleton House, held a reception, or an "At Home: a social function which is a novelty to the people of Widnes. Although the town has not yet attained to the dignity of a municipal borough, it is yet qualified to . take a position amongst the proudest of them, both by the extent of its indus- tries, and the importance and wealth of its and the Town Hall in its unfinished stet? is from many. points of view well adapted for the social gatherings that are inseparable from the title of Mayor. This latter fact, no doubt, but princi- pally the laudable desire to draw together a portion of the population in pleasant intercourse, prompted Mr. Deacon to hold a reception, and which it is to be hoped that the success that the first • attained, will inspire a continuance. In issuing his invitations Mr. Deacon acted upon a fixed principle, and the guests included members and officials of public bodies, clergy, profes- sional men, and leading residents of the town, together with their wives. Guests commenced to arrive shortly after half-past seven, and for their convenience a covered way had had been erected from the carriage road to the entrance to the Putplic Offices. As the guests arrived they were announced and welcomed by Mr. and Miss Deacon in the ante-room on the upper floor, and they could then saunter through the suite of rooms and inspect the curiosities and works of art that were displayed for their enjoyment. The building needed little aid from the decorator's art to give the interior a most handsome appearance, and when the well-dressed company had assembled the scene was charming. On the walls of the Board-room were hung a number of beautiful paintings, lent by Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. Deacon, but the keenest interest was manifested in por- traits of the late Mr. William Gossage and the late 11r. Henry Deacon, who were pioneers of the trade of the town. In the large committee room were a number of powerful microscopes, through which numerous objects of interest could be viewed. Mr. V. C. Driffield had been instrumental in getting this collection together. In another room were engravings by Albert Darer, Earlon, Stockpoole, and others, and an original drawing by Bar- tolozzi. These were chiefly lent by Mr. Driffield. There '-ere also some valuable etchings and interesting an- cient and modern books. The following programme of music was gone through in the Board-room " Brightly dawns our wedding day" .(" Mikado"), Sullivan, Miss Lucie A. Jones, Miss Kate Meredith, Mr. Morrison, and Mr. Cantor; song," The heart bowed down" ("Bohemian Girl"), Bake, Mr. Heyes ; romance, "The harp in the air" (" Maritana"), Wallace, Miss Lucie A. Jones; humorous song, new sketch, "A journey by rail," West„ Mr. Josef Canter; trio, Zitti (` 6 Barber of Seville "), Rossini, Miss Lucie A. Jones. Mr. Morrison, and Mr. Cantor; "The prettylittle flower and the great oak tree" (" Rud- digore "), Sullivan, Miss Kate Meredith; humorous song, "Two spoons," Caldicott, Mr. Josef Cantor; quartette, "The fisherman's good night," Bishop, Miss Lucie A. Jones, Miss Kate Meredith, Mr Morrison, and Mr Cantor; solo violin, " Bourree," Beetzle.y. Mr. A. Thorpe ; song. "The lost chord," Sullivan, Mrs Lawton; recitation, "Yes or no," Loathed. Mr. Harry Cookson ; song, "Come into the garden Maud," Balfe, Mr. Morrison; humorous song, "Love unrequited," Sullivan, Mr. Frank Ather- ton; song, "Revenge," Hatton, Mr. Heyes ; duet, " Maying, Alice Smith, Mrs Lawton and W. Morrison. The company appeared to derive much pleasure from , the admirable singing of the various vocalists. From half-past eight to ten o'clock refreshment were provided in the surveyor's office upstairs, and in a convenient room on the ground floor. Mr. A. Parkes, of the Central Hotel catered for the refreshments. We have not spacefor the list of the invited guests, but may state that the majority of them were present.

PRESCOT BaD OF GUARDIANS. The monthly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whisten, on Thursday forenoon, when there. were present: Mr. J. Fisher (chairman), Rev. T. Chambers, Rev. Dean Fine- gan, Messrs. J. Lowe' J. Ranson, T. Musson, E. Syder, W. G. Ashton, R. A. Graves J. W. Wareing, T. F. Hill. ' R. Tyson, C. B. Johnson, W. Tyrer, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Burchall, J. Whalley, W. Swift, J. Buckley, and S. H. Hartley (Clerk.) GOVERNMENT CONTRIBUTIONS.—The Clerk read com- munications from the -Local Government Board stating that they had paid to the treasurer of theirinion the sum of £1,993 12s from the Parliamentary grant towards the cost of maintaining pauper lunatics: and £3l lOs from the grant in respect of additional fees paid to registrars of births and deaths; both for the year ended 29th Sep- tember last. • THE PARR VACANCY.—The Local Government Board wrote that they would shortly issue an order for the election of a Guardian for the township of Parr in the room of the late Mr. Jos. Jackson. AN EXTRAORDINARY COMMITNICATION.—The Clerk read la long letter dated "Leigh Villas, Lower Walton, near Warrington, February 28th," and signed "Sam. B. Stringer," stating that when he called at the house 78, Walmsley-street, Widnes, owned by him, and occupied by Thomas Rawlinson, he found that person had re- moved, and the house was occupied by a fever patient under the care of Mr. Treacey, relieving officer, who had written to him stating that the Relief Committee declined to acknowledge any liability in the matter, for rent or repairs. The letter concluded as follows,:—" The com- mittee must be very innocent gentlemen to think that in a land of law and order they can take possession of a house, furnish the same, put a person in charge, pay that person to do their work' keeping it as long as they like, and then: turn round to the owner of the house and say, We don't accept any responsibility for rent.' It is i simply ludicrous. The case throughout s a gross reflec- tion upon somebody. To think that we should have an infectious hospital within sight of the house in question, built and supported by the ratepayers, fully equipped; with, I believe, two nurses and a servant, and at the time in question not a sinle patient in, and, as soon as disease springs up, to find its doors locked and bolted, and over its portals, inscribed in red tape,' No admittance.' It is a scandal on the powers that be; rejeot it who maw.,—The Clerk said the Widnes Relief Committee had done perfectly right in repudiating any liability. As a matter of fact, the relieving officer did not take the house.—Mr. Hill moved, and Mr. Leatherbarrow seconded, that the action of the Widnes Relief Committee be confirmed.—The Rev. T. Chambers remarked that he did not think it right for any committee to take a house, fill it with sick patients, and ' pay no rent.—The Rev. Dean Finegan said they had not done that. There would be no difficulty in proving that they newer took the house. Fever hid broken out, in the house, and the owner wanted t 9 throw all ro3" ponsibitty on the Guardians and put it irk ft p 1•6154 tag dition.—The motion was then passed. Senoot Arrpauxce.—The Clerk submitted the esti- mate,of the probable sum required by the School Attend- ance Committee for the next three months, amounting to 03 ss. The estimate was approved. THE ATIDPI".—The Clerk reported that since the last meeting Mr. Haslehurst, the Government District Auditor, had audited the books and accounts of the Union, and found them all well kept and in a satisfactory condition. There were no surcharges on the Guardians and the auditor expressed himself eminently satisfied with th manner in which the Guardians looked after their relief work, and the manner in which the books were kept. div.p: FOOTBALL.

• • Secretaries e Football Clubs are requested to note that rep:rts of snatchee played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warringten, not later than ten • o'clock on Wednesday morning

RUGBY RULES. RUNCORN "A " TEAM V. ROCHDALE HORNETS "A " Tytm.—Played at Runcorn, on Saturday, before a large crowd. An unusual amount of interest was taken in this fixture, owing to the Hornets being looked upon as the champion, "A" team of Lancashire, and having a splendid record. The game was very even throughout, and was a good exposition of football. For. Runcorn S. Booth played a splendid full back game. Crompton was the hero of the day, and played grandly throughout. Both halves played well, passing and saving well. The forwards one and all showed up well. Bamford, Barton, and Sugden, for the Hornets, strove hard to avert de- feat. Shortly after the commencement of the game Crompton made a m tgnificent run through the thick of his opponents, and grounded the ball between the posts. Booth added the premier point. In the second half Crompton dropped a goal, and Bamford for Rochdale followed suit. A good game ended Runcorn 2 goals, 2 minors; Rochdali 1 goal, 1 minor. Teams :—Runcorn: Full back, S. Booth; three-quarter backs, Cookson, Crompton, and Lunt; half backs, Hollingsworth and Evans; forwards, Bowyer, Gatley, P. Riley, Cox, Raffe, Abrams, Ford, Whmyates, and Hampson. Rochdale: Full back, Thorpe; three- quarter backs, Tattersall, Bamford, and Hawksworth ; half backs, Barton and Pilling ; forwards, Rhodes, Par- kinson, Oldham, Forster, Ashworth, McHugh, Pilling, Sugden, and Haigh. RUNCORN V. ROCHDALE HoasYrs.—Some five thousand spectators lined the ground at Rochdale on Saturday, when the above teams met to pay off their return match. The ground, owing to the rain over night, was very slippery, making it rather bad for the back play. It was 3-15 when the following teams appeared :—Hornets Pennington, back; Hastings, Smith, and Whitehead, threequarter backs; Smith and Nuttall, half backs; Groves, Melladew, Wild, Griffiths, Scholes, Leech, Mutch, Holt, and Rev. Ormrod, forwards. Runcorn: Brazen- dale, back; Riley, Woods, and Cawley, threequarter backs; H. Hughes and Whitby, half backs; Hughes, Clarke, Faulkner, Wainwright, Hancock, Gayter, Dolan, Andrews, and Stubbs, forwards. Referee, Mr. Marshall, Bradford F.C. Hastings won the toss, and played with the wind. W. Hughes kicked off, when for offside rule infringement a scnmmage was ordered in centre' when Brazendale saved cleverly. Faulkner dropped out,when a forward rush was made by Hancock and Gayter, and Pennington saved the ball near the line. Quick pass- ing by Nuttall, Whitehead, and Hastings was checked by Riley, who confronted Hastings and fairly held him in check all the game through. Tall kicking by Brazendale and Pennington was put in, when the ball rolled in touch. Hostilities were confined to centre, and the for- wards had some very severe scrimmages. Groves drib- bled nicely, which Riley stopped, when Nuttall threw back to Whitehead, who took a drop at goal, which proved a near thing. Woods made his mark on the goal line, and dropped to Smith, who claimed a mark. W. Hughes returned well in touch. Consecutive runs were put in by Hastings and Cawley, when the ball got in the home quarter, where occurred some passing by Andrews, Hughes, and Faulkner, who almost got in, the movement, however, being baulked. Woods and Brazendale.both shot at goal, when Pennington touched down. Wainwright, Brazendale, and Pennington ex- changed kicks, and play raged in the home half until some passing among the Hornets backs brought the ball to the Runcorn end, when Brazendale touched down. • Play still continued fast, when H. Hughes relieved well by a screw kick in touch, half-time being announced soon after. Wild re-started the game, and kicked over the line, Brazendale saving. Some good play was put in by Faulkner, joined by Wainwright. The ball was taken down the ground, Smith saving. Later the ball was kicked towards Pennington, who failed to hold it. Wainwright, racing up, got the ball, and after a short sprint scored. No appeal whatever was made until the try was got; then, on an appeal to the referee, the Hornets got the verdict. Hughes, however, in view of an appeal to the Union, took the,kick at goal, -which failed. After this, play became fast. H. Hughes made a couple of strong efforts to score, but to call of time neither could get a winning point. The Runcorn backs played a eapital game, saving and collaring most fearlessly. Riley's collaring of Hastings was very safe, saving the game frequently. The forwards played well against their heavy opponents, following up and tack- ling the home backs repeatedly. Pennington and Hast- ings were in grand form for the Hornets, and Groves, Leech, Wild, and Scholes were very prominent for- ward. WARRINGTON V. OLDIXAM "A" Tsams.—The return

match between the above teams was played an the Wil- derspool ground on Saturday, a large number ol specta-; tors being present. It will be remembered that the Warrington "A " team suffered their first defeat of the season at Oldham, in December last, by one try; but the visitors paid the penalty on Saturday, Wamngton put- ting on thfil tall score of 1 goal, 3 tries, and 6 minor points to nothing. Two 25's being agreed upon, the home captain lucked off from the railway end of the field at 3-30, the ball going into touch. From the lineout Adam- son secured and put in a kick. Wrigley returning. Whittle threw to Evans, who ran strongly,and passed to Sanson. the latter kicking to the visitors' 25; but White- head, Chapman, and Gardner replied by a dribble to centre, the ball going into • touch. The visitors broke away from the lineout and invaded Warrington territory, but Evans relieved with a short run, Whittle passing to Antrobus, who got nicely away and transferred to Ap- pleton the latter player kicking, and McDonald mulling the ball, Bate and Adamson missed a good chance of scoring. Whittle passed to Evans, who put in a short kick over Wrigley's head, and following up had hard lines in not scoring, the ball going into touch-in-goal. Whitehead dropped out, but the ball had to be scrim- . . . . . .
maged on the N;iflitors' 25 line through off-side play. Lowe took the ball to centre, but a splendid screw kick .by

Sanson again located play in Close proximity to the visitors' goal line, the full back saving by kicking dead. Whiteheadkdropped out, Antrobus returning into touch. Whittle next put in a good run and passed to Sanson, • theilatter kicking to Cook, who was held by Chomley. ' The Warrington forwards dribbled to the line,but Clough saved by touching down. Whitehead again kicked eff, Evans running the ball back to centre. Whittle now threw nicely to Evans, and this player, going off at a swinging pace, dashed aside all opposition and grounded the ball over the line, Isherwood's kick at goal failing. Whitehead restarted from centre, play again resting near • the visitors' quarter flag. Whittle got away and passed to Sanson, who gave a long , punt, but Cook sent the leather into touch in midfield. The Oldhlrn forwards

now came away with a grand dribble, and appeated to 'be dangerous, Whittle saving hi the home 25. Donohue, Adamson, Dillon, and Lloyd worked the ball back to centre, but Lowe again returned with a kick into touch. Intrelsus next ran well, and passed to Appleton, this - player kicking to Clough, who was held by. Bate before he could return. Whittle was next to the front with a long run to thp visitors' full back, when he passed to Evans, but the latter failed to take the opportunity. Evans' kick being charged down, the home line was again placed in jeopardy, but Samson got the ball away with a splendid screw kick, and on call of half-time the score stood—Warrington 1 try and 2 Minors, to Oldham nothing. On change of ends the visiting captain re- started, Jolley returning with a gigantic punt, a scrim- mage being formed in the Oldham 25. Lowe and Cook • dribbled to centre, but Molyneaux, Donohue and Jones responded, and ;from a scrimmage, in the visitors' quar- ters Whittle gained possession and passed to Evans, who, • on being tackled, passed to Appleton, the latter player being pushed into touch on the line, a dead ball being scored soon afterwards from a kick by Sanson. Stott and Mellor now made a good dribble, hut Jolley replied by a tremendous punt, and Clough mulling, Dillon grounded the ball over the line, bu,t the point was dis- allowed. A scrimmage was formed near the line, from which Whittle secured and passed toEvans, who planted the ball over the line near the corner-flag, Isherwood failing at the place kick. Warrington continued to have the best of the game, and from a scrimmage in the Old- ham 25, Antrobus made a beautiful run in between the posts, Isherwood again failing to land the premier point. Whitehead restarted, the ball going into touch, and from the lineout the oval was sent to Evans, who, after scat- tering two or three of his opponents, put in a high punt, Clough returning to Samson. The latter player made a short run and kick and following 111), re-secured the ball and ran in behind the posts, Appleton this time kicking a goal. Antrobit9 returned the kick off, and Lowe was applauded for a run and kick into touch. The visitors pulled themselves together, and rushed the ball into the Warrington half, but Jolley got the leather away with a good kick, and Thornley dropping ODI Clough prevented that player from returning. Splendid passing on the part of the home backs continued; another dead ball be- ing registered from a kick by Sansou. On call of time the score stood—Warrington, 1 goal, 3 tries, and 6 minor points to Oldham nil. Teams :—Warrington: Fullback, Jolley: threequarter backs, Appleton, Evans, and San- ado: half backs, Whittle (captain), and Antrobus ; for- wards, Dillon, Molyneaux, Thornley, Isherwood, Jones, Lloyd, Bate, Adamson, and Donohue. Oldham: Full back, dough' threequarter backs, McDonald, Wrighley, and Buckley ;half backs, Lowe and Chadwick • for- wards, Whitehead (captaia), Giles, Chapman, Gardner, Mellor, Sixsmith, Stott, Buckley, and Cook. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM. In brilliant weather Warrington made the journey to Oldham on Saturday, to bring off the return fixture with the representatives Of the spindle town. The home club had mustered a strong team, having enlisted the services Moseley and Wood, of Wemeth, and Logan, of Rat!- Warrington were placed at considerable disad- >, being without Barnes, who, it is feared, will :gain this season. This player has never as- al in a match against Oldham away from 'urner was also away, but a substitute 1,. Barlow, of St. Paul's, who was at the last moment. Arriving at A was found to be in a wretched
not 0:-a sist,ed home.
was found' drafted into Clarksfield, th, • condition. At 3-30, before 37 motion. The kick-0 ,a few moments the ip
tators, Mills set the .ball in p ed in its careek, and for ilk a very loose character,

The Warringtonians carried the first scrimmage to the home quarter flag, and. Jolley supplemented their smart tactics by a huge kick to the Oldham line. Moseley tackled Massey with the leather in his possession, but the latter made amends shortly after, for a huge kick by him was well followed up by the visiting forwards, and Broadbent mulling the leather, Bandies took advantage and scored the first try for Warrington. From an easy place Speakman missed. Povey replied to the drop out with a neat dribble to, the Oldham 25, and Mosely mo- mentarily relieved. • Fair. Turner endeavoured to snake headway, but smart tactics by the home team found play in Warrington territory. Davies, however, assisted by Speakman, took the leather back, and Jellev gaining possession at half-way by a brilliant run crossed the line, but, unfortunately, failed to gain the 'verdict of the referee. This decision was severely commented on, and all good judges honestly admitted the try to be a fair and legitimate one. However, only a minor resulted, and, from Mills' drop-out, Speakman again placed Oldham on the defensive. Moseley put in some strong work, and, from some loose play which followed, Davies conceded a minor. The latter player dropped out, and a splendid combined dribble by Ashton,.. Littlewood, and Hayes looked like scoring, but the ground was sadly against them. A bad pass served as a relief to Oldham, but off- side play by the home team placed Warrington on the aggressive. From a pack at their opponents' quarter flag, Ashton and Littlewood dribbled to the line, and Ashton, when in the act of putting the finishing touch on this smart piece of work, had the ill-luck to have the leather kicked from under him. The game went merrily on, and although stnenuous efforts were made by Jolley, Turner, and Povey to add to the visitors' score, no addition was made up to the call of half-time, War- rihgton then leading by 1 try and 2 minors to Oldham 1 minor. Fair Turner re-started the second half, Holden returning to centre flag. Quick passing by Jolley and Turner gained ground, and thistsmart work was supple- mented by a good rush of the Warrington forwards, in which Littlevfood playel a prominent part. Oldham retaliated to mid-field, and a good run by Mosely ended in another minor being credited to the home team. The drop-out brought little relief, for the Oldham men seemed to be quite at home in the mud, whilst the Warring,to- nians were severely handicapped. Johnson put in some sterling work for the home team, and a good dribble by Lees transferred operations from the Oldham 25 to the Warrington 25. Speakman and Warren, the latter of Whom had gone to half back, shone individually with smart work, but a good dribble by Wood ended in Mills getting over. The place was in a favourable position, but the kick failed. The re-start from the quarter-flag fourtd Povey making tracks for the home team's line, and a pass from Mills to Johnson ended in thelatter punt- ing to Massey, who as promptly kicked back again, Bar- low and Bandies preventing Broadbent returning. Speak- man made his mark, but this availed his side little, for Johnson by a huge kick scored the third minor for Old- ham. From this point to the call of time, despite the efforts of each team, neither was able to add to the score, and Warrington had to be content with a draw, the score sheet reading—Oldham, 1 try 3 minors; War- rington, 1 try 2 minors. On behalf of Warrington Speakman was the best of the backs, whilst Nevins performed creditably. Massey had very little work, whilst Warren seemed out of place. Jolley plays a strong game at centre, but certainly ought to indulge in a little more passing. The ground told sadly against the forwards, but under the circumstances they played a good game, Povey deserves special men- tion, whilst Ashton, Turner, and Littlewood each played a determined game. On behalf of Oldham, Moseley, Wood, Broadbent, and Lees were the pick. . The following were the teams :—Warrington: Full back, W. Nevins; three-quarter backs, J. E. Warren, J. Jolley, and J. T. Massey; hhlf backs, T. Davies and W. Speakman; forwards, Fair. Turner, H. Ashton, W. Dil- lon, W. Hayes, W. Povey. W. Bandies, R. Littlewood, R. Eyes, and A. Barlow. Oldham: Full back, T. Broad- bent; three-quarter backs, P. Moseley, G. F. Logan, and W. Johnson; half backs, G. H. Holden and J. R. Mills; forwards, J. Armstrong, P. Ingham, W. Lees, G. Wood, H. Woolstencroft, A. Mayers, W. Hankinson, tcourt, and Blomley. WEST LANCASHIRE CUP. _ _

Winu,s y, FpniElirox,—Widnes journeyed to Pember- ton on Saturday to dedide their tie in the above competi- tion, and took with them about three hundred spectators. They had only a weak team, Kid& atid Parkinson—two of their best men—being unable to play. Moorfield, of ' the Pemberton, was also absent. The field is of a very awk- ward formation, and in many parts resembles nothing better than a miniature morass, which on Saturday was in a wretched condition. From the first the game waS stubloornly contested, Widnes eventually winning by one goal ind two minors to one minor. In the first half Widnes played against both wind and Slope, and scored a single minor, the same as their opponents, but they had by far the best of the game' and karrell had hard lines for a goal from a "place" by j. Bingham, the ball missirfg the posts by about a foot. With the advent of the second half the excitement was intense. Widnes attacked frequently, and Plamptcrn and S. Bingham essayed their luck for a dropped goal, but to no avail. Towards the close, when the game was still undecided, Barker, of Widnes, ran splendidly to the home line, where he was collared just outside. At last, about five minutes from the call of time, Wilkinson ob- tained a free kick near the touch-line, from which Plumpton endeavoured to place a goal. The kick, though a good one, failed, but the forwards dashed after the ball, and in the melee Harding secured a try in a good position, from which Farrell placed a goal, much to the chagrin of the Pembertonians, who expected to .make a drawn game. The play was of a rough and tumble character, the home team doing their utmost to keep the ball in the pack. The referee had to caution them for rough tackling. Teams: Widnes—S. Bingham, back; Plumpton, Farrell, and Harding, three-quarter backs; Wilkinson, and Barker. half-backs; Smith (cap- tain), Hardman, Hughes, J. Bingham, Woods, Barber, Gandy, Pennington, and Williams, forwards. Pember- ton—Clarkson, back; J. R. Calderbank, Clough, and Kay, three-quarter backs; Fairhurst and Adamson, half-backs; Sharrock (captain), Worthington, Wilde, Heaton, Freeman, Cheetham, Modrfield, Hilton, and Wright, forwards.
