div.head: WARRLNGTON FARMERS' CLUB.
div.p: WARRLNGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A meeting of the committee of this club was held at the Corn Exchange, Bewsey-street, on Wednes- day evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. Per- cival, and there were only about half a dozen mem- bers present.—The SECRET4RY (Mr. J. L. Stelfox) said that some action had been taken in regard to two 'of the resolutions recently passed by the club. In regard to the one dealing with the alleged adul- teration of American cheese, Mr. McLaren, M.P., had asked a question in the House of Commons, and had received a reply to the effect that the attention of the Government had been called to the matter, and that the Foreign Office had already been asked to obtain reports from the Consular offices in the United States as to the prevalence of the alleged adulteration. A question had also been asked in the House with regard to the frau- dulent sale of &ad meat, about which a circular had emanated from the club. That circular had done considerable good, and had set the pork- ieutchers in motion. Those in Manchester had al- ready formed an association to protect themselves from those butchers -who sold American pork -and hams as English.—During a discussion that followed the CHARMAN said he considered it a pity that the public should be • so gulled by the sale of foreign as English meat, and Mr. JOHN DARBY- SHIRE said he thought that the club had now gone far enough, and thatlt behoved the public to stand in their own defence.—..4. resolution was then passed thanking Mr. McLaren for the interest he took in agricultural matters, and for the assistance that he bad rendered to the farmers by putting questions to Parliament in their behalf.—The meeting then proceeded to discuss the desirability of making the law more stringent for the punishment of manure manufacturers and seedsmen who adulterate their articles to the injury of farmers and of the national wealth, and it was decided that it would be advis- able for the club to take action in the matter —This was all the business before the meeting.
At the Glamorganshire Assizes on Wednesday, David Davies, seaman, who some weeks ago cut his wife's throat at Swansea, causing her death, was acquitted on the ground of insanity.

div.head: F-I: V' UT 1,? THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1888.
div.p: F-I: V' UT 1,? THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1888.
THE "FAIR TRADE" FARCE.
BY H. WHITHeklf.

Numerous friends, ere I left Warrington, made a special point of requesting that I would give a little attgntiop to the question of Protection when I had go fladd in my new home. In fulfilment of my promise to do so I forward the following for their perusal. • _ . -

Thal I call the Fair Trade movemeni, a " farce " need surprise no one. Readers of the -T‘ Examiner " will remember that your correspondence column has, times out of number, heaped contempt on those who, for the merest party gain, would sacrifice their country's urgent and instant necessities on the altar of so shallow and hollow a device as the cry for Fair Trade. A cry i only it has been, for, as Lord Salis- bury said n his speech at Derby, "until the de- mands of those who ask for Fair Trade are embo- died in the clauses of a bill presented to Parlia- ment," we are all justified in doubting the honesty of all who put such propositions forward. True, it may bothat a feverish anxiety has possessed people of all classes, and even so desperate a remedy as Protection may have seemed to offer a remedy for the depressed state trade has been in since the six years of power held by Lord Beaconsfield; but responsible legislation should not be the outcome o! panic. As Lord Salisbury said, "Protection is ab- solutely out of the bounds of political possibility." Your neutral contemporary has, I hope, so far as Warrington is concerned, given it and Mr. Lawren- son their death blow. In the use of strong language, which must have been very unpalatable to the small and obscure exponent of Fair Trade princi- ples. your contemporary is not sparing. To have it said that "The great bulk of the 'tail' of Tory journalism, as distinguished from the brain centre, seized upon the Fair Trade' phantom simply be- cause it had a nice look, and an honest nanie ; the editorial cranium being a blank to the elementary princinles of political economy, to say nothing of the fiscal history of the country for forty odd years. 1 The' Fair Traders' were rudely awakened to a sense of their hopelesness and insignificance when they found themselves slighted by Lord Salisbury, and even deserted by Mr. Chaplin," is surely bad enough, but to be termed •' the noble band of itinerant gab- bless employed by the Fair Trade League, and the rag-tag and bob-tail of the provincial Conservative press' is surely enough to make Mr. Lawrenson throw down the pen in despair. The Fair Trade bubble having burst through the constant prickingof the Radical press. it by no means follows that the feverish anxiety to which I have referred is allayed, and it may be that agents, who protest too much, may, with a wonderful amount of self-abnegation, still act the Protection farce for the landlords' interest. To counteract this work, I will try to show what is done in this county, where I find the battle on this question is be- ing waged with a surprising amount of bitter- ness. .

Political parties in the States may be divided into two, the Democratic and the Republican. Each in its turn appeals to the working-class element, and each lays before its followers, through its selec- ted organ in the press, such arguments as appeal most forcibly to the wage-earner's pocket. The President's recent address, as touching Protection, has caused quite a flutter in the Republican or Tory , breast. It seems to augur, as indeed it does, the death knell of Restriction, and the speech delivered in the Senate by Senator. Frye exposed the hand of American political Protectionists. He declared, em- phatically, that" England had never in one single instance evinced any sympathy for this country'," and that she had "never permitted an opportunity to injure America to pass unimproved." He further declared that "the counsel, advice, and, friendship of Great Britain to any nation in commercial mat- tens, hati invariably resulted in injury to the nation which adopted it," The extracte I give prove be- yond question that the root of distrust of the Ameri- can towards the British nation is jealousy. Whem the English press quoted the address, the American Protectionist cried out that "his ears were deafened by their cries of ' Hear! hear !' and he set to work to disprove the transparent truth " that a duty is a tax paid by the'consumer." How ridiculous Protectionists make themselves is seen when the lumbermen come forward and ask for a dis- criminating duty of ± cent per pound on sugar in hogs- heads as against sugar in bags, so as to stop the growersl from buying pauper English bags." It happens that in this particular form of lumber, the country has more of the commodity of its own production than can be sold at a profit in home markets.. The lumbermen fail to see that a restristion of imports is a restriction of exports, and that trade is simply exchange of commodities. Con- gressman Miliken asked the pertinent question, "What right has Government to raise itsrevenue from the neces- sities of a poor man and the needs of his family, &less his wages are enhanced by as much as it takes from him through this method of taxation?" Just so; this is a plain way of putting it, and it may be further asked, how are the farmer's wages increased in purchasing power by his being made to buy dear an inferior cloth, lumber, or implements? The same may be asked of the carpenter, the mason, or the day labourer. I can assert from a careful study of the Government returns that skilled labour has ceased coming this way from England, and why is this? Simply because the English mechanic gets more in commodities for the same amount of his labour-product than the AmeriCan. I am proving that each time I spend a dollar. "In all coun- tries wages are lowest in protected industries. In the United States they are much lower to-day on the average than they were under the revenue tariff of 1860. There is probably not one 'protected' industry in the land but would to-day be employing doulsle or more than double the labour it actually employs had the non-obstructive tariff of 1860 remained unchanged. Could that tariff be restored to-morrow it is probable there is notione of those industries but would 12efore the end of Cleveland's second term employ double the labour it employs now, and on a far more favourable basis of remunera- tion."

Take the question of sugar from coal tar. Dr. Fahrberg was recently in London seeking to establtsh a factory for its manufacture. He says America is greatly ham- pered by the duty. If the duty were abolished, it could be used to make cheaper grades of sugar out of the whole glucose product of America, saving to the country many millions now paid abroad for cane and beetroot sugar. The original factories would have been built in America, if the tariff on raw tuaterials, coal tar, and sul- phuric acid had not been kept up by the chemists' ring." This is so, and a list of the industries killed and driven away by the rings and monopolies would beVartling to your readers. Lord Salisbury said he "did not know what fair trade meant," nor does any other man. There is but one way to solve the:problem—allow competition to work its own certain cure.; that will ultimately collie out of the half- developed ideas floating somewhere in the brains of the Socialists t For myself I have ceased to care very much which takes the stump, Free Trade or Protection. In either case the capitalist will receive the lion's share of the product of labour, and we shall still continue to exist after the same hand-to-mouth fashion as at present. The tariff discussion brings out at times humorous features, as when the Ways and Means Committee enacts the time-honoured farce of having the manufacturers be- fore them. Every delegation wanted a little more tariff. Your readers will be surprised to know that the rice growers of South Carolina wanted a raise on the broken rice used by brewers. I suppose this tickled Mr. Hewitt, for he asked each delegation whether it was their habit to pay higher wages when they got higher prices for their products, and whetherthey employed newly ar- rived Hungarian and Italian labourers when they had difficulties with their workmen. ' •

There are signs abundant that the Protectionists are gradually breaking up as a party. The pork butchers are against the salt boilers, and the New England iron manufacturers are disposed to throw over the Pensylva- nian coal producers, while the woollen manufacturers and growers are at open war. Of course the landlords come in here as at home, and they are "going for" thee edge wool manufacturers, some of whose articles are now protected by a duty of 200 per cent. So long as the re- form of tariff could be put off, the whole gang of tax- eaters seem to have hung pretty well together. Now they ate quarrelling over the division of the spoil. I could weary your readers, Mr. Editor, with detailed in- cidents 'connected with almost everything that enters into the life of this much protected country. It never seems to have been conceived that while the baby may need protection, in the adult it is a sign of weakness.

Here, as a consequence of Protection, smuggling from Mexico is no secret, and high priced articles such as silks and clothing are carried by tons across the Rio Grande and distributed through the United States. Attempts have for years been made to influence the British farmer, and persuade him to go in for Protec- tion. With the ordinary hard working farmer, nothing was easier than to lay the persuasive words "Fair Trade" before him. They carried conviction with them without any argument. Who could resist Fair Trade ? Put the phrase into actual shape, as Lord Salisbury sug- gests, and you have Protection as a result. The farmer has America pointed out to him as a place where corn can be grown and exported, and that the American farmer will ultimately ruin the British farmer. Well, there is a grain of truth in this, but this truth will only be found when the English farmer, like the Irish farmer, adopts the Plan of Campaign. What are the actual facts respecting the American far- mer? In Michigan, out of the 90,603 farms 43,079 are mortgaged for 60 per cent, of their value, and "the far- mers and delegates to the Nebraska Farmers' Alliance meeting have sent in a strongly worded petition to Con- gress asking for a removal of the duty on iron, lumber, sugar, wool, salt, and woollen goods. In the document, ; which Is indorsed by the National Farmers' Alliance and State Granges of Illinois, Indiana, and Pennsylvania, the husbandmen point out that the statistics of Illinois show

that from 1880 to 1888 eighty-seven of the richest agri- cultural districts of that State suffered an actual loss in population, and that 50,000,000d015. was lost on corn in the past live years, thus proving that the farmers worked without earning even a day's wages. Under the present system the petitioners urge that farms are being mortzaged, and the farmers are being reduced to the condition of the unhappy tenantry in Ireland. The ex- isting state of affairs, they claim, Is duo mainly to the protective tariff system now prevailing, vhich taxes the farmers of the nation for the aggrandizement of manu- fa.cturors on the plea of protecting American labour; whilst white labour is left free to come from all parts of the world In conclusion, the farmers allege ,that the agricultural products are sold in the open markets of the world in competition with the cheapest labour, whilst the manufacturers, throtigh the operation of the protec- tive tariff, receive a bonus of from 25 to 100 per cent, on the wares."

These statements may cause some of those who have hugged the Fair Trade farce to their heart to pause .in the hugging process. Men are asking here in very serious tones, "How is it, and why is it, that home competition has reduced wages, has also reduced manufacturers' profits, but has not reduced prices? Seven-tenths of the country being agriculturists, how is it that manufactured goods are supplied to them no lower, though the prices of their own products have shrunk from one-fiftit to one-third ? " At present, only the owners of timber lands are getting nch. Here, as in England, report says, iron manufacturers are not making extravagant profits, but the mine owners are. It is be- coming clear that the greatest part of the profits from Protection do not go to either the capital or the labour engageli in the converting of raw material, but to the owner of the raw material. _ _

Take the question of wool growing, and I can assure your readers that it is a most important one. Winters in the East are fearful. Where blizzards are, top coats should be plentiful; but seven, eight, and nine pounds for an overcoat put them out of the reach of the poor. The same high prices rule for blankets and women's under clothing, £8 being required for a good pair of blankets.

The wool growers of Mendocino have through their chairman issued a document in which they say "The tariff protects the manufacturer only, and provides him with legal weapons to oppress labour. 'Phe manufacturer knows just how much his employee can sustain life on by parsimonious economy, and you may increase his pro- tection until he is enabled to increase his profits tenfold, and the labourer will still be held down to wages just sufficient to maintain an existence." This is the whole philosophy of " protection to labour." It is to support such protection that the wage-slaves of Pennsylvania will be herded to the poll this fall by the masters who keep out the products of pauper labour and import the pauper labour itself. Theiarmers' eyes are opened at last, and the State Granges of Illinois, Indiana, and Pennsylvania are taking action, and cite the interesting fact that eighty-seven of ' the richest agricultural districts in Illinois suffered a loss in population between 1880 and 1888, and that in the last few years 50,000,000d015. had been lost on corn, showing that the farmers worked all that time without, earning even a day's wages. They called attention to the lact, undisputed except by a San Francisco school of econo- mists, that agricultural products were sold in the open markets of the world in competition with the cheapest foreign labour. To equalise, to some extent, the burdens of the different classes, they demanded the removal of the duties from iron, sugar, lumber, wool, salt, and woollen goods, and protested against the 'abolition of the taxes on whisky and tobacco. Men holding these opinions are not likely much longer to be content with the present state ot things. The duties on wqollen goods average about 70 per cent, and the "Philadelphia Record," in urging their repeal, says :—" With free wool the manufacturers in the United States ciuld compete with the manufacturers of the world in the quality and price of their woollen or worsted products. The home manufacturers could not only keep the home market to themselves, but they could cope with the manufacturers. of Great Britain and Continental Europe in their own markets., If wool should be admitted free' of duty, it would make little difference whether the tariff tax on woollen or worsted goods should be high or low; it would not pay to import such goods." I should like your readers to get hold of Dr. Wallace's ",Land Lessons from America," In this pamphlet they would see that the land question is looming up, and will soon ecome a burning one. In a further letter I may touih upoli it, Rita 0,180 give my apialQw) as to the kind of people who should come out, and dwell in "the gar- den of the Lord." On Protection I think I have said my last word to English readers, unless it may be in answer to questions. lam happy to say, sir, that We are all "first rate. Things are looking brighter. With an ahnostr tropical sun at mid-day, vegetation is springing up even on the desolate-looking mountains, and the climate seems to agree wonderfully with the children. I enclosed cutting from the "San Francisco Chronicle." It contains a re- markable verification of my statements respecting Mrs. Parker's ill-judged mission; and I hope you will find room for it. I receive your papers, arid even a "Neutral" is welcome from any old friend. Feb. 18th, 1888. 2,305, Taylor-street, San Francisco, ' Cal., U.S. • . _
[Extract.] SIXTY WOMEN rIIOM GREAT BRITAIN.HITNTING POSITIONS AN REAMERS AND LADIES' COMPANIONS.

Margeret E. Parker, of Penketh, Warrington, Eng- land, paid a visit to California a year ago, and, while here, became impressed with the need of a more general supply of working women for domestic service. This requirement, she thought, could be readily filled by drawing on the thousands of unemployed girls and i women n Great Britain, and from the many others who earn only a scanty pittance, and at the sametime a great service would be done to the toiling poor of her sex. On her return to England she therefore set to work•organiz- ing parties to come here for that purpose. Her material was chiefly sought in the field of the British Women's Temperance Association. Three of these parties were organized; and two of them, numbering about sixty, have arrived in this State.. Leaving the pars at Los Angeles they were taken under the protecting wings of the WomerN Home of that city. Their arrival had been eagerly awaited by the housewives ,of Southern Cali- fornia, some of whom had promised in advance wood wages to the new-corners and steady situations. "'You see," said a gentleman from Los Angeles to a " Chro- nicle " reporter yesterday afternoon, "our people have been paying the highest wages to servant girls. They are very scarce and they command from 25 to 45 dollars a month. So when these girls came on from England we thought that the problem of domestic service had been solved, and we hastened to avail ourselves of the assistance of the new arrivals. Judge of our astonish- ment wtfen we found on application to their agent that the would accept properly recommended posi- tions as companions, governesses, and readers for in- valids,' but were far above the degradation of menial service as domestics." "Well, are they getting employ- ment in their chosen occupations ?" asked the reporter. "No ; 'they have come to the wrong town. If our familieswere all composed of people of leisure and means they might do well enough, but imagine sixty lady's companions and governesses for a place like LosAngelcs. I offered one of the girls 35 dollars a month as maid-of- all-work, but she only smiled at the tempting proposition. I am told that a few have been employed for light work; that others have come on to San Francisco to seek em- ployment, while a few are very much disappointed with the result of the enterprise and will go East to find posi- tions or return to their native land."

div.head: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.
div.p: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.

Preaching at this church on Sunday evening, in aid of the funds of the Infirmary, the Rev, John Yonge referred to the generosity of the poor to the poor, and said that some of his hearers might recol- lect a picture representing a blind beggar at the door ot a fisherman's cottage 'on the east coast. The old salt was depicted sitting before his cottage door busily menyling his nets. There were traces and signs of his hard life and very humble lot, but he could not resist the appeal of the blind beggar, and so he was putting money into his grandchild's hand in order that she might give it. It was a simple picture of age answering to the appeal of helplessness, and teaching childhood to be kind and generous to such as could not help themselves. It was not much that the poor could give, but they would always give what they could. It was a great mistake to suppose that before a , man could afford to be generous he must become well-to- , do. There were multitudes of people in the world, and ' in the church, unluckily, who kept a clOse hold won I what they possessed, and Could get, because they thought I they could not afford to give any, of it away. They would I like people to believe that really in their souls I they were very generous, but in refusing help to needy Cases they were restrained by their pover- ty. He wanted to remind them that night, on the occa- sion of a charitable collection, that nothing was ever lost by being sympathetic and generous. He wanted I also to urge the truth that sympathy that was not prac- tically allied to generosity was a very spurious kind of sympathy, and that the sympathy which found practi- cal expression in the way of giving, however small the gift, was alone worthy of the name. Sympathy meant help—unselfish and generous help. Many people com- plained of the many calls and claims which are connec- ted with religion and philanthropy, and, unfortunately, they heard of some people who simply refused these claims all-round, assuming that philanthropy belonged only to the rich, who had a superfluity. They needed to be well upon their guard against the spirit Of selfish- ness. It was inevitable that there should be many claims upon their generosity. Let them understand that what they possessed was not for their own selfish, exclusive use, but that it was a trust from God, to enable them to help their fellows. That night it was the suffering, the stricken by disease or disaster, who appealed for help, and he urged his hearers to make a generous response. •

THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
No. 9.—THE CANAL AT LATCHFORD.

It is probable that there are few places between Eastham and Manchester whose outward and visible appearances will be more completely changed by the Ship Cana l and its subsidiary works than the residential, or—may we say?—the fashionable parts of Latchford; and, although we last week traced the course of the canal throuji this district, it may, perhaps, help us to get a still clearer comprehension of all the changes if we consider them from another point ef view. As we cannot .bring the future to us, any more than Mahomet could bring the moun- tain to him, we may itdopt a device similar to that which found favour with the Arabian prophet, and, in mind at all events, coney ourselves to the future.

div.head: 'PROSPECTIVE_ RAMBLE.
div.p: A 'PROSPECTIVE_ RAMBLE.

Let us suppose, therefore, that on some fine July or August Sunday evening, some six or seven years hence, we, after having listened to an appropriate discourse by the pastor, come out of Christ Church into Wash-lane, and, with the intention of enjoying an hour's ramble, turn our faces southward, that 18 in the direction of the present level crossing. In going up the lane the first thing that will almost of necessity catch the eye will be a huge embankment running at right angles with the roadway, with, it may be. on the top of it a train passing from the direction of Warrington to Lymm, or, perhaps, from the latter place to Warrington. This will be a por- tion of the great embankment that is to be made from Warringt3n nearly to Thelwall, in order to carry the railway over the Ship Canal at a point near Cross-lane. We will pass through this em- bankment by an underbridge with a span of some- thing like twenty-five feet and a height of thirteen feet. Once through it and a few yards farther on, we shall be upon the site of the present level cross- ing of the railway that is to have its course altered. in foretelling what we will, see here it would per- haps be judicious to indulge in a little Sybilline in- definiteness. As to whether the old and disused rails will be there or not it would be hard to say. but it is more than probable that they will have disappered, and perhaps with them pretty nearly all indications which would show that trains had ever run over the spot with the frequency that they now do. This at all events seems a reasonable in- ference, seeing that, in these commercial days, the rails might at least be disposed of as old metal, and the land on which they lie, if divested of its infer- tile covering, turned to profitable uses. Leaving, however, these conjectural problems to be solved by the course of events, and, going on a few more yards, we should, were things then as they are now, have a choice of three ways—one to the right, another to the left and the third straight ahead. But then will not be as now, as we have already seen, and the road to the left—along Common-lane—would simply bring us in a very short time to the northern bank of the Ship Canal, and, as there would be no provision in the shape of a bridge by which we might pass, wt would of necessity have to retrace our steps. A walk to the right—alongside the Baptist Chapel—if we wished to go through the fields would end in the same fashion, the barrier, in the way again being , the waters of the canal. As a matter of fact, then, there would be little choice but to go straight ahead up Ackers-lane, and even in this road we should go only about two hundred yathe before we come upon the 'ubiquitous canal, but in this case, should no vessel be passing at the moment, a swine bridge will span the canal and, across this we should pass. NO SHIP TO BE SEEN.

It may haps be imagined by some people that if Latchford be dised eAddivid 1w a momtfg embankment,there will at all events lid Soinewhat of a compensation in a frequent view of what is .„al- ways an interesting and pleasing sight to a lands- man—a fine ocean-going vessel fresh from success- ful struggles with Atlantic storms gliding past them almost within arm's length. But those who en- courage anticipations of this sort will be disap- pointed, 80 far as Latchford is concerned at any rate, for, through the whole length of this locality up to Latchford Locks, vessels will be hidden from view in a deep cutting, to all but those who stand on the very verge of.the canal. All tbat will be seen by those who are more than a few yards away will probably be the floating pennons and iihe upper parts, of the masts. The "jolly tar" who wishes to perceive the beauties and outward characteristics of Latchford, or to exchange greetings with some ad- jacent "land lubber," will need, like Shakespeare's ship-boy, to climb the "high and giddy mast." As for the passenger, he will, for this particular part of his voyage, have to give up the pursuit of land- scapes, and betake himself to geological studies, for which his surroundings will be more or less favour- able.

div.head: DEPTH OF CUTTINGS.
div.p: THE DEPTH OF CUTTINGS.

_ At Ackers-lane, for instance, de swing bridge will be some thirty feet above the level of the canal waters. But before reaching Ackers-lane an inward bound vessel will have passed some even deeper cuttings. On the Chester-road, between Wilders7 pool and Lower Walton, and near to Tom Paine's bridge, the waters will be twenty-five feet below the level of the road, but between Tom Paine's Bridge, and Twenty-step Bridge at Stockton Heath, the new waterway will pierce sokne high- lying ground—the site of the station from which in Roman times Agricola's legionaries dominated the neighbouring regions—and at this point the waters will be no less than forty feet below the adjacent land. So low indeed will be the level of the new canal that its surface will be four or five feet lower than the bottomiof the present Runcorn and Latchford canal. A person passing over the Stretton and Warrington-road at Stockton Heath will notice the canal twenty-six feet beneath him. To the east of Stockton Heath the level of the ground declines somewhat, so that the waters get to be at about twenty-feet below it, but further on it again rises, and at Acker's-lane it is, as already stated, about thjrty feet above the canal. ALONG THE NEW ROAD.

Having crossed the swing bride--Eil-A.cker's-lane, let us turn to the left along the new road, which will be made here. While going along this road we shall have the canal close to us on our left, while further away in the same direction there will still be seen the great embankment already alluded to, ever getting higher and higher towards the past, and indeed this will, by itsi very size, if for no other reason, be the dominant feature in the landscape of this locality. Keeping along the new road, whose foundations will be partly laid on what is nqw the field of the Latchford Cricket Club, we shall soon find ourselves in the upper part of Common-lane, which will lie to the south of the canal and to con- nect which with Acker's-lane the new road we have just traversed is to be made. At Common-lane the waters of the canal will still be thirty feet below the level of the ground. NEAR LATCHFORD STATION.

'lf we, continuing our ramble, wend our way up Common-lane into that portion! of Ackers'-lane which rune east and west peat the houses of Mr. Dun and Mr. Wallington, and thence turn down Grappenh all-lane in the direction of Latchford station, we shall again be forcibly reminded of the changes incident to the• making of the canal. 'lt will here be noticed that the house of Mr. S.' Gaskell still remains, but the pleasant gardens in front and between it and Latchford station have been swept away by the channW of the canal, in close proximity to which the house will stand. The canal here will still be thirty feet below the level of the roadway, which *ill be carried over with a swing bridge. It may te noted incidentally that none of the appara- tus for the manipulation of , the bridge is on the south side, for it is provided in the Canal Company'S Act, for the protection of Mr. Gaskell, that the company shall not place or ix on the southerly side of the canal any engines or machinery for opening and shutting the proposed swing bridge near the house of the said Samuel Gaskell.' ' It is also provided that no ivharf- constructed by the company on the, southerly , side of the canal, so far , as it abut% on any land of Mr. Gaskell, shall be used for the loading.or unloading of manure, nightsoil, or other offensive matter. .It is sti4l further laid down that tile company shall construct and evOr afterwards maintain between their works and the whole of Mr. Gaskell's ',laid between, Common-lane and Grappenhall-road, a good rubble stone wall of not less than four feet six inches in height as a boundary fence ; • and any towing path or road that may be made on the side of the canal is to be kept ten feet •at least below the natural level of the soil during its course through Mr. Gaskell's land. (To be Xontinued)

div.head: LEGAL DIFFICULTY.
div.p: A LEGAL DIFFICULTY.

Mr. Farwell moved, in the matter of "Yates v. Walker," on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Bekewick, in the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, on behalf of plaintiff, for an injunction to restrain the de- fendant, who is the contractor for the construction or the

Manchester Ship Canal, from trespassing upon certain lands at Ince, in the county of Chester, and from com- mitting any Acts of waste or damage thereon, either by himself or by his servants and agents.—His Lordship ob- served that, from the notice of motion he had before him and what the learned counsel had just said, the matter sounded like a question of title.—Mr. Farwell said there was no question of title concerned.—Mr. Bardiwell (with Mr. Moulton, Q.C.) stated that he ap- peared for the defendant. The trespass had ,begun on the 4th of March, and it was not until Friday morning that he had seen the willldavits that had been filed by the plaintiff in support a the motion. He must ask, there- fore, that the matter should stand over until next week, to enable his client to answer the affidavits.—After a short I argument, the motion was postponed, the defendant giv- ing an undertaking not to cut up the plaintiff's land in the meantime. ACCIDENT AT HOLLINS GREEN. Early on Saturday morning a serious accident hap- pened to a man named John Jackson, who was employed on the Ship Canal works at Hollins Green. He was en- gaged in removing some trucks and by some means or other fell underneath one of them, the wheels passing over both his legs. A spring, cart was obtained, and he was conveyed in it to the Warrington Infirmary, where, upon examination by the house surgeon, it was dis- covered that the left leg was completely smashed be- low the knee-joint, rendering amputation necessary, and that the right leg was also badly fractured. As Jack- son is a man well advanced in years, it is extremely doubtful whether he will recover. He now lies in a pre- carious state.

THE ROADS AND THE TRAFFIC. ,At a general meeting of the Warrington District High- way Board, held on Wednesday, Mr. Hartley asked if any of the roads in the Board's district had suffered in consequence of the increased traffic that had followed upon the construction of the. Manchester Ship Canal.— The Surveyor (Mr. Thompson) replied that the roads had not as yet 4 suffered any material damage; traffic had been heaviest at Holhns Green, but. up to the present it had done no damage there.—Mr. Royston said that he had seen three or four traction. engines about, and he thought that there was no doubt they would make good use of Manchester-road.—The Surveyor: They will soon have their own lines of rails all along the canal, so that they can bring their own goods.—The . subject then dropped.

THE SHIP CANAL AT EAUFIAII. Rushing along in a cloud of white; Shrieking and hissing, enough to fright; Making hideous both day and night, Near the Ship Canal at Eastham. Train of waggons round winding curves, Moving en masse vast heaps as it swerves, Souring the tempers and shaking the nerves Qf all the good people at Eastham. Navvies are there that, driven by steam,. , Tear out the earth with huge bucket and beam, Deposit in waggons, which then (with a scream From the engine) are borne off to Eastham. A small tipping engine is then in reqtiest,' Which, taking eaCh one on its iron-bound breast, Runs up to the tip and deposits to rest The earth on the foreshore at Eastham. Huts are now built where lately grew trees, Onoe beautiful grass is now mud to the knees, And hundreds of men are now busy as bees Marring the beauty of Eastham. Miles of sleepeis and rails are now seen • Skirting the estuary, over the green, . A navvy might call it a picturesque scene, But not so the people of Eastham. Its beautiful ferry now used as a dock, Its gardens for teas have received a rude shock ; • The monstre of Progress its quietude mocks— He is now reigning monarch at Eastham. , The Liverpool children and lovers will grieve For loss of their walks on long summer's eve ; The quiet repose 'neath its branches and leaves For a while hath depnrted from Eastham. No more shall the bluebell be sought in the glade, The primrose no more glads the heart of the maid; Whole woods have succumbed to the axe and the spade. 'Ahi theovvies.are working at Eastham t And soon where grew oaks the deep waters will flow, • Steamships and sailors, with life all aglow; The oldest inhabitant scarcely will know In a few months the place he called Eastham. March 14, 1888. 3. PEACH MORRIS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Ihnttd Was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. The Rqir. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Houghton, Blackhurst, Jolley, Heaton, Voisey, Bonnell, Derbyshire. Isherwood, Harrison, W. Houghton, Ratcliffe, Clarke, Hum- phries, BaMarry, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

THE LATE MR. =OWN, The CHAIRMAN said that before beginning the business of the meeting he should like to express his personal regret and sorrow to hear of the death of their vice- chairman, Mr. Brown.- He had heard since that the case had been aggravated by the furthet decease of Mrs. 'Brown, some two days after the funeral of Mr. Brown, and it must be very distressing-to the family to lose both parents, one so soon after the other. He heard that there were no young children, and that was a happy feature in the case. It wonld afford pleasure to every one of them to pass a resolution of sympathy with the family in their distress, and in doing so that Board would feel very much the loss of Mr. Brown. He was a man who had leisure at his disposal, and took a very great interest in the work he had undertaken in his dapacity as vice- chairmaff':of the Board. He had been not only vice- chairman of the Board, but also' chairman of the House Committee, and one or two other committees. The chairman then proposed a vote of condolence with the family under the distressing circumstances.—Mr. BLACIIHURST, in seconding the proposal, said he had known Mr. Brown almost as long as he knew any man in Warrington, and he had always found him a straight- forward and honourable man, and a man who was always ready to do the best he could for the poor people of the Union.—Mr. jolley. Mi. Harrison, Mr. Ratcliffe, and Mr. Darbyshire also supported the proposal, which was agreed to unanimously.—ln the course pf the discus- sion, the CHAIRMAN incidentally mentioned that it was 28 years since Mr. Brown was first elected a member of the Board, though there had been one break in his period of service.

'FHB BOUNDARIES QUESTION. The CLERK said the Honourable Mr. Pelham would attend at the Town Hall, Warrington, on the 9th April, with regard to the question of the boundaries of Lanca- shire and Cheshire,. He remarked that this matter of boundaries was of the greatest importance as it affected the rateable value of the extra municipal tortion, if, not the municipal portion of Warrington' geeing that it was a question whether the townships of Latchford; Thelwall, and Grappenhall were to go to -the- credit of another Union or to still remain with that Union. It was essen- tial that they should consider What course they should take with regard to the meeting ,of the Commissioner, but by' the next meeting of the Board they would have the advantage' of the Local Government Bill being made public, as he noticed that Mr. Ritchie, the president of the Local Government Board had given notice that on Monday next he would apply for leave to intnaduce the bill to Parliament. His (the Clerk's) opinion tended very much in the direction that parochial or poor-law business would be left in tho hands of Boards of Guar- dians, and that the other buSiness at present transacted by Boards of Guardians would be transferred to County Committees.—/n answe to a question the CLERK paid he thought ,the meeting" at the Town Hall would be THE SHIP CANAL AND ACCIDENTS. The CHAIRMAN remarked that although we had recently had such severe weather he was glad to find that there were only 340 inmates itt the workhouse.— The CLERK said he was sorry to hear that the Warring- ton Infirmary was very full, and he was afraid they would be wanting to remove persons who became con- valescent from there to th 4 workhouse. It was a little hard that people wko came from outside the Union to the Infirmary should have to come to that workhouse:— Mr. Joiiny saiokthat the governors of the Infirmary had had a special metting on the previous day, and they had made provision for utilising wards which liad, hitherto, not been occupied, and he thought that would tide them over the summer. He felt sure that the efforts that were to be made at the Infirmary would meet all requir- 'ments, although, as large works were to begin near Warrington, they expected it would be very much used. —Ms. RATCLIFFE asked if the Ship Canal people sub- scribed to the Infirmary.—Mr. JOLLEY said they did not, but he had heard a gentleman say that Mr. Walk, the contractor, had very liberally subscribed double the amount he WKS asked for to an infirmary near a place where he had been carrying out wine work.—Mr. HEATON said he had reaton to believe that Mr. Walker would readily give a subscription to a hospital.

VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN. The CLERK read, a letter from Mr. Cooperoiaccination, officer, at Newton, with regard to the 13 cases of iiqn- vaccinated children referred to at the previous meeting of the Board. The letter stated that one-of the children.

had been vaccinated, in six cases fines of 5s each kaj been imposed, but the children had not yetbeen vaccior ted ; in three cases vaccination had been postponed fat time that had not yet expired; and in three cases it he• been neglected to get postponement certificates. these last three cases he did nyt think the children Wen fit to be vaccinated, but the parents had promised have them vaccinated when well.—Mr. HARRISON askeu what authority the officer had for saying the children were not fit.—The CLERK said he visited and knew the cases.—The CHAIRMAN thought theaccount was a "ve'i, one.—Mdr. Btacm the iunsr suggested that tand over tt see if the parents complied.—*" matter satisfactory stand r RATCLIFFE said it appeared from the Medical officer's re' port to the Newton Commissioners that they had not n single case of infectious disease in the township and ke. believed that in the last 20 years they had only had eiSt cases.—Mr. VOISEY said the report of Mr. Cooper vi,dt satisfactory as far as the 13 cases were concerned. 13_71 thought, however, that those who had been fined an",, had not complied should go again before the court. was, no doubt, a hard thing but if they persisted An' getting fined it could not be helped. The Guardians lte'; a duty to perform and they should not mince it in way. It was his opinion that vaccination could be vref, and thoroughly done and it was only a question of hol'' it could best be done. He thought that some obligation should be imposed on medical officers to satisfy the Board that it was done as it should be, and lie sugge.stet that those who were opposed to vaccination should dad; their efforts towards having such an obligation imposen' —Mr. CLARKE thought Mr. Voisey was under a mistake' Vaccination could not be enforced; it was merely / matter of money. A person who had plenty of morel could keep his children unvaccinated as long as he liked; Ao their Clerk said at the previous meeting it was ny'' the wish of the Local Government Board to make mar tyrs of any person. They sent a letter some time age, down to that Board and also to man; other Boards saying that they 'did not wien' when people really had conscientious objection/ to vaccination, to make martyrs of them. fl„e was sorry that his friend was so persistent in trying bring these people up again and again. He (Mr. Clarke/ knew that there were persons who would obey the law all other respects, but in this one they were determine not to obey it, and the Local Government did not wig] to make them.—Mr. HARRISON said that was news to h:ol3' —Mr. CLARKE said itwas stated at a previous meetal that he was no authority on that subject. He did 0 profess to be, but if they would allow him at some future time he would.bring the authority of other people to SI port every statement he had made.—ln reply to re"' Harrison, the CLERK said that Mr. Clarke was substao tially correct in what he had said .with \regard to tin Local Government Board. That subject had been _re peatedly before Parliament, and the tendency of all to, speeches had been in the direction Mr. Clarke name,' and the Local Government Board themselves issued ,1 letter of advice or instruction upon the subject to Boar' of Guardians. They said that the vaccination officer were not to proceed to a second prosecution without th express instruction of the Board of Guardians, and tbe. did not think it was a desirable thing to continue thee prosecutions one after another. The Board could if the: , liked continue to prosecute time after time, but the Lod Government Board did not advise it. In Warrington few years ago he had occasionally to appear before tb4 magistrates to press for convictions, but they did n persist, and he believed he was justified in say7ag tbs. objection to vaccination had wholly gone out in Wel drington. (Hear, hear.) He certainly believed that the Iliad now a very improved condition in Earlestown, an as long as this improvement was being evidenced it vd, better to be mild, and he believed the opposition wow gradually decrease.—Mr. CLARKE said that some till no. the House of Commofis decided against repeate penaltiel by a majority, while in the House of Lords thi were only kept up by a majority of one.—The Cx.se said he believed that under the new Local Governmel Bill vaccination would be left to the Sanitary Authoritl and it would be very much more satisfactory that tl Newton Commissioners should have to deal with till question. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN said they shon act according to the spirit of the law on that questid and the Local Government Board were very- Cl upon it, while the House of Commons and House ' Lords were very much divided as to repeated prosecution He thought that on the whole they had better let ti matter drop.—The matter then dropped. This was all the business of public interest.

At the Occasional Courthouse, Warrington, .°..° riles Marson and Joni' Tnesday, before Messrs. vT,‘ W a WWI Rylands, John Matthews, a traniT; 1141 -gar • stealing from the person of Annie Boyeic sth, a white shawl, the property of Elizabe, Elizabeth Mee stated that she was a domestic st At vant in the employ ot W. Airey, at Lowton. about four o'clock on Sunday afternoon,' March bt''' she was walking in Crow-lane,Newton, in cbmpatli, with a friend named Annie Boyer, with the shalt' rin her possession. She asked Boyer. to hold itaielliel she fastened her bonnet. They had then just passe: the prisoner, who was locking' into a field. He caille behind them and snatched the shawl from her friend's arm, after which he walked quickly awaPs She called to two young men who were in front 0' her to stop him, but as the wind was strong in the 00°. 1 site direction they did not hear. She called to the PriS(r ner that she would give him in charge when she saw constable, upon which he threw the shawl over the rah= into the chapel yard he was pas Sing, and swore that he would cut their throats. They ran away. she after' wards got the shawl, and, seeing P.C. Spencer the sane evening, learned that the prisoner was in custody II another charge.—Annie Boyer gave Corroborative °v!' ence.—P.C. Spencer stated that in consequence of a cony ljalroint made to him by Elizabeth Mee he went to Earle 1 town Poßce Station on the Monday morning in'questio°' where tlgo prisoner was in custody, and charged 103 with stealing the shawl, to which lie made no reply!, 1 Prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for OW' —He was then charged with having stolen a watch, value 10s 6d, from the person of Thomas Glover, at Nov ton, on Sunday, March 4th.—Thomas Glover said tiil! he was a wheelwright's apprentice, and lived with h.': parents in Earle-street, Earlestown. The watch waS property. He was walking in Crow-lane at about foile o'clock on Sunday afternoon, with another boy, wh the prisoner came up to them and said, "Will .you to' me the time, young gentlemen ?" On his taking the watch out of his pocket, prisoner snatched it out bf hand, breaking the chain, and'carrying part of it with him. He ran off across the fields. He (Glover) and hie companion called to some other lads who were a clistanc.e, , away, and they ran after him. Prisoner turned and sav 1 something to them, which sounded like a threat. The others caught him and made him go with them to the police station. He went quietly. On the way they me! P.C. Spencer, and gave him in charge.—Joseph Howarnr 19 years of age, said that he was a blacksmith's appren- flee, and lived with his parents in Crow-lane. On the: afternoon in question, about four o'clock, he was sitting With some companions on the bridge in Crow-lane. He heard Glover call, and saw the prisoner running across the fields towards Ashton. They ran after him, and sag' him crouch behind a hedge. They could not see what he was doing. He remained there for two or three ml' mites, and then ran off in the same direction as before. He and another boy went behind the hedge where the' prisoner had been, and found the soil had been disturbed near the foot of the hedge. They dug it up; and found the watch and a piece of the chain. The watch was the one now-on the table. He called out to his companions "I have found a watch." Prisoner was then about 1O yards away. He stopped, and came back to them, and said, "Get me locked up." They started off towards Newton, and met P..C. Spencer, and told him about it, giving him the watch.—P.C. Spencer said he was near Newton, on Sunday, about 4-30 in the afternoon, when he met the boys with the prisoner. He charged him with stealing the watch from Thomas Glover. The prisoner replied I had nothing to eatto-day, and I wanted some- thing."—Prisoner, who declined to answer the charge, was committed to the Quarter Sessions on this charge also.

The second volume is now published of English Writers, or what Prefessor Henry Morley modestly rule "In attempt towards a history of English jterature." The whole work.is to be completed in tour Volumes; and the publishers (Messrs. Cassell Co.) announce that Professor Morley "hopes to to-get volumes -three-and four ready for issue durings' the course of the present year. In the °lame before us we have the history Of our litera- ture placed on record from Ccedraon to the Con- quest; and and it need 'hardly be said to those , who have given any attention to the subjeet that the period is one which is fruitful in the development thelanguage, and especially of English verse. ;13001 II opens with an account of " Widsith," which known also as "The Traveller's Song," and is be- lieved to be one of theoldest poems in First English. .4,9 e second chapter deals with the Scop, the poet of 'lle generations Who lived before the Norman inva- t"3/1. The Seep was a singer and actor as well as ;Aker of verse ; for we learn that" he was thi best bse°l3 Who had the best invention, the best ear for andlhe best skill as an actor." Homer and Irgil were, of course, the great Scops of their day. resent day ballad makers who cannot do without a re- may point to the fad that the refrain was tharac- ieristic of the earliest forms of En,giiskverse ; it came in b7l before rhyme, which was not used until the most I been made of accent, alliteration, and assonance. " The Lament of Deer," we. have as refrain "That „waa got over,and so this may be,"a piece, of sound philo- '°l3bY in the way of consolation which puts to shame illolue of the maudlin laments of the nineteenth century. • orefessor Morley givesa translation of "The Sea-farer,"one the finest of our earliest alliterative poems. One verse as follows, and how modern it is in its recognition of the charm and 'mysterY of the sea! There is no man among us So proud in his mind, Nor so good in his gifts, Nor so gay in his youth, Nor so daring in deeds, Nor so dear to his lord, „ That his soul's never stirred' At the thought of sea-faring, • Or what his great Master Will do with him yet. He hears not the harp, Heeds not giving of rings, , Has to woman no will, ' Arid no hope in the world, Nor in ought there is else, But the -wash of the waves. He lives ever longing, Who looks to the sea. Other chapters in this valuable volume deal with First teachers of Christianity,"" Tp the death of Bede," ,` The mother Tongue," "Exeter Books," " Cynewulf," Alfred," "Monasticism," "The Northmen," &c. Pae volume includes an exhaustive bibliography and tite.a, and leaves the istudent longing for the next issoe. The Pictorial Scrap Book which is being issued bk. .„"`essrs. Cassell and Co. is a capital way of pleasing Children and of saving parents trouble. There are to be Will at 6d. each ; .and the volume, when complete, include rio less than 3,000 beautiful pictures.—Part ','Wo is to hand of "Milton's Paradise Lost," illustrated the Gustave Dore. It is edited with notes and a life by te late Rev. Dr. Vaughare It is hardly necessary to say at this edition is unique. Dore's drawings, like the text,often soar into the sublime. Jack's Yarn, or Perils hithe Padfic " is a capi- ""2 story for boys published by Messrs Griffith, Farren, and Co. It is a handsomely bound volume of 350 pages, and is froralhe pen of Mr. Robert Brown, A.B.' author ct!' " Spunyarn and Spendrifir &c. It is full of adven- ute ; the exciting incidents are throughout admirably el "e^sevibed, while the *titer's wide experience and techm- cal knowledge enable him to preserve at all times an air of reality. The book is one which the young will read With avidity and with profit. It should be added that Jack's yarn" is profusely illustrated by Mr. R. T. • rritchett ; mad that paper, type, and printing leave no- thing to be desired. carlyle's "History of the French Revolution" is now ,o,47ing brought within the reach of the masses. Messrs. ' 4.01'd, Lock, and Co. have just issued a shilling edition of Vs extraordinary work of an extraordipary man. When "la stated that there are over 600 pages of letter-press, 1 will be seen that the book is in every respect a won- derful one for tile money.—Part 40 of Ward and Lo.l's Technical Journal and Industrial Self-instructor has fcr • frontispiece a series of charming little chromes illustra- tive of form and colour aa applied to dec varlve design. The illustrated articles include instractions for the car- penter, and the ornamental draught ;man ; and there are • besides, papers for the machinist, Vie bricklayer, the iron-worker, the market gardener, ko. Part 17 of the History of Lancashire, • which is edited by Mr. James Creston, and pnblished by Mr. John Hey- woodq contains details of the'ecclesiastical history of the Hundred of Salford—Man-chest& Parish, with accounts ,o;)i the Free Grammar SchOoI„ the Hulme Trust, Chatham's y°sPital and Library, and other Manchester and Sal- charities. The part is rich in illustrations; includ- -1,4 portrait of the Rev. Henry Newcome, and view of eat Crumpsall (the reputed:- birthplace of Thigh Crumpsall flail, Clayton Hall..Chetham's Hos-

, and Library, and Manchester Royal Infirmary. o,fsr. T. B. Browne, of 163, Queen Victoria-street, Lon- O, E.O , has just issued a new edition, for 1888, of his aluabie " A vertisers' A. B. C.," one of the most per- and valuable guides of the kind in print. We notice, !I's,eng others, the following improvements hi the new °lame :—(1) several literary articles bearing specially Pon newspaper matters; (2) A greatly amgmerfted list 91 colonial and foreign papers; • (3) A series of complete Lsclices, fully classified, and extending to. n,early 300 Vas. The getting together of thd material for so ex- austive a work has necessarily been a. great task, and it suist be admitted that the editorial work has been ad- rairably performed. Messrs. C. Mitchell & Co. of London, the pioneers in he field of Press Guides, having first issued "The News- paper Press Directory" in the year 1846, have made sPecial efforts, in their issue for the present year, to eclipse all previous numbers. In an extensive supple- /pent, treating solely of Colonial and Indian mattera, 'sets and figures are given which cannot fail•to be of in- terest to the British trader. These, in turn, are sup- Plemented by maps showing our world-wide posses- sions and the various steamer routes by which they are reached. Needless to say that enterprising adver- tisers, seeking fresh outlets fpr their trade, cannot find a more reliable guide than Mitchell's well-known 'rectory. ____

LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY STATIONS. ' Sir,—For some time past I have heard various vague rumours abqut some change that is likely to take place with regard/to the position of the stations of the London and North-Western Railway Company in this town. There canbe no doubt whatever that the present sta- tions are as inconveniently out of the way and as utterly devoid of centrality as they possibly could be, and the site of the Bank Quay Station seems to have been specially selected with a view to getting as far out of town and as far away froth the travelling public as pos- sible. Latterly, railway companies have opened their eyes to the advantages of putting their stations in the midst.of the people and as centrally as possible. If the company are about to centralize their stations, allow me to make a suggestion to them through you, which would, I think, benefit themselves and also the town, and tend to the convenience of travellers. (1), Divert or rather continue the main line from the Bridge over the main line near the Horse and Jockey down the old Dallam-lane coal lines to Foundry-lane and Winwick- street,' and place a station there as near as possible to the present Central Station, so as to form a really grand central railway system right in the most central part of - the town. (2), From thence, strike across to a point on the main line somewhere between Froghall-lane Bridge and the present Bank Quay Station. In following the courses I have suggested the company need not go through much valuable property, and the improved posi- tion that such a central station as I have suggested would give them would be enormous.—Yours truly, A TRAVELLER.

THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION. Sir,—lf I might. venture an opinion, I should say that your anti-teetotal correspondent, who signs himself "Bellerophon." is—if he has any clearly-formed con- victions on any other subject than the virtues of liquor—a Nihilist or Anarchist in politics, and in private life something either much above or below the common run of men. The most" disgusting thing" he knows is the " meddling.with other people's concerns" of the teetotallers. Now, there is, as far as I know, only one school of politicians or thinkers on public matters which finds anything to disgust them in the" meddling with other people's concerns," and that is the Nihilists or Anarchists. Other sections have, or ought to have, an ideal which they wish to see realised, and the only way in which it can be realised is by " meddling with other people's concerns." "Bellerophon " will; I expect, ad- mit that in times past some good things have been done by legislation and law-making, yet I will defy him to mention a single instance in which that good has been done without" meddling with other people's concerns." Your correspondent agrees with the teetotallers in one - thing—he hates drunkenness. But why does he hate drunkenness ? Not because it is a good, but because it is art evil thing. In fact, he hates drunkenness just as he hates leprosy, cholera, and small-pox. It is, like these diseases, injurious to the community, and mostly fatal to those who suffer from it. But here comes in the difference between "Bellerophon" and those he cri- ticises. He hates drunkenness, and would proteet it; they hate it, and would, as far as possible, do away with it. For the same reason that he would protect drunken- ness, he would protect cholera and small-pox, for there is no way by which a community can be protected against any one of these diseases, except by " meddling it with other people's concerns." In the one case you have by compulsion to put in force sanitary restriction, and in the other you have, by the same means, to restrict the vending of liquor, the cause of the disease. Now, with regard to" Bellerophon's " code of private morals. He says he once asked a teetotaller if he had never tasted a glass of ale, and he said "Yes, but he dropt it because it became expensive"; and, wonder- ful to say, your correspondent finds something in this answer which excites his contempt. Yet what, in effect, did the teetotaller say ? Was it not this, that drinking was to him, with his income, an expensive habit, that he had no desire that in his old age he should live as a pauper on public charity, or a dependent on the precarious be- nevolence of relatives, or—which is still more humiliat- ing—the sponger or parasite of his former friends and • -,uals. Yet this is the sort of man which " Bellerophon " professes to hold in contempt, and, vte may assume, that the reverse sort of man--the man who, that he may enjoy a present indulgence, is quite willing to spend a future of shame and ignominy—is the one whom he admires.—Yours, &c.,
Warrington, March 15, 1888.
CADMUS.

WARRINGTON CO - OPERATIVE SOCIETY. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to say a few words re- specting this question of co-operation? lam a grocer, and I had thought of entering into the controversy to prove that the members of the stores gain nothing, so far as our trade at least is concerned. Your correspon- dent "A Member" has, however, saved me that trouble. Everything that I wanted to prove he has proved for me. He admits—as does another of your correspon- dents—a difference in price, and when he admits a dif- ference of 2d in the shilling, ho admits enough for my purpose. He—kind, good, obtuse man—fails to see that 2d in the shilling is 3s 4d in the £, or more than he re- ceives in dividend at the Stores. Rally, sir, he had better have refrained from quoting Carlyle. He should have remembered the proverb about playing with edged

Just a word or two as to his complaint about sugar. The Stores don't give any dividend on sugar, hnd yet the sugar they sell is very much inferior to what is sold by the grocers. He must think the grocers are awfully soft, to suppose they would oblige him with cheap sugar, when he gets his other goods at the stores. His simplicity is most engaging. And then to" judge of his dismay," you know. He surely doesn't suppose that grocers exist for the special convenience of members of the Stores—or is he only poking fun? As to the other articles he names, he is altogether in error in supposing that the grocer would refuse to sell them alone. They . are amongst the most profitable articles in the trade, and must yield the Stores an enormous profit at the prices ...-they sell them. In conclusion, I would ask why the Stores don't sell at -..the same prices as the leading shops? I understand that • co•eperation was started with the idea of its members getting the profits the tradesman got. According to the advicitssions of its members, they clout They only get tibacka portion of the extra prices tbey pay for their goods. Then, who gets the rest ? Masking you for your courtesy, and "A Member" for his entertaining letter, I am, sir, A GROCER.

Sir,---Being one of that much-abused class who appear to be the pet aversion of some of your correspondents viz., a 'tradesman or middleman, I have naturally taken an -interest in the correspondence about the Co-op- erative stores. Evidently, sir, the schoolmaster is abroad, for one of your correspondents quotes the late Lord Beaconsfield, and no less than three others quote Carlyle. I little thought the Chelsea sage was so popular in Warrington; and I as little expected to find such an -amount of erudition on the part of one who used to pat ronize a " tommy shop." How he could ever have man- 'aged his affairs with such a want of intelligence, being himself so intelligent, as to go to a " tommy shop," I can- not conceive. He says that he owed £3 10s, and he ap- pears to have a grudge against the "tommy shop" for being indebted to it. Whose fault was it, his or the shopkeeper's, that he was so indebted? But it generally is the case that those who inflict an injury on another are the last to forgive. They always assume a tone of injured intiocence. Surely "One Who Knows"does not mean to imply that tradesmen find it to their interest to incur bad debts. I

can assure him that nothing in my business causes me so much worry and anxiety as bad debts. I hate debt, as cordially as he does, and although I, as a tradesman, set my face dead against ,credit, yet I find it absolutely impossible in all cases to avoid it. And let me assure Mm that all the members of the stores are not as honest as he claims to be, for after running on an account with me, when some one or other in the family has been out of work or laid up with sickness, or a death has occurred in the family, I have kept them for weeks, and have ad- vanced money for funeral expenses, without a penny of interest, and they have then left me, but not as "One Who Knows" says he did, for they neglected settling their accounts first. It is also a fact that several mem- bers of the stores who were my personal friends, would, now mid again, give me an order out of good-fellowship, and, out of good-fellowship, I suppose, would allow it to remain in the books six and twelve months before

settling. Will "One Who Knows" give me credit for sincerity, when I tell him that I am so desirous of seeing the lot of the masses improved, of seem" them in possession of greater comforts, and of seeing the evils incident to their position ameliorated, that I would gladly welcome any measure calculated to bring about so desirable a result. Honestly, I don't object to co-operation, and I don't fear its competition, providing its competition is fair. People have a perfect right to buy where they like if they pay their way. What I object to is that its competition is not fair. It is not fair to tradesmen and it is not fair to its members. The whole secret of its success is the " divi," and this " divi" is notaderived from the legiti- mate profits of the business, but from extortionate prices. Notwithstanding the disclaimer of "One Who Knows,"l say emphatically that this is a fact ; and I say further that the quality of many of the articles sold at , the Stores is much inferior to what can be bought from respectabletradesmen at much less money. I have made a number of purchases there this week to test this, and I go so far as to say that, after allowing for the " divi," , purchasers are out of pocket. Will "One Who Knows" kindly explain what becomes of the legitimate profit after the " divi " is paid.? The 5 per cent, so much bragged about is only 5 per cent. per annum on deposits; and the members can get 2i per cent in the Savings Bank, so that really a man who has £lO in the stores only netts 5s per year more than he would in the bank. Will " One Who Knows "explain why, when made my purchases I got no " checks " for sugar, and such sugar! I defy him to get such poor sugar at 2d. per lb., at any large grocer's shop in the town. Lest" One Who ICncisfs " should forget, I will again ask him what becomes of the profits such as the tradesman makes after paying all expenses? It was to; save this that co-operation first started. It was this that was to be divided in the form of " divi," amongst the members,

after paying the expenses, but the" divi" they get is only the extra prices which they pay week by week as they make their purchases. Since "One Who Knows" appears to be so fond of Carlyle, I would commend the quotation he gives about fools to his further considera- tion,—l am, sir,
A TRADESMAN. "One Who Knows:" look over his figures again? They were quite wrong last week.

Sir,—l fully expected somebody would have to come to the rescue of "A Member," as he had cut such a sorry figure in defence of the Co-operative Society. He has not even attempted to deal with the facts I have given. If they are true, and he cannot deny that, why not admit it? If untrue, why not challenge their un- truthfulness? It will not be worth my while to discuss any further with him, as I have not the time nor the disposition to write for the sake of writing. I admit that there are men who are thrifty, prudent, and intelligent, who are in connection wiih the Stores, but there are hundreds equally so who are not members and in no way connec- ted with it. But it does not follow that even these thrifty and prudent ones may not be deceived. Ido not aspire to be a leader of men, neither am I a Daniel, and it is quite possible that amongst the 2,000 members there are some equal and superior to me. I am _quite sure "A Member" would consider himself to be much superior, but I think with all his knowledge he is in the estimation of some a great simpleton, and that he is. without doubt, being juggled, as he calls it, out of his money. This, I thought I had fully proved in,my last letter. I may say here that the members did not care ;or his advocacy, and have admitted that he gave no One Who Knows" finds fault with me for giving a list of prices, which effect the working-man very little. Let us see. Does not the working-man bake his own bread very largely? Does he not eat cheese? Do his chil- dren never have such a thing as treacle? Does not he use oatmeal? Does not his wife use articles such as mustard, pepper, starch, soda, &c.? I can purchase good cheese at 841 per lb. at any good shop in town, whereas the lowest price at the Stores is 8d per lb. Yes, I think the prices of these articles do effect the wokking-men not a little, but a good deal, and these are they • A Member" and "One Who Knows" takes such interest in. All the members are not of this class. There are those who use pastry flour and self-raising flour, and if not in such large quantities, the reason is not far to be found. Many of them tell the shopkeeper they can buy much cheaper than at the Stores. As to the interest of five per cent. per annum for all trading members, I think it paltry in the extreme, considering the prices they get. Let me tell "One Who Knows" something he does not know. Is he aware that the Stores are getting is per dozen profit on all the pastry flour they sell, or 81 per, cent.; on McDougall's ed per dozen, or equal to 30 per , cent; on oatmeal 8d per dozen, or equal t 0 30 per cent.; and giving 5 per cent. ! I should hope they could afford to pay such dividends after getting so much profit. Lean give a long list of articles besides the above. I say, without fear of contradiction, it is all a farce to be told that the Stores are such a benefit to the town. Let "One Who Knows" spend 10s in any good shop and I guarantee he will save 2s and get better value for his money. •Itis a new thing to be told if he did not spend his money at the Stores he might spend it on something.he could manage to do without. As to the hated credit he speaks about, how main' families in these bad times would have had to break up their homes, and part with all they had, if the shopkeeper had notaent I money free of interest and a few weeks' goods, believing when they got work, and times mended, they would pay for them? I know of many such cases, and I wonder how much money they would get and how many weeks' trust at the Stores? There are not a few members who forget to pay their shop account, and there are others,when they have cash, I will pass by the shop which helped them when they had none. It would have served them right if they were treated like a tradesman treated one of these considerdlte persons. An old lady went into a shop and inquired the price of Indian corn. Finding it cheaper than the Stores, she told him he might send her down a load. On asking if she intended paying for it, she answered " Ne." So he then told her she had better get it at the Stores, where she usually traded. I may tell "One Who Knows " that the Stores would be quite welcome to all those who spend a few shillings there, and a few elsewhere in order to avoid being put ' into the court as soon as ever their " tommy book" ac- counts were settled, as the tradBman viorla be only too glad to get rid of them. But should they leave ht b fore settling, and take all their money to the Stores. I think "One Who Knows" wotild be one of the first to take them to the County Court if they owed him any- thing. I was greatly amused with the manner in which the half-penny check was treated. Take notice; the half- penny checks are not considered to be worth the cost, either in money, time, or trouble, the judicious house- wife always arranging to keep her expenditure out of the half-pence. How thoughtful ! But, supposing a man has not such a wife, why, then the Society must reap the benefit at the expense-of the purchaser, which I think is too bad. If the members are satisfied with the above prices, Sze , well and good—but lam not.—l remain, sir, yours,
A' LOOKER ON.
PULPIT REFERENCES TO THE LATE • SIR RICHARD BROOKE.

In memory of the late Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., of Norton Priory, a muffled peal was rung on the bells of Runcorn Parish Church. on Sunday, and the services throughout the day, were suitable to the occasion. The vicar, -the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, preached in the morning, tlnd selected for his text the first and second verses of the second chapter of the first book of Timothy. Alluding to the death of Sir Richard Brooke, the vicar said that not only had he, naturally as it were by the position to which he had been born, held the first plate in that part of Cheshire, but he had by his kindly and gentle disposition endeared himself to allwho knew him sufficiently well to appreciate his character. Sir Richard would be very greatly missed by all who were brought into any close as- sociation with him, especially by the members of the Church of England in Runcorn. The position occupied by the late Sit Richard Broeke as lay rector of that widely stretching parish could never be looked at without showing its importaace, nor, had he or his predecessors ever forgotten the claune, of the parish upon them' as occupying that position. Wiry last autumn assistance was given to them by the late baronet in cleansing that church and only so recently as Ash Wednesday morning last Sir Richard, entirely unsolicited, had sent to him £lOO for the perfecting of St. Michael's Church, or for any other object failing that, that he (the vicar) thought might be best for the parish.. In losing Sir Richard Brooke their schools and their charities had lost one who, had helped them for very many years, and they could ill afford to lose a friend who gave so unselfishly where it was needed. At the conclusion of the service, the organist, Mr. J. Johnson, rendered the Dead March in "Saul." At Halton Parish Church, on Sunday morning, the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar, also referred to the sad event. He remarked that according to the baptistnal register, Sir Richard was baptised in their " chapelri " of Halton, on the Mich? of December, 1814, so that he would be at his death 73 years of age. His father died in his 81st year, in 1865, so that the late Sir Richard had been at Norton Priory some 22 or 23 years at the time of his death. As was said of his father in 1865, so now might it be truly said of the son in 1888. He took a kind and personal interest in the welfare of histenants and their families, and studied, by every means in his power, to increase their prosperity, and to add to their comfort. He was , always ready to dispense the hospitalities attached to his life, whether the parties wereof his own rank, or whether the recipients were of a poorer class. At the evening service Mr. Lockweod again made the late baronet the subject of his discourse, the text being 1 Chron. xxix. 28 And he died in a good old age, full of days, riches and honour, and Solomon, his son, reigned in his stead." • The preacher said that for a long time the parish had had the late baronet's kind in- terest and pecuniary help. As long as he was able there was a regular attendance at church to his credit—that was in the morning—and he was most regular in his at- tention to duty as regarded the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper. The fabric of the church, too, the organ choir, and services generally, each came in for a share of his in- terest. The schools were largely supported by him, and he dreaded the very idea of there ever beim, a School Board in the parish, or Board sChools', hence 'his being president, a trustee or manager, of the various establishments for public education. Speaking of the Dowager Lady Brooke Mr. Lockwood said her ladyship would be more missed in the parish than her departed husband, for ort account of old age, land a natural disposition to retirement, Sir Richard did ! not takejor some years past, a very active part in parish matters, although he was never behindhand in assisting with his purse. Her genuine sympathy with and help in all cases brought under her ladyship's notice would lead him (the rev, gentleman) to occupy too much time. ' The church and the day ache* would also, in many ways, experiencA a loss not easily made good, and espe- cially with so many excellent daughters, who had been always ready to co-operate with her ladyship in any work she took in hand. They would pray for her, that she might be sustained in her time of bereavement, and have as happy and as long a future as was'desirable. God bless her no/, and always.

Evidence was given that the prisoner admitted that he stabbed his wife, and said he told his father-in-law, who refused to let her live with him, that he would have her dead or alive.
