div.head: NEW GERMAN EMPEROR.
div.p: THE NEW GERMAN EMPEROR.

Frederick William Nicholas Charles of Hoben- zollern—till recently Crown Prince of Prussia, the, eldest son of the newly-deceased German Emperor —was born at the Nene Palais of Potsdam October 18th, 1831, and had, therefore, ftppzcoached the age of fifty-seven, when, in the prime of a strengthful manhood, he was attacked by a throat disease that has baffled the greatest surgical scientists of the age, of Germany dnd of our own country. He is ad- mired throughout the civilised worldfor his high per- sonal qualities, and in England he is familiar by his visits, the reputation of those deeds and character- istics which Englishmen most admire, and fpfpeci- ally because he was the husband of our own Princess Royal. In Germany itself his popularity is unbounded. To everyone he is "Unser Fritz"-- our own Fritz. Most Germans learn a trade, and " Fritz " was not made an exception by his duty- loving parent, who selected for his heir the trades of carpentering and bookbinding, which he learned o under professional teacherst. He studied at Bonn University after leaving the excellent tutor 0' his early years, Dr. Curtin, an able historian ol Greece.

COURTSHIP AND MARRIAGE During his student life (1850-1) the Prince several times visited England. In the latter year he visited this country to take part in the first International Exhibi- tion, which so largely occupied the interest of the Prince Consort and was to inaugurate the Millennium. It was then that his heart beat towards the Princess Royal. The Queen, writing the story in "The Leaves from a Jour- nal," writes under date 27th September, 1855:—" Our dear Victoria was this day engaged to Prince Frederick William of Prussia, who had been on a visit to us since the 14th. He had already spoken to us on the 20th of his wishes; but we were uncertain on aceetuAl'of her extreme youth, whether he should spPex to her himself, or wait till he came back again. However, we felt it better be should do so, and during our ride up Craig-na- ' Bau, this afternoon he picked a piece of white heather (the emblem of good luck), which ke gave to her ; and this enabled him to to make an allusion to his hopes and wishes as they rode down Glen Ginnoch, which led to this happy conclusion." Princess "Vicky,' as she was familiarly termed, was thenilittle more than fifteen years old; her lover was seven years older. The marriage was celebrated at the Chapel Royal, St. James's, on January 25, 1858, in the presence of kings and queens,.of many princes and dig- nitaries, and was preceded and folleired by truly Royal festivities. The heart of the young bride was heavy at parting with her mother and her home, and her tearful face did honour to the warmth of her affection. At Ber- lin the child-bride was received with enthusiasm and some jealousy. She yriust have felt the change from thp cOmparative easo 9nd lionniinto4 of cur own royal circle to the stiffness and restraint of the German Court. THE CHILDREN. The first child of the rnarrage, Prince Vrederick 'William, now Crcrvru Prince, was born On January 27, 1859. prince willianif, in. February, 1882, married the Princess Victoria of Sehleswig-Holstein-Augustenburg, born 1860, and is the fath6f of four boys, born shc- cessively 1882, 1883, 1884, and 1887. The other children of the late Crown Prince a.i.Nl the Princess are—the Princess Charlotte, married in I,':sbruary, 1878, to the Prince of Saxe-Meiningen ; Prince Henry, born 1862, and engaged to the Princess Irene, daughter of the late Princess Alice and the Grand Duke of Hesse; Princess Victoria, 1866; Princess Sophie Dorothee, 1570; Princess Margaret Beatrice, 1872. Prince Francis, born in 1864, died in 1866; Prince Waldemar. born 1868, died in 1869.

div.head: MILITARY EXPLOITS
div.p: MILITARY EXPLOITS

In 1858, Frederick William and his young wife lent their full influence to the accession to power of his father as Regent, succeeding his • incapacitated brother. They were on the side of constitutional rights, but mat- ters did not go well, and the young couple had political troubles which have not even yet been fully explained. The Prince therefore welcomed the campaign in Schles- wig-Holstein in 1864. In this little war the Prussians and Austrians were allies. Two years later they be- came foes. The question at issue was the rtmoval of Austria from the _German Confederation, in which she interfered only to avert reform. The struggle was brief but decisive. We here merely note that Fritt led an army 01125,000 men against the Austrians, and arriving time- 'ously on the field of Sadowa decided the fortunes of war. •

Fritz's services throughout the Franco-German war were most conspicuous. Burin," the four years of peace he had visited 'Palestine and Egypt on the occasion of the opening of the Suez Canal. Ills visit to Jerusalem and the holy places touched him deeply. The Franco- German war broke out in 1870. At the close of July the Crown Prince was on the Rhine frontier, in command of the Third German Army, about 200,000 men and 500 Funs. He won VVoerth, and then marched to take part in a still more famous engagement. At Versailles, which the l.rown Prince assisted to in- vest, he was in October created Field Marshal, an hon- our from which princes d the reigning house had hitherto been excluded. On- the 18th January, 1871, King William of Prussia was in the palace of the French kings at Versailles proclaimed German Emperor. On this occasion the Crown Prince of Prussia had conferred on him the title "Crown Prince of the German Empire," with the prefix of "Imperial Highness." On the triumphal entry into Berlin, after the conclusion of peace, his Imperial Highness received the Grand Cross of the Order of the Iron Cross.

div.head: HABITS AND CHARACTER..
div.p: HABITS AND CHARACTER..

When in November last the telegrams from San Remo startled and distressed Europe, the following estimate was made by a sympathetic and discriminating pen, which ventured the hope that he would survive the projected operation of tracheotomy :—The gallant • and gifted husband of our beloved Princess , Royal comes of an exceptionally vigorous stock. Like his father and grandfather before him, he is a man of great stature and powerful build, vast muscular force, and robust consti- tution. With the exception of a low fever which endan- gered his life some sixteen years and a half ago, at the time when the Prince of Wales was stricken down by typhoid, no malady of any real gravity.has afflicted the Heir-Apparent to the German and Prussian thrones from the days of his happy boyhood down to those of his honoured middle-age. He has led a temperate and healthful life, replete with active exercise, and singularly free from all the sensual indulgences which impair vita- lity and sap the recuperative forces of the human micro- cosm. It may, therefore,, be confidently hoped that he . will triumphantly surmount the delicate, but not peri- , lons, operation of tracheotomy, and will be spared to his family and fellow-countrymen for many years to come, in the full possession of his splendid physical and intel- lectual faculties. Seldom has a nobler or more inspirit- ' ing spectacle, indeed, been presented to the eyes of man- kind than that afforded by the, heroic patience and devout trust in Providence with which Frederick William Nicholas of Hohenzollern has borne his heavy burden of pains and privations. THE JUBILEE PROCESSION.

Few would -1.;;:e -4-x(7-tight—who saw the Crown Prince riding foremost amongst the escort of mounted princes on the day of the Queen's Jubilee that he was suffering from an incurable disease. His Ana form and command- ing presence excited general ad&iration as he sat in his white Prussian uniform on his splendid charger, a thorough soldier every inch. The Crown Princess sat with the Princess of 'Wales in the carriage with the Queen, who was delighted to have her eldest daughter so long with her. "How fond the Queen is of the Crown Princess," a gentleman observed who had been inside the Abbey. and who noticed that when the Queen saluted all her family circle after the thanksgiving service, she kissed the Princess twice.

The largest passenger steamer in the world was launched on the Clyde on Thursday. It has been built for the Inman and International Company, Liverpool, and was "christened" the City of New York by Lady Randolph Churchill. Accommodation is provided for 2,000 passengers. ROYAL Miaataor AT BOIJUNEMOITIM.—The marriage of Prince Oscar of Sweden and Mdlle. Munck was solem- nised at St. Stephen's Church, Bournemouth, on Thurs- day morning. The church was crowded. The party included the Queen of Sweden, the Crown Prince of Denmark, the Duchess of Albany, and the Princes Carl and Eugene of Sweden. The Swedish Ambassador represented King Oscar, and the bride was given away by Colonel Munck, her cousin. The; Swedish National Anthem was played at the opening, and Mendelsohn's " Wedding March " as the royal party were leaving the church. The wedding wag private. ,
THD SMALL-PDX EPIDEMIC: ALARM- ING OUTBREAK IN MANCHESTER.

It is satisfactory to see that local lodging-house keepers are being looked up. Several persons were brought inte court at Warrington, on Monday, and lined for overcrowding. There cannot be too much care exercised at the presgot moment when an epi- demic of small-pox is stalking through the land. At Manchester there are at least 100 cases of small-pox in hospital, and it is probable that ahother 100 cases are under private treatment. The authorities have sent out circulars urging the inhabitants to re-vac- cinate; but it is not generally known that the disease has obtained such a footing in the city. Two fresh cases of small-pox have been admitted into the Small-pox Hospital at Blackburn, making 33 in the borough and 30 in the Hospital. Two fresh cases of small-pox have also occurred at the Borough Hospital at Stockport. The accommoda- tion for such patients at that place is now nearly exhausted, and the authorities are,on the lookout for supplementary accommodation.

THE MANCIVSTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) THELWALL. Steady progress continues to be made with the work at Thelwall, and it is evident from the preparations that are being made near to Morris Brook farm and the offices and other erections that are being put up diet this is to be a sort of headquarters from which large operations will be directed. It may be mentioned that it is directly. to the west of where the offices are being built that Latchford lockswillbe made. As yet no steam navvy is at work in this neighbourhood, though one is apparently all but ready, and the various parts of others are on the ground. Lines of rails have been extensively laid down, ; and to the north of Thelwall village piles are being driven into the bed of the river to support a line of metals which will connect the works on both banks. MOORE. The wintry weather which has prevailed during this week has somewhat interfered with the progress of work on the Stocktou Heath section of the canal, nearly all the men being on short time. At Bob's Bridge the work seems to be carried on amid a bed of mud several inches deep. The German navvy continues to make headway and the embankment grows perceptibly larger week by week. At Moore meadows men are busy at work with the spade and barrow removing the loamy soil from the top and placing it on each side for future use.. ACTON GRANGE. At Acton Grange the steam navvy has made a cutting some 29 yards wide, 60 yards long, and 4 yards deep, and seems well adapted for the loose, sandy soil which lies on the top of the red sandstone. Beforelong another line of rails will be laid, and then the navvy Will be able to fill waggons on both sides and the work will proceed more rapidly. What was known as Bellhouse-lane has entirely disappeared, and a deep cutting now exists in its place. A person looking in the direction of Walton Arches may I form some idea of the width and shape,of the new canal, as there is a slopeemade on each side of the cutting some four or five yards deep, the cutting being about half a mile in length. At the bottom of the present cutting rock of a good quality has been come to, and will be found useful for the work of the canal or other purposes. On the land near the railway at Acton Grange are to be built houses for the workmen' smiths' and itters' shops, engine shed to accommodate half a dozen engines, offices, &c., and also a large store, near to Ball's Wharf, where already an immense quantity of material has arrived. The accommodation road under the railway arches, near Farm, is nearly complete.. This has been cut through hard rock, and blasting with powder has had to be resorted to to loosen the rock from its solid bed. This road is for ths purpose of bringing some mil- lions of tons of earth from the bed of the canal between the railway and Lower Walton. We understand that Sir G. Greenall does not consent to tipping in the vicin- ity of Morley Common, and the debris consequently will have to be taken a long distance down towards the Old Quay Canal and be disposed of on the low land there. LOWER WALTON. Some 50 or 60 men are already at work on the east side of the railway, and gradually making headway to- wards Lower Walton and as time goeion a larger num- ber will be set to work. LYMM. Of what was well known to Lymm people as "Mick- ley Bill," yery 111 Qiylneeil:ll; M right away as far as Thelwall men are 116* efigagg, .r?"4oYleg the ellrfef'e soil and making gullies, ready for the steani na,744§ commence work. At Thelwall side of the island a quay has been erected, on which is stationed a steam crane for landing the ballast trucks, timber, rails, and other. heavy materials, which are brought up the river on bar- ges: The railway is rapidly being laid on the Cheshire side of the canal. At present there are no locomotives or steam navvies on this section of the works. Work is provided here for a number of Lymm men, who are able to earn s, much better wage than at the fustiant trade, though the work can only be done by those who have a strong physique. Among those so employed are men who have been gardeners, farm labourers, &c, thus showing the scarcity of work in the neighbourhood. Among the joiners at work is also a cabinet maker, who, having worked for ..many years at that trade, and though a good workman being unable to find employment at his usual trade; he took " Hobson's choice,' by doing heavy joiner's work in the open air exposed to all sorts of Weather, in preference to starving. At a short distance from the line of works, near Statham Pools, a large wooden hut has been erected, by the enterprising land- lord, who has recently taken the Star Inn. Groceries of all kinds are here sold, and in a room adjoining- are several tables, arranged wjth rows of knives and forks, and plates, with ‘ot pot." and a variety of other dishes, ready for the navvies at knocking-off time. , _

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

The work of constructing the Ship Canal in the neigh- bourhood of Runcorn l's proceeding yerysteadil7, but the winterly weather whicllhas been experienced during the past week has had a teAdency to interfere with the pro- gress made. No fewer than six locomotives are running about incessantly during tile day, conveying the laden trucks from the scene of operations to the marsh, where the soil, &c., is being deposited. Three steam navvies are at work, and about' three tons of rubbish :are being removed per minute. In addition, a num- ber of water tanks have been erected for the purPose of supplying the engines with water, and pipes have been laid to the steam navvies. Steps are being taken to still further extend the supply.

WEST)N.. 'The workshops and offices for this section have been erected at Weston Point, and• are now occupied. The offices are particularly commodious and em ' nfortable and have been handsomely furnished. The workmen'shnts are also approaching completion. It is likely that operations on a large scale will soon be commenced at this spot, and vast quantities of wood and other material is being unshipped there each day by means of a power- ful steam crane. BARTON. _ .

A commencement has this week been made with the construction of the Barton section of the canal works. Upwards of 50 men started operations in the meadows at Salt Eye, Barton, on Monday, and since then the num- ber has been augmented. Three or four wooden joiners' workshops, &c., have been erected, and a machine for cutting timber has been fitted up, so that the erection of a number of huts by the contractor for the accommoda- dation of navvies will shortly be proceeded with. The navvies are engaged mak* the necessary excavations for the construction of a ballast line, and shortly it is ex- pected that one or more steam navvies will be got to work. Large quantities of railway rails, timber, bar- rows,,&c., arrived in the meadows named last week, and several boat loads of waggons arrived. The work in connection with the construction of the Salford section on the Manchester side of the Barton aqueduct has been much, retarded owing to the unfavourable weather. The contractor (Mr. Walker) has purchased the Iron Chapel on Patricroft Bridge, now being used by the United Methodist Free Church denonunation, which he proposes to have removed to Barton for the navvies to worship in. The denomination named contemplate the substitution of a stone chapel on the same site.

• A BREACH OF THE LAW. At Lymin Petty Sessions, yesterday, Mr. T. A. Walker, the contractor fbr theiShip Canal, was charged with 'hav- ing, on the 23rd February, unlawfully caused to be erected a steam engine within a distance of 25 yards of the highway, such engine not being within any house or building, or behind- auy fence, &c., so that it might not be a danger to horses and passengers. P.C. Dutton said that about ten o'clock on the morning of the day named he was on duty in the Warrington-road, Thelwall. near Morris Brook farm, when he saw a portable steam engine closp by the road without anything to hide it from view. He saw a gentleman going along in a horse and trap; the horse shied, and the gentleman had to call to the engineman to stop the engine, which he did, and the ,horse then went past. Witness asked the engine driver why it was that the engiOe had been erected so near to the road, and he replied that he did not know. The next clay witness saw a ganger, and he said that Mr. Walker had ordered the engine to be put up. He added that the engine was on the day afteF covered up. Mr. Watkins, solicitor, Manehester, who appeared on behalf of Mr. Walker, contractor, said that the engine had been put up by Mr. Walker's agents in ignorance pf the statutory requirements. Mr. Walker would, however, take care that such a thing did not occur again, as notice would be sent all through the route of the canal. A fine of lOs and costs was imposed. LORD EGERTON'S LAND.

The value of the land required for the Manchester Ship Canal at §alford belongmg to, Lord Egerton of Tat- ton has In ascertained by arbitration. Mr. Sohn Clutton, theumpire in the case, has awarded theamount due to Lord Egerton as compensation at £63,240.

At Warwick Assizes, on Tuesday, George Timms, 53, a labourer, ilvas indieted far the murder of his wife. The case was ordered to stand over until the next assizes, pending inquiries into the prisoner's state of mind.
ALLEGED CONCEALMENT' OF BIR,TIL

At an Occasional Court, held at Warrington, yes- terday, before Mr. Edward Greens 11, a girl named Mary Jane Whitby (20), a domestic servant, was charged with having, on the 20th of February, con- cealed the birth of a child of which she was the mother. Evidence was given to the effect that prisoner, who was employed as a domestic servant by Mrs Sarah Astbury, of Dutton, near Runcorn, I was repeatedly accused by her mistress of being pregnant, which she denied. On the morning of the 20th February, after an hour's absence from the house, prisoner returned trembling with cold, and, suspicion being aroused, a search was made, the re- sult being that a dead child, which had had a separ- ate existence from the niother, was found in a pan on a shelf in a shed adjoining the kitchen. Dr. ,Smith, of Weaverham, said that he was distinctly ,of , opinion that want of proper attention had caused the death of the child. Prisoner was com- mitted for trial,.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER,.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER,.

[FROM OUR OWN CORRBSPONDENT.I 17, Union Court. Old Broad-street, E.C. The chief subject of interest during the past few days has naturally been Mr. Goschen's conversion scheme and its bearing upon the market generally. When first Mr. Goschen brought forward his proposal it was received with coldness, if not with direct opposition, that boded ill for its future succe.s. Bankers and financiers would have nothing to do with it, and at one time it looked as if Mr. Goschen would have to abandon it. However, after various private interviews and discussions of the leading bankers, the opposition vanished, and henceforth Mr. Goschen's scheme was received, if not with enthu- siasm, without opposition. The secret of this marvel- lous change of front was due to the recognition by Mr. Goschen of the ner.essity of paying a commission. The marvellous part of the whole affair is Mr. Goschen, who has been a financier all his life and made his income out of commission, did not iecognisethis important factor at first. Having now done so, however, he has removed all discontent, and has only the helpless holders of con- sols to contead with, and if there is any opposition in this quarter it will verrsoon be overcome. The holders of console are certainly deserving of sym- pathy, for they have had at one blow their income re- duced by one-twelfth. This sympathy is all the more deserving of greater consideration than Mr. Goschen has Mown because it affects a class of people who can ill- afford 'such a reduction. The fact of Mr. Goschen's scheme has had a decided effect on the market. Consols, , after a small rise, have since relapsed on heavy sales by the holders who have rushed to obtain something better for their investment than consols will afford. ,Home Rails have been most affected,•and the rise in some of the leasing lines has been as Amuch as 4on the week. Ever,: first-class security shows a rise in value, the natural desire being to obtain such sound security as will enable investors in Government Funds to at least realize something better than 21 13er cent. In mining shares the gamble is still kept up in dia- monds, and De Beers is made the pawn on which so much as at present been quoted. 34 to 48i has been the rise in these shares during the past fortnight, and the statement that one of the leading financial houses was at the back of this speculation, is cortfirmed by the fact that at the settlement, which concluded on Thurs- day, nine-tenths of the names passed as purchasers of De Beers was that of the Rothschilds. This is evidence that, at any rate, Rothschild s are not "bears," and there is a possibility that the anticipated jump to 50 may yet be realised. At the same time, we can only advise our readers not to be tempted or dazzled by the false glam- our surroundlug speculation. Copper during the past week has been particularly steady. Rio Tintos are well maintained at a fraction over 19. The more dazzling market in diamonds has caused these shares to take a second place. That a fall in both these markets is inevitable there can be little doubt. In miscellaneous mining shares there has been some steady buying of Indian gold mines, and Mysore Gold shows arise of nearly 1 since attention was first called to them. In South African gold mines there has been little doing, and prices generally are flatter. In Industrial and Commercial Companies the market has been generally flat. Hotchkiss are down, as also are Spratt's Patent. Pavilions also have been sold, and are lower than a week ago. These shares should be sold withopt delay. •

The nomination for the Melton Mowbray division of Leicestershire was, on Friday, fixed for Wednesday next. •

Mr. J. C. Flynn, M.P., was on Friday released from Cork Gaol, having undergone a sentence of three weeks' imprisonment under the Crimes Act, for advocating the plan of campaign. He took refuge at the house of Mr. Joicey, M.P., nearby. 074,WRECK OF A BARQUE.-A Montrose correspondent says that the barque Letterewe, of Liverpool, from Hamburg for the Tyne (in ballast), drove ashore on Friday morning on BuddOn Rocks, four miles south of Montrose, and IS likely to become a total wreck. The crew were saved by rocket 'apparatus. . . _ _

BLOWN TO PIECES.—A man at Melyn Crythan Tinplate Works was working up some dynamite in his hands on Friday morninc, previous to blasting, when the whole lot exploded. 'l'he man was blown into the air, and fell into a pool 20 yards away, his limbs, head, and body falling in separate fragments. LIBERAL UNIONISTS AND TEE ARREARS BlLLS.—yester- day a meeting of Liberal Unionists, presided over by Lord Hartington, was held to constder the Arrears Bills to be introduced by Mr. Russell and Mr. Parnell. Mr. Russell explained his views, and urged the necessity of arrears being dealt with. , After a discussion which lasted nearly two hours, and .in which Mr. Chamberlain sup ported Mr. Russell's views, Lord Hartington said he would convey to the Government an intimation that if they simply contented themselves with opposing the bill. introduced by Mr. Parnell they would not have the sup- port of a large number of Liberal Unionists.

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE LATE EMPEROR.
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE LATE EMPEROR.

• The cold in Berlin on Friday morning was again in- tense. This did not deter the many thousands who gathered in Berlin from taking up positions in the streets along which the funeral cortege passed. The tolling of the church bells, announcing the commencement of the funeral obsequies of Emperor William, began throughout the city at a quarter-past eleven o'clock. At the entrance to the cathedral stood a colossal statue, draped in black, representing Christ pronouncing the Benediction. Every window along the Linden Avenue was full, and mourn- ing flags and black draperies were suspended from houses and at street upasings. The route of the pro- cessi9R pregentel an itnposmg_ aspect, entirely in keeping with the deep sormvf 0414 11.31r9rVIT? fclt, Iv' the Ipeople. BERLIN, FRIDAY EVENING. The removal of the re- mains of the late Emperor from the Cathedral to the Royal mausoleum at Charlottenburg took place this afternoon. The pageant was most solemn and impres- sive. The Emperor Frederick, Prince Bismarck, and Count Von Moltke were absent from the procession. The weather wag bitterly cold. BRITISH SIGNS OF MOURNING.

*On Friday about noon, in honour of the funeral of the late German Emperor, salutes of ninety guns were fired in all garrison towns in the Ilnited‘liingdom. In Lon- don minute guns were fired from some of the pieces in the tower, and flags on all official and many private buildings were hoisted half-mast high. The Mansion House, Buckingham Palace, and Marlborough House were very conspicuous in their sicms,of mourning, all blinds being down and the Royal 'elandard floating half-mast from roofs— Many Germans resident in London wore cornflower37.the favourite flower of the deceased mon- arch, and German merchants and shopkeepers Rut up black shutters on windows of their butness premiseS. A special funeral service was held in Westminster Abbey, at whiclrthe dean delivered an eloquent eulogy of the late Emperor. The congregation Netts very large, and included Mr. Muntiella, Earl and Countess Kilmarey, Mrs Gladstone; and many members of the House of Com- mons. A special service in menrory of the late Emperor was held in the private chapel at Windsor Castle, at which were present the Queen, Princes a Beatrice. Prin- cess Christian, Prince Henry of Batt,enberg, the Court, and, the Royal household. The choral part of the ser- vice was rendered by the choir of St. George's. Chapel, and the dean of Windsor preached the Sermon.

The House of Lords met at four o'clock. The Pharmacy Acts Amendment ,Bill was read a third time. The Railway and Canal Bill was read a third time,, after which the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. ' The House met at half-past three. ' QuesrloNs.-7Mr. SMITH, replying to Mr. F. Powell, said the question of issuing a Parliamentary report on technical education would be considered by the Royal Commissioners on Education next week .—Mr. W. replying to Mr. Bannerman, said the Government inten- ded ta adhere to the intentions already expressed with regard to the renewal of the goat and Wine Duties Bill. AN IMPROPERTROCEEDING.—Mr. H. FOWLER infOrmed the Speaker that he had received a post card from. an lion. member asking him how he intended to vote on the motion with regard to the alleged grievances of artificers in Woolwich Arsenal. ' He wished to know whether such a proceeding was proper.—The SeizAkmr said the pro- ceedingras contrary to the usages and traditions of the 'House.. NEW B/zs.—Colonel Sanderson brought in a billj for the better regulation of certain articles of linen manu- facture, woven upon handlooms. The bill was read a first time.—Mr. Macartney .brought in a bill to'aniend the law relating, to land held in pernetuity at variable rrts in Ireland. It was read a first time. WAYS AND MEANs.—The House went in Committee on Ways and Means. A vote' of £11,000,000 out of the Consolidated Fund was agreed to after ii short dis- cussion.

_ Tna CONVERSION DILL. —The CHANCELLOR Of the Ex- CHEQUER moved the second reading of the National Debt I Conversion Bill.—Sir C. Lewis opposed. He thought more time than a week should have been allowed to all those deeply interested in the scheme. He pointed out the hardships the bill occasioned to the poor, who would be deprived by it ,of alinost daily bread. He moved "that, having regard to' the great loss and injury sus- tained by a large number of persons who hold small amounts of stock interest on which is proposed to be reduced, and the small annual reduction in the burdens affected by the proposed conversion this House thinks it inexpedient to make the change proposed." Mr H FOWLER wanted to know why the bankers who were SO strong in support of a system of conversion which, when it was proposed by Mr. Childers, was denounced as unfair, unjust, and detestably bad.—Sir It. H. F,ow- LER thought the scheme of the Chancellor of the Exchequer a masterly one. Sir J. LUB- BOCK .said the creation of one large stock had the general approval of bankers.—Mr. TYSSEN AM- HERST and Mr. S. HOARE criticised the provisions of the bill—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said althoup there had been some adverse criticism the general basis of the measure was not assailed. He did not see why the country shouldlay three per cent for money when it could be borrowed at a lower rate. He explained some modifications he proposed to introduce in the bill.—The amendment was afterwards withdrawn, and the bill was read a second time. Tin OATHS BILL.—The Committee on the Oaths Bill was postponed from Tuesiay, the 27th March,iuntil the 10th April.—The sitting then suspended. The House resumed at nine o'clock.

the fact known to Lord Salisbury. In all that he did i Egypt he acted in his private and not public capacity', and he denied that he ever received a fee from the cc" Ithadive after he was appointed as Judge Advocate General.

A JOKE WHICH BROUGHT TEARS TO HIS EYES. - Three commercial travellers sat over their wine and cigars one day after dinner, in a comfortable inn in Devonshire. They were "jolly good fellows," knowing each other as Tom, Dick, and Harry. After comparing notes on the state of trade, etc., jokes and stories went around, till, at last, Tom and Dick began chaffing Harry on the shabby condition of his head.o.for his hair was fast falling out, and the sparse quantity he still retained was quite gray, and both de- clared he had dee,eived them concerning his age, for his scanty gray hairs proved that he had already "fallen into the sear— the yellow leaf.' Dick declared that he knew of a sure remedy. Harry innocently and anxiously inquired what it was. Dick told him: "Cut half a dozen red onions into thick slices; rub your head thoroughly with them, and—leaving the slices on your head—sit in the hot sun for three hovrs I" "Nonsense 1" Harry objected. "Well, if you don't choose to try it, go bald I" Harry secretly resolved to try it, and did. The next day his mischievous friends spied him sitting in the sun, in the stable yard, his head plastered with onions, his eyes full of their juice, and streaming with tears. The shout they set up :old Harry that he was sold, and but for Tom's interference Dick's head would have stood in need of a plaster. Dick apologised, and made amends by informing Harry of the admirable qualities of Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's ITair Re- storer, which never fails to restore the hair to its natural colour, prevents it from falling out, and gives it the luxuri- ance and silken glossiness of youth. It can be had at,..any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the world. It should always be kept on the toilet table for dressing the hair. It is delicate and agreeable,

• THE HEALTH OF WIDNES. Dr. Cooper, medical officer for the township of Widnes, has just submitted his annual report for the past year to the Local Government Board and Local Board. It states that the number of deaths registered in the township of Widnes. during this year was 697, and calculating on a population of 30,000 persons to the driddle sf 1887, this gives a death rate of 23.23 per thousanof The deaths from the seven principal zymotic diseases numbered 147, or 49 per thousand of population, and were as follows: —Scarlatina, 2; measles, 63; whooping cough, 2; diptheria, 2; diarrhoea and dysentry, 62; typhus fever, 1.; typhoid fever, 15; total, 147. The deaths of children under one year, including pre- mature births, numbered 202.,0r 6.73 per thousand, and of those between the ages of one and five years 178, or 5.93 per thousand. The hirths registered during the year numbered 112, or 384 per thousand of population. Twenty-four inquests were held daring the year. Two cases of smallpox occurred during the year; one in November did one in December. Neither of these .cases proved fatal. Every precaution possible under the circumstances was taken to prevent the spread of the disease. A severe epidemic of measles occurred during tbe months of May, June. and July. The fatal cases were chiefly among infants, and were very numer- ous, 53 children falling victims to measles and its complication during those months. There were eight cases of typhus fever during the year, happily only one proved fatal. Diarrhoea and dysentery were exceptionally fatal, particularly the lat- ,ter during the months of July, August, and Sep- tember. Scavenging has not been done safisfactorily, but the supply of water to the township continues pure and abundant.
